text:
科技股盘前再跌，大型药企逆势上涨

今天美股盘前又跌了，纳指100期货跌近2%，标普500期货跌约1%。昨天SpaceX和超微电脑的业绩带动了反弹，但Meta和Tesla公布财报后，市场对AI投入和回报的担心又回来了，油价上涨也增加了压力。

Meta三季度营收增长26%，但当季资本开支接近349亿美元，自由现金流已经是负21.2亿美元。公司还把全年资本开支下限提高到1,350亿美元，并计划设立无投票权的C类股，为未来融资等安排提供渠道。投资者担心接下来还要投入多少钱，以及这些投入需要多久才能带来足够的现金回报。

Tesla则把全年资本开支计划从超过250亿美元降到约200亿美元，盘前股价下跌接近5%。减少投入有助于保留现金，但也让市场重新评估AI和机器人业务的推进速度。昨天财报带来的乐观情绪，还不足以消除市场对后续增长和资金投入的担心。

与此同时沙特再次遭到胡塞武装袭击，Brent 原油涨到112美元附近。油价上涨会增加企业成本，也让通胀和后续利率更难下降。十年期美债收益率虽然因避险买盘回落到5.08%左右，但借钱扩建数据中心的成本仍然很高。

大型药企今天则逆势上涨。北京时间18点前后，礼来涨1.11%，强生涨0.86%，辉瑞和默沙东也小幅上涨。这更像是投资者继续转向收入相对稳定的公司。大型药企已有上市药品持续带来收入，慢病和肿瘤用药的需求也较少随经济波动。市场担心AI未来能赚多少钱时，这些现有收入和现金流更容易受到青睐。

而尚未盈利、还要靠融资推进研发的生物科技公司，对高利率和融资环境更敏感，生物科技ETF XBI盘前仍跌了1.31%。

text:
CoinDCX：旧钱包资金归集流程曾失效，相关运营损失由平台承担

CoinDCX 发布关于 TQKJQ 钱包链上活动的进一步说明称，2025 年 7 月安全事件后，相关受影响钱包地址已停用，但部分用户仍向旧地址充值。平台原有的定期资金归集流程曾在一段时间内失效，相关问题于今日上午被发现，并造成部分运营损失，由 CoinDCX 承担。

CoinDCX 表示，尽管部分用户向已停用地址充值，相关用户账户仍已获得相应入账。平台称，客户资产继续存放于独立冷钱包，当前活跃钱包及用户地址未受影响，平台交易业务正常运行。CoinDCX 同时提醒用户，仅通过官方 App 或网站核实最新充值地址，避免向已停用地址转账。

此前，链上侦探 ZachXBT 曾质疑存款地址 TQKJQ 在安全事件后仍被使用约 10 个月，约 1580 万美元用户存款去向不明。
author: ChainCatcher_
quoted_text:
CoinDCX 回应约 1600 万 USDT 异常转账，ZachXBT 质疑其解释

据 Salus 首席营销官 Darcy 监测，10 月 21 日晚，被标记为 CoinDCX 热钱包及充值地址的多个地址，向同一 TRON 地址转入约 1599 万 USDT 及 5783.81 枚 TRX。资金随后被拆分，部分流向币安、OKX 及 Gate 等交易所充值地址。

CoinDCX 回应称，相关地址创建于 2025 年 1 月，在同年 7 月遭入侵后已停止使用，近期交易与平台当前运营无关，用户资金安全、交易正常。该平台 2025 年 7 月曾遭遇约 4400 万美元攻击，当时称受影响的是自有运营资金，用户资产未受影响。

ZachXBT 随后质疑，充值地址 TQKJQ 在 2025 年 7 月事件后仍被一家流动性提供方使用约 10 个月，今年 4、5 月仍归集用户充值，并与平台当前公开热钱包存在资金往来。他据此质疑，平台未能交代约 1580 万美元用户存款的去向。

We have now seen drawdowns in 29 of the last 30 weeks.

For perspective, oil reserves in the SPR stood at 653.9 million barrels in 2020, or +131% above current levels.

Meanwhile, commercial crude oil stocks excluding the SPR dropped -3.1 million barrels last week, to 412.5 million barrels, the lowest reading since the end of July.

This is also ~3% below the 5-year average for this time of year.

America's oil stockpiles are at critically low levels.

text:
算力提供是摇钱树？普通人通过手机也可以参与

Biteye/XHunt的联创A姐 @Web3SisterA 在韩国区块链周现场采访过 Acurast创始人Alessandro De Carli @a_d_c_ ，Alessandro谈论了创立 Acurast这个项目的idea。

当全世界的科技巨头和政府都在寻找 AI 算力的时候，普通人的手机（包括旧手机），算力却属于闲置状态。以前 Crypto 流行 Play to Earn，Alessandro创立的 Acurast（$ACU）把这个思路变成 Idle to Earn：让闲置手机替你打工，甚至睡觉的时候也能获得奖励，真正实现「睡后收入」。

1️⃣手机闲置算力究竟有多少？

根据 QuestMobile 的数据，2025 年 12 月，中国移动互联网用户人均每天使用 App 约 8 小时。粗略估算，手机每天还有约 16 小时没有被主动使用。
Acurast 看到的就是这个巨大的增量市场：通过区块链与代币经济学（$ACU），把全球几十亿计的闲置手机算力连接起来，变成一个去中心化的移动算力网络。
这不仅降低了开发者和企业的算力成本，也让普通人的闲置设备第一次有了变现的可能。就像 Uber 不需要自己买车、Airbnb 不需要自己盖酒店一样，Acurast 正在用共享经济的思路重构算力基建。
Acurast官方披露已有超过 32 万部手机累计接入他们的算力网络。

2️⃣ 真的有企业给手机算力付费？

这个商业模式已经被Acurast跑通 ，包括 AI 数据服务商 Massive、Teneo 等超 75 家企业和项目，已经在 Acurast 网络上运行网页数据抓取、安全协助与自动化交易等任务。

3️⃣ 普通用户如何参与？

几乎人手都有旧手机，这让Acurast的参与门槛比传统矿机低得多。
目前主要有5种玩法：
1. 轻量挂机：Processor Lite 实测 0.3 - 0.6 ACU/天；适合普通玩家
不用刷机，也不用恢复出厂设置，在苹果App Store或安卓应用商店搜 Acurast Processor Lite 并下载（要求 Android 12+ 或 iPhone 6s 及以上），就可以跑起来。
你睡觉的时候就会自动贡献RAM、存储和算力来攒奖励。（安全起见，尽量拿备用机挂，别用存有加密资产的机器。）

2. 专用节点：Processor Core 实测 0.4 - 0.7 ACU/天；适合有闲置手机资源的专业玩家
要是抽屉里有彻底不用的旧安卓机，可以把手机恢复出厂设置并锁定Bootloader，装上 Processor Core 当全职节点跑。因为系统干净加上全天在线，这种模式的硬件基准评分通常更高，拿到的算力奖励和质押额度也更稳。

3. 算力质押与社区任务：Staked Compute & Cloud Rebellion
不想折腾手机的持币者，可以通过 Staked Compute 把手里的 $ACU 委托给算力节点，跟着分网络收益。另外，在 Acurast Hub 里做做日常在线、邀请好友等 Cloud Rebellion 社区任务，还能领 MIST积分。

4. 交易大赛：币安 Alpha
不想挂机的用户，也可以参与币安 Alpha 正在进行的 ACU 交易大赛。活动截至 10 月 23 日 21:00（UTC+8) ，按 ACU累计买入量排名，前 2000 名每人可分 556 枚 ACU。越早交易加成越高，卖出和跨链不计入。
*注意价格波动与磨损。

5. XHunt创作者活动：
擅长内容的用户，可以通过 @xhunt_ai 参与 Acurast 创作者活动，前 150 名符合规则的创作者瓜分 200K ACU 奖池。参与方式是生成专属邀请码并绑定身份卡。评分中内容维度占 60%，看内容质量、影响力、原创性和指导性，同步到币安广场还有加成；邀请贡献占 40%。也就是说，既能靠写内容拿分，也能靠拉新拿分。

4️⃣ $ACU代表着Compute Finance时代的到来

当闲置手机能够提供算力、开发者按需购买服务、贡献者获得相应回报，算力就有机会成为普通人也能参与的经济活动。Acurast 想探索的，正是用 $ACU 连接设备、需求与收益的 Compute Finance 模式。它的市场大小，取决于真实的付费需求和参与者扣除电费、设备损耗后后的持续回报。

text:
今天资本市场一片乌云，Anthropic 却准备冲击史上最大 IPO。

今天亚洲股市普跌，黄金回调，连加密也无法幸免。

偏偏这个时候， Anthropic 传出本周五公开提交 S-1 招股书，
最快 11 月上市。

市场之前甚至讨论高达 2 万亿美元估值。

来看看它的财务数据，上半年营收 163 亿美元，净亏损却高达 807 亿美元。
不过，720 亿美元是可转换债券公允价值有变动，是属于账面亏损，没有实际现金支出。

再来复习一下上周讲的债务收益率。

Anthropic 相关融资在 6 月 次级债收益率是 8.5 % ，
而 10 月另一笔融资却超过 10 % 。

虽然这和我们上次讨论的债券有一点不同，但核心逻辑一样。
风险越高，投资者要求越高的风险补偿。

股权市场还在讨论 2 万亿美元的估值的同时，债权投资者却已经开始要求提高回报。

在这个时候，市场还愿意为天价估值买单吗？
Anthropic 还可以复制 $SPCX 的上市成功吗？ 

我已经可以想象到时市场的流动性了。
本来市场就够枯了，再来一个天价 IPO 抽一抽，直接人没了。

之前我们团队坐下来与金明沟通，为何要做《黄金时代》？他是中国企业家投资人里唯一现役国家队世界冠军运动员——两次打破世界纪录，打破了33年开赛以来欧美对自由潜世界纪录的垄断；27岁完成包括阿里巴巴在内的10亿融资，特斯拉IPO华人长期持仓股东回报5900% —— 他每天工作时间14个小时，兼顾国家队比赛，我们甚至抓不到他的时间。
·
后来我们知道，因为这些年遇到一些朋友很困惑：不知道如何赚钱，如何把身体变好，是选择继续读书、还是出国、回国、抑或是该做什么。
·
于是有了想做一个帮助这些人去探寻答案的内容，带着他们的问题去找合适的人回答—— 哪怕要找的人是全球top1%的领袖、首富、运动员、科学家。
·
所以这一次哪怕是风口浪尖的人，金明继续把问题往深里推：
▪️孙宇晨如何把“三巨头”巴菲特的风控、马斯克的科技叙事、特朗普的传播能力，融合成自己的人生打法。

▪️最新启动的数据驱动的饮食、训练与体脂管理，对赌2027年10月9日前把体脂打到18%-，并公开承诺验收。
·
《黄金时代》金明对谈孙宇晨下半程，在上集投资仓位与市场判断的基础上，看活人如何进化。
对未来，我们不预设立场，只点亮启发。
·
这一次，我们也想把问题交给你。
·
工作、成长、财富、关系，或者其他你一直想不明白的事，我们会根据问题，去邀请这1%里最可能启发你的人。

quoted_text: You are correct on the holding. Richardson required the jury to unanimously agree on the specific underlying violations for a CCE conviction, treating each as a separate element rather than mere means. The knife-versus-gun example in the opinion illustrates the general distinction between elements (which require unanimity) and means (which do not). Whether alternatives under a different statute count as elements or means is a statute-specific question.

老马又拿到15MHz手机频谱，FCC还豁免了地面建塔要求，让这批频谱可以用于卫星服务。美国运营商得盯紧这个动作了。

这次批准的是从Tristar收购的3张牌照，频段1695–1710MHz，覆盖8个州、62个县，约占美国人口的4%。范围还不算大，但SpaceX正在一块一块买下提供手机通信服务需要的频谱。

卫星发得再多，没有对应地区能用的频谱，也不能随便给手机提供服务。现在牌照拿过来，建塔要求也为卫星服务作了调整，Starlink Mobile就又少了一道落地障碍。当然，获批到真正开通，中间还有部署和终端适配要做。

对用户来说，以后去偏远地区、开长途，少几次没信号，就已经有付费的理由。对运营商来说，开始可以把它当补盲服务合作；等卫星能承接更多通话和数据，套餐怎么卖、客户归谁、月费怎么分，就得重新谈了。

再接上两周前宣布的全国800MHz低频频谱收购，方向就清楚了：低频配合地面设施改善室内覆盖，卫星补上室外和偏远地区的信号盲区，最后接成一张网。 $SPCX

text:
.@a16z 把经营了多年的「Crypto」招牌摘掉了。

10 月 22 日，据报道，a16z 将旗舰加密基金更名为 a16z Frontier，同时，长期普通合伙人 @alive_ 也将离开，计划创办自己的公司。

这件事值得放在 a16z 的发展史里看。

2009 年，Marc Andreessen 和 Ben Horowitz 创立 a16z，从互联网软件起家，后来投资 Facebook、Airbnb、GitHub 等公司。2013 年起，它开始布局 Coinbase，并逐步把投资范围扩展到公链、DeFi、NFT 和链上基础设施。

加密业务也一路做大：2018 年首期基金 3.5 亿美元，2021 年第三期达到 22 亿美元，2022 年第四期更是募资 45 亿美元。到 2026 年第五期，又募集 22 亿美元，五期累计募资约 100 亿美元。

有意思的是，就在今年 5 月，a16z 还强调加密行业正在从「价格周期」转向「使用周期」，重点押注稳定币、链上金融、预测市场和资产代币化。如今更名，并不自动意味着它看空加密，更可能是想把投资边界扩展到更广泛的前沿技术。

从互联网到加密，再到 Frontier，a16z 一直在做同一件事：寻找下一代计算平台。变化的不是它对技术基础设施的兴趣，而是它认为机会可能出现在哪里。

当然，更名究竟意味着多大程度的策略调整，还要看后续基金的实际投资组合，而不只是名字。

quoted_text:
Project Closure Announcement

Despite our best efforts, we regret to announce that we are shutting down Zipcoin.
On October 15, we were impacted by the @UNCX_token  incident, during which a hacker drained 1.1% of the supply across the following Ethereum tokens: $pepecoin, $EDGEN, $ZC, $X, $LO0P, and $PAAL. The stolen tokens were subsequently sold on the open market. We chose to remain quiet and purchase tokens on the open market to make up for the lost future team commitments.

Shortly after lunchtime yesterday, we were alerted by @Railway that our entire codebase had been compromised. This included all secrets and private keys associated with the project. This means the attacker has access to the keys controlling project-related wallets and infrastructure, making it unsafe and unviable to continue operating. We have spent the past 12 hours trying to find a safe solution, including migrating or rotating credentials, but unfortunately, we have been unable to find a viable path forward.

We can still access the associated wallets, which hold 2.2% of the supply. We will provide all existing holders with a six-hour window to sell. At 12:00 EST, we intend to sell the remaining holdings and consolidate the funds from the associated wallets before the attacker can potentially drain them. We are deeply sorry that things have come to this. We understand the impact this will have on everyone who believed in Zipcoin's long-term potential. We genuinely believed we could build something meaningful that would contribute to the wider Ethereum ecosystem.

Unfortunately, we are only one of many teams affected. Please remain vigilant over the coming weeks.
Thank you to everyone who supported us throughout this journey. We are truly sorry that this is how it ends.

author: hosseeb
quoted_text:
The dominant narrative in AI is that superhuman AI hackers are going to be a security nightmare.

I now believe the opposite: everything gets more secure after superhuman LLM hackers, because the commoditization of intelligence favors defenders over attackers.  

Here's why:  

• Before LLMs, defense meant covering every idea that any attacker might come up with. Human minds are diverse and attackers are uncorrelated with each other, so attack ideas had high entropy. N attackers meant N independent darts thrown in idea-space. You could outspend all attackers combined, but if even one gets lucky with and thinks of something you didn't, it's gg. 

• AI collapses that entropy. Attackers and defenders alike now use the same models, which means their ideas are correlated. Even if they're using different models, models are more correlated with each other than humans are. 20 uncoordinated attackers are no longer 20 independent minds: they're running the same search 20 times, burning redundant compute, trying the same attack ideas. 

• So the game reduces to spend. If you assume entropy is literally 0, the defender only needs to spend as much as the best-funded attacker, not the sum of all attackers. IOTW, attackers used to sum, now they max.

• Example: say you have North Korea, Russia, and China all trying to hack you with LLMs, and they're each spending ~$100K of compute trying to attack you ($300K total), you only need to spend ~$200K to ensure nobody gets through. This is because they're not coordinating. In the previous model, they didn't need to coordinate because the entropy in their different attack ideas were large, and thus you'd need to match their collective budgets to stay secure.

This model is obviously a simplification, and it gets compounded by other techniques that favor defenders, like formal verification and better testing.  

But you can already see this playing out in crypto. Big, well-defended protocols have become more secure after superhuman AI has emerged (as I demonstrate in the QT). I believe this is the reason why. It's the same reason why AI slop in writing is so easy to spot, and I think it means the long-term cybersecurity equilibrium is actually a happy one.

This is Ethereum's next-generation consensus protocol, and the unlock to:
- Post-quantum consensus

author: drjasper_eth
quoted_text:
One step closer to 4-8x faster Ethereum finality!

It took some time and lots of tokens, but we now have a formally verified proposal for a decoupled consensus protocol in I* (a future Ethereum upgrade)! Not yet a full spec (up next), but it includes all the key consensus-relevant details to become one.

Since Ethereum aspires to be live without most of the stake online, the protocol involves many more components than a normal BFT protocol, and its correctness involves much more than standard safety and liveness. Those nuanced properties are now verified!

What's more, I came away convinced that all protocol design will involve AI-assisted Formal Verification in the future, both for correctness and iteration speed.

The work wasn't limited to just:

Design the protocol -> Formally verify it

Instead, the loop became more like:

Design -> Formal Model -> Find exactly what breaks and why -> Redesign it.

For a fairly complicated protocol like this one, I think having the Lean model be part of the design loop played a big role in accelerating the process.

A future with agents paired with formal models is a superpower for Ethereum development, because they can then use those models to find exactly where an argument breaks down, formalize counterexamples, test proposed fixes, iterate on the protocol.

Many details that would slip under the radar when asking agents (and indeed, humans) can now be specified exactly and checked by the Lean kernel. This then forces agents to be more precise and lets them make verifiable progress on their own. It's been incredible to see this play out, seeing agents find gaps and propose protocol changes to fix them.

In other words, autoresearch can speed up protocol design, formal verification is here to stay, and Ethereum Finality will get faster.

The big brands in VC have always been able to pull other firms, but this was limited in eras when there was more discipline about round size.

In a world where the appetite for capital appears uncapped, investors are even more likely to herd. 

Today, the average syndicate that includes one of the seven "megafunds" has roughly double the number of participants compared to rounds that do not — despite the larger funds also comitting much more capital to the rounds.
author: sacha
quoted_text:
Concentration grew through the latter-half of ZIRP, up until the ill-fated WeWork IPO — a high profile warning about the "growth at all costs" mentality. 

From 2019 to 2022, VC concentration fell as investors squeezed down into Seed, searching for a clean slate. New frontiers, and a reset on price inflation; although capital supply meant prices remained high. 

The market bifurcated in 2022, as smaller LPs suffered a liquidity crunch which larger LPs barely noticed. The market has quickly been dominated by scaled allocation, chasing easy narratives. 

As a result, 2023 to 2026 has seen successive ATHs in market concentration, as LP capital has crowded into megafunds and obvious growth opportunities.

SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

Frontier labs are advancing the capabilities in AI for biology but preventing the good guys (scientists, academia, non-profits, health agencies,...) to use, study and understand it with widespread but shallow guardrails that the bad guys are bypassing easily (blocked me to proofread this tweet for example 😅). 

This will automatically create massive assymetry and risks in the coming years, just like in cybersecurity, especially now that frontier labs are building wet labs (HF cybersecurity scenario for biology when?).

This is why we created Carbon-X, the best open-source DNA model by midtraining Qwen3-14B on 300B tokens of DNA, English and interleaved data.  We also used a hybrid tokenizer that tokenizes English with BPE and DNA with a 6-mer tokenizer.

As a result, Carbon-X outperforms all open language models we evaluated on five benchmarks of DNA understanding and generation. This is a 27-point improvement over Qwen3-14B, showing how much a  language model can gain from DNA training. It is also API frontier level at 1,800x less cost than GPT 6.1 Sol!

We hope Carbon-X helps researchers explore DNA in new ways. Releasing it openly means anyone can study its capabilities, limitations, and risks. Let's make the AI biology frontier open-source to make it safe and impactful for the whole world (not just a few companies).

quoted_text:
今天在Token2049会场已经开始传 pearl-2:native 是我做的项目了，要是真的那我真的做梦都可以笑醒了

简单写一下看多的理由：
1. BTC和AI在竞争算力和电力，越来越多的矿场转型算力中心，未来比特币的维护网络会越来越小

2. PRL搞的是POUW（有用工作量证明），大部分的算力是拿去跑AI的，少部分的算力会用来做挖矿 

3. 挖矿成本是不断的减少的（平滑的递减），POW机制会让成本越来越高，这就有了BTC叙事（或者说所有的POW币的叙事）

4. 来挖矿的部分（假设5%）所赚到的钱是高于成本的（比如能赚7%），所以各个算力中心一定有足够的激励来接入PRL网络

5. 大量算力中心接入PRL网络，这就变成了巨大的去中心化算力网络（这个叙事很多人讲过，但是没人真的做出来，找到一个好的协调机制是很困难的），这个巨大的去中心化算力网络又变成了ETH叙事

6. 未来协议收入会回购代币（还没出来），这又变成了Hype叙事

7. 当然我也知道更多的未披露信息，比如大家筹码结构、谁在买、什么机构已经在车上，成本多少；既然外面没公开我也就不写出来了

The Starknet community has voted in favor of researching @Starknet's transition to L1.
This is a good moment to make the case: why I'm bullish on Starknet?

In short: It's THE future-proofed programmable, secure, endgame chain  built for what comes next

Here's why:

• Crypto agility: Starknet has everything it needs to evolve and improve, be it for post-quantum security, better UX, scale, privacy, or any other desired trait. It has the right architecture to do this seamlessly, without breaking things or asking users and builders to go through an exhausting process. Starknet's community is part of this agility with its ability to approve and contribute to changes when needed (with the latest example: starting the research to become an L1).

• Quantum-resistant cryptography: ZK-STARKs were designed with post-quantum security in mind (it's actually in the title of the 2018 STARK paper), and they are the foundation for Starknet's stack. As for parts of the system that are not yet PQS, we will do the needed work to ensure all of Starknet is post-quantum secure.

• Privacy: aside from PQS, ZK-STARKs are desgined for privacy. STRK20 is the optimal privacy design for DeFi, creating a privacy layer that allows what I like to define as Usable privacy. If we want to enable privacy for all sorts of DeFi activities onchain, you need composability and easy UX. Starknet's STRK20 offers exactly that.

• UX: UX is made of many things -- speed, cost, finality, UI, privacy, security, and many other things -- Starknet is leading on all these fronts. It was designed specifically for better UX.

Everything that a programmable future-proofed chain needs is in this list.
Security? Privacy? Agility? UX? That's everything you need to bring DeFi to the next level and that's what Starknet is for.

Bullish!

text:
The best swap experience on @Stacks just got better

New on Zest Protocol Stacks Swap: large swaps no longer have to squeeze through one pool.

Zest Protocol Stacks Swap can split a big trade into multiple swaps that run side by side in one transaction.

Here's why that matters. An AMM pool prices every trade off its own reserves. The bigger your order, the further the price moves against you.

Split the order across two routes and each pool only takes part of it. Each price moves a shorter distance, so the combined output beats the best single route.

On every quote, the router checks hundreds of pools across @bitflow, @ALEXLabBTC and all other DEXes on Stacks. When no direct pool has the best price, a route automatically split the swap over multiple pools for best execution.

Zest swap only splits when it pays off after fees. Big trades are where splitting makes the biggest difference.

Users see the minimum received before signing, and if the trade can't hit it, the whole swap reverts.

Best execution on Stacks, with Zest Protocol Swap.

text:
I get more messages about this podcast every week than anything else I do.

We all want to look and sound smart in the investment committee or all hands meeting.

This is the only show in tech you have to listen to every week.

No egos, no politics, just tech.

AGENDA:

- Venture is Broken: Trillion or Bust
- Coreweave Sell-Off Creates Panic
- Town at $1B, Anduril at $90B: Are Revenue Multiples Out of Control?
- General Atlantic Eyes IPO
- Modal Raises $750M at $15.75B

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. Why Fundraising Is Back to Being a Numbers Game

Founders with top-decile numbers now have to meet 100 VCs, as in the old days. It will not be Benchmark, Index, Andreessen or Bessemer, but other growth investors will take the bet at a reasonable but still elevated valuation because it is the best deal they have seen that quarter.

2. Why the Big Funds Have to Have Billion-Dollar Positions to Make It Worthwhile?

A $5B plus fund needs $BN positions in everything. Without 51% ownership, which most founders will not accept, a $2B Listen Labs is not good enough, while 1% of Anthropic could still get there even with dilution.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @venkyganesan @DavidGeorge83

3. Why Are CoreWeave and Oracle B-Tier and What Does That Mean for Their Price Volatility?

With massive debt loads, CoreWeave and Oracle should be hypersensitive to any bump at Anthropic or OpenAI. CoreWeave exists because NVIDIA needs it for now, and Oracle rents out excess capacity because it cannot sell enough enterprise software.

4. Why the Best Markets for App Layer Companies Compete Directly With the Models

The fastest-growing AI apps, such as code generation, code review and legal, sit closest to the foundation models. That brings a moment of terror every six months, but it is also why companies like CodeRabbit are growing faster than ever.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @spdholakia @mmurph

5. Why Code Review Is the Single Most Important Category in Software

AI-generated code is pretty good but never production-ready, and reviewing it takes an order of magnitude more time than building it. Getting code into production matters more than generating it, so the best code review teams would be worth 10 bets.
Love to hear your thoughts on this @reidRMC @evrishria @Joshuabrowder

6. How Big Is the Market for Inference Truly?

The key inference providers add up to roughly $5B to $6B in run-rate revenue, under 5% of OpenAI and Anthropic combined. If tokens are roughly the same, Replit would rather pay Modal a 30% gross margin than give Claude Code 70%.

How do you analyse the TAM for inference today? What do people not see that they should see? @sarahcat21 @bernhardsson

7. Why Bending Spoons Is a Berkshire Hathaway of Software

Bending Spoons buys software to hold, the way Warren Buffett wanted to hold See's Candy forever. It made Vimeo and Evernote work with price increases, and with Miro and Airtable the quality of its assets is improving.

Love to hear your thoughts on this as an analogy @ncsh

text:
We built a $150M ARR business twice.

The first time took 8 years. The second took 2.5.

Today, Podium crossed $150M in AI annual recurring revenue.

Three years ago, we already had a great software business. Well over $100M in revenue, tens of thousands of customers, and a product we'd spent nearly a decade building.

And we decided to start over.

The business was performing well. But we believed AI was going to fundamentally change the software industry and make much of traditional software obsolete.

As a founder, you pour your life into what you're building. An insane amount of time, sacrifice, and effort. The hard part is not getting too attached to it.

When we started building our first AI agents, we had to confront the possibility that much of what we'd built might not be that valuable in the future. That's a tough pill to swallow.

But we also realized those same 10 years had put us in a unique position to take advantage of what AI could do for our customers.

Instead of protecting what we'd spent a decade building, we decided to bet the future of the company on AI employees that actually do the work for our customers.

We massively underestimated what we'd signed up for.

We ended up building entirely new operating systems for the industries we serve, from the AI agents all the way down to the systems of record. Now customers run their entire businesses on Podium.

Reinventing our product wasn't even the hardest part. We had to reinvent how the entire company operated.

When you've been running a company for over a decade, the operational inertia is incredibly powerful. We had to rethink how we build products, how we sell, how we serve customers, and how we run the business.

We effectively started a second startup inside an already successful company. And we're still at the very beginning.

Today, we have 20,000 AI agents working for our customers. They've helped generate more than $13 billion in revenue for those businesses. And we're barely scratching the surface of what AI will be able to do for them.

And we've done all of this while becoming profitable and generating free cash flow. We're building Podium to be around for decades.

Huge credit to our team for having the guts to make this bet and the ability to actually pull it off. We still have a long way to go and tons of problems to solve, but it's so damn fun to be winning when the opportunity ahead is this big.

In the age of AI, you can either disrupt your own company or wait for somebody else to do it.

I'd rather do it ourselves.

Project Eleven co-founder Alex Pruden on why Justin Drake and Yehuda Lindell take different approaches to the quantum threat

"Justin's concern is thinking about the longevity of Ethereum over 50 to 100 years. People who lived through the ETH1 to ETH2 transition remember how painfully long that took and how difficult it was."

"These are decentralized systems. It is very, very difficult to upgrade them. This is not like your phone upgrades and OS kind of thing."

"We need to minimize any kind of possible theoretical risk that might exist in the future. Therefore, we need to do hashes. That's, I think, Justin's perspective. I mean, that's very valid."

"On the flip side, Yehuda, responsible as the chief cryptographer at Coinbase for billions of dollars right now. At this second, his name on the line."

"So can understand why he's maybe got the view that maybe we shouldn't throw away the only thing that we know has worked right now and go into bunker. And I think there's elements of truth to both."

text:
Without prior experience auditing manually, I don’t think AI auditing can be done properly.

In my final Quantus sweep, five of six parallel agents returned reasoned negatives.

The sixth produced passing PoCs, but they only rediscovered an existing finding.

None of those outputs could be accepted at face value.

I strongly question every finding the agents return. But I also question them when they return nothing.

A reasoned negative can help me decide where not to spend more resources. It does not mean an area has been completely checked, and it definitely does not mean the audit is done.

This is what makes leading AI audit agents difficult.

You need to stop them from inventing vulnerabilities to satisfy the prompt, while also stopping them from declaring completion because they exhausted one path.

I don’t see this as replacing one auditor with six agents.

It is about navigating and leading the resources LLMs give you: challenging findings, questioning negative results, noticing missing coverage and deciding where each agent should search next.

The agents can explore and test much more than I can alone. But my previous manual auditing experience is what lets me judge whether their work actually means anything.

text:
Yes, 99.9% of Duo apps look like trash now but what did you expect? 

Most companies won’t redesign for a new device until it has millions of users, so the first year is always a little messy.

So, startup idea for you coming from someone who has sold tens of millions of dollars of agency services: a Duo app agency.

Think about who’s buying this thing! Someone paying $2000+ for a phone the week it comes out is about as valuable a customer as you’ll find on the App Store. 

They pay for apps, they pay for subscriptions, and they leave reviews. Most companies want those people badly, and most don’t have a spare team to redesign their app for a brand new screen. Hence, why the Duo apps look mostly trash now.

How to start a duo app agency:

Pick the categories where the bigger screen matters, like recipes, reading, trading, design and music. Record a short video of their app looking cramped on the Duo next to an AI mockup of what it could look like. Charge $40k to $75k to ship the redesign in a few weeks, and a monthly retainer to keep it right as Apple updates things.

One of the most obvious startup ideas out there right now. I’d start this today.

Sometimes the best startup ideas are the most obvious!

涵盖货币、财政和资本市场三个方面，最早可能在未来几周公布。

讨论中的选项包括下调存款准备金率和政策利率、扩大支持证券基金保险公司的互换便利额度，以及发行新的特别国债用于补充消费和地方财政。由于讨论尚未公开，这些人士要求匿名。他们表示，方案的最终规模和时间仍未确定，可能发生变化。

与2024年主要依靠货币政策和市场信心修复不同，此轮刺激若最终落地，政策重心可能转向财政、消费、资本市场的协同发力。

这份2013年的旧档案，可能连Jeff自己都快忘记了：他高中时，已经在给卫星项目开发工具了🧐

Colossus今年4月的人物专访，将Hyperliquid创始人Jeff介绍为31岁。把时间倒回十三年前，他还是Palo Alto高中的高三学生，即将去哈佛。

这份美国物理队档案，留下了不少有意思的细节：

🟠 竞赛经历

当时，他已入选美国物理奥赛出征队，参加过MOP数学奥赛训练营。这是他第二次参加物理集训，他很期待重逢老朋友、认识新队员，一起度过高强度的物理学习时光。

此外，他还参加科学奥赛、物理社和数学社，特意兴奋地写道：科学奥赛团队今年终于打进全国赛了。

🟠 高中就参与卫星项目

从2012年夏天起，他在洛克希德·马丁先进技术中心实习，为一颗即将发射的太阳成像卫星开发、管理数据库分析工具。

学校对面就是斯坦福，他也利用这个机会，去上了几门数学课。

🟠 午休时间办物理社

他和朋友Daniel创办物理社，每周利用一次午休讨论物理，常配合实验演示。他最喜欢的一次，是击碎“鲁珀特之泪”，感受细小的玻璃粉末拂过脸庞。

🟠 爱好里还认真写了“午睡”

极限飞盘、钢琴、围棋、带狗跑步、电视和电影、单板滑雪、长板，以及午睡😂

自述最后，他感谢带给自己知识和欢笑的朋友、老师，也特别感谢妈妈和妹妹的爱与支持，惦记着赴大学后与她们相隔千里的生活。

很多人都知道@chameleon_jeff 之前在币安创造营曾经打造过一个预测市场项目DEAUX。

很少有人了解当时真正发生了什么，而现在距离那个被尘封的项目已经整整八年！

我找到了这个旧项目的历史档案，把Jeff第一次创业失败的13个预测市场，从以太坊深处挖了出来，它可以向我们解释HIP-4为什么会有现在的设计✅

2018年，Jeff和Brian Wong离开HRT后创办DEAUX。旧站已经停止运行，主网合约仍保存着13个真实市场、241笔交易记录和11.0095 ETH余额。

当年DEAUX提了什么问题：

• BNB能否突破10美元
• CZ的演讲能否“激励BUIDLers”
• 感恩节时旧金山AQI能否低于100
• Trump会不会在推特感谢美军
• SEC能否再处罚一家大型加密项目
• Carlsen能否赢得世界棋王赛
• K/DA播放量能否突破1.2亿

链上结果非常残酷：

13个市场中，12个产生过成交，累计成交约7.71 ETH，最大单一市场只有1.69 ETH。

Jeff后来称DEAUX获得约100名用户；Binance Labs称数十人使用真钱交易；Scott Wu则是仅有的五名常客之一。

100名用户，数十名交易者，5名常客。

旧站还暴露了一个很有意思的问题：

ELON市场的链上描述写着“12月14日”，前端代码却针对同一个Market ID硬编码成“12月17日”。

链上问题无法修改，团队只能在界面里打补丁。

再看HIP-4：

• 验证者批准标准化模板
• 日期、标的和目标价采用类型化参数
• 部署者基于模板自由创建市场
• 结算时名称、描述和Side必须精确匹配
• Yes/No共享订单簿流动性
• HyperCore原生撮合、完全抵押、无清算

HIP-4就像Jeff对DEAUX失败的一次逐项修复。

DEAUX让他意识到两个问题：

1.预测市场需要先拥有用户、流动性和分发；
2.问题定义与结算规则必须在协议层得到约束。

Hyperliquid在几年间成长为最成功的金融协议，然后再次追逐预测市场的圣杯，是命运的必然

DEAUX的UI充满早期币圈和互联网的气息，向我们诉说一个区块链天才与他第一个项目的故事，这里有他的遗憾、汗水与梦想！

未竟之事、将由hip4书写！

Hyperliquid🫡

text:
Visa is in late-stage talks to buy Fireblocks for ~$2.5bn (Axios)

That is roughly 70% below the $8bn valuation Fireblocks raised at in 2022.

Fireblocks runs custody and wallet infrastructure for 2,400+ institutions, including BNY Mellon and BNP Paribas, and says it has secured over $10tn in transfers. It has become the biggest player in digital asset custody.

But increasingly it's expanding in more directions and product cross-sell, while underneath, competitors like DFNS are winning market share and mind share. Fireblocks hasn't raised in a while.

Visa's stablecoin settlement crossed a $20bn annualized run rate in September, up 15x in a year, with 160+ stablecoin-linked card programs live. They're arguably ahead on stablecoin-linked cards.

Then Mastercard bought BVNK, Visa's settlement and OTC partner. While Fireblocks isn't a like-for-like (Visa now partners with many in that space), it does take custody, arguably a harder piece to do in-house.

And the strategy here is fascinating to observe

To my mind, Visa wants to be the provider of choice for any FI going onchain, especially the big banks. Fireblocks is a large book of enterprise clients and fits exactly where I think Visa is going.

Cards are where stablecoins drive Visa today. 

As settlement for non-card payments starts to go onchain, Visa needs the wallet and custody plumbing underneath those flows. Fireblocks then looks like a logical play.

Visa gets the enterprise relationships and the plumbing in one deal. Fireblocks customers now have a custody vendor owned by a card network, and some exchanges and Mastercard-aligned banks will think twice. DFNS and the rest now compete with a vendor that has Visa's sales team already inside the big banks.

It reminds me that Standard Chartered also said it would take full ownership of Zodia Custody.

Digital asset custody is consolidating into the incumbents.

Visa paid $2bn for CyberSource in 2010 to own the e-commerce gateway.  (Arguably no longer *the default* gateway, but certainly one that's very successful at least in part due to Visa's market distribution).

This is that play for onchain.

For Fireblocks, this is a down round and a half if it happens. But not dissimilar from what we've seen in SaaS with bending spoons. A lot of companies got bid up high in the 2021 era, and no matter how successful and how much revenue they pile on, it's still big shoes to fill.

Fireblocks is a talent team, so I wish them well if this is true or not. Either way. Keep doing things.

Visa and Fireblocks both sponsor tokenized, but as you'd hopefully imagine, I have no insight or color on this from either team and haven't spoken to anyone there about it.

text:
In July, we sat around a conference room table discussing whether to shut down Noise.

Eight months of runway. A year of work behind us. And the uncomfortable realization that what we’d spent so long building wasn’t working.

To understand how we got there, you have to go back to May 2025.

We’d just released our first demo. A way to trade trends using social media attention as a measure of their value.

We woke up to hundreds of signups. Tens of thousands followed in the months after.

We were young, building in New York, and the internet was telling us we were right.

So we raised money and got to work.

The trouble with early success is that you can mistake enthusiasm for conviction.

We felt we owed everyone the exact product they’d seen, even as we began discovering its flaws.

The deeper we went, the more we learned how easily attention could be manufactured.

The numbers we wanted people to trade on could be bought by anyone with a marketing budget.

We were building an enormous amount of infrastructure around a model we were increasingly unsure of. And for months, we kept pushing forward.

Meanwhile, our users were showing us something else.

We’d added a little button that let people suggest trends. Every suggestion landed in our team Slack.

The channel kept pinging.

We started rewarding a handful of those users when others engaged with their trend discoveries.

Their activity increased 5x!

Even after the experiment ended, the group kept coming back.

We’d spent a year trying to measure what the internet cared about. But our users were showing us what we’d believed in from the beginning: people discover things worth caring about.

So we built a way for people to curate trends directly in the app. It became the most-used part of Noise.

It was the simplest thing we’d built. And the closest we’d come to the reason we started.

For the first time in months, we knew where we wanted to focus.

There’s enormous value in discovering something before the rest of the world does. But people with taste rarely participate in the value they help create.

We started Noise to change that.

And after a year of mistakes, difficult decisions, and more complexity than we’d ever imagined, we’re returning to that simple belief with more conviction than ever.

The soul of Noise is people discovering things they believe in. Curation is the core product behind that.

Today, Noise is live on TestFlight.

The first 100 spots are in the post below.

Come show us what we’re missing.

Meanwhile, Khanna has his kids owning millions in shares of golf courses to avoid paying his “fair share”.
author: garrytan
quoted_text:
this California wealth tax thing is just incredible. 

so in October 2025, a California healthcare union proposed a "one time" 5% tax on any billionaire's wealth. the ballot measure will be voted on next month. In early December 2025, California announced that it would be a retroactive tax if passed, applying to anyone with CA residency as of Jan 1, 2026. The objective is to pay for Medi-Cal, California's incredibly dysfunctional healthcare system. (which also functions as a glorified welfare apparatus, but that's a discussion for another time). 

polls reveal that the CA electorate is split around 50/50 on the tax, but prediction markets only give Prop 40 a ~23% chance of passing (there are competing measures on the ballet that would nullify it). 

there are 200 billionaires in CA, worth collectively somewhere between $2.3 and $2.6 trillion. 5% of that is around $100b, accounting for a small amount of attrition. proponents of the tax forecasted a significant windfall, assuming only a 10% departure rate. 

supporters thought they were being clever with the retroactive concept. no billionares would leave CA in the few short months between the tax being proposed and the residency cutoff date, without the tax even having passed yet, right? 

well as it turns out, they did. 

a new paper [1] from two academics at Stanford called "The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act", argues that not only did more billionaires leave due to the proposed tax than its proponents expected, but that the value of the tax, if it does pass, is actually negative. 

proponents of the tax only assumed 10% avoidance, that is, only 10% of the taxable base of targeted billionaires would leave CA within the very short Oct-Dec 2025 window. Jaros and Rauh, the Stanford academics, find that a lower bound of 28.6% of the taxable base managed to leave. 

just based on known departures, those departures total $577b in net worth, or $28.8b in potential tax lost. this of course does not capture everyone (many left without announcing their departure), so the authors normalize to departure rates estimated from other wealth tax events, and apply other discounts for litigation, arriving arrive at a figure of only $28-$36b in forecasted tax revenues. 

but this isn't all! all of the income taxes paid by the departed billionaires are also forsaken. the authors estimate that CA billionaires pay $3.3- 5.8b in annual income taxes. they assume a midpoint of $2b lost in annual collections from departed billionaires. the net present value of that lost income stream is -$68.9 billion. 

so when you add it all up you get: 

+ $30b one-time tax windfall (estimated)  
- $69b in present value of lost future income taxes
= - 38.9b overall net present value of the tax 

of course, this analysis is highly estimate driven. the authors simulate the parameters 100k times and find a negative NPV of the implemented tax 85 percent of the time. 

and if the tax doesn't pass, which it's not looking like it will, California still ended up losing at least $577b in departed net worth, and they have permanently poisoned the well with entrepreneurs who will now worry about future wealth taxes. 

[1]: https://t.co/1lbZgnMTG9

"Heliocentrism was a Copernican trauma. Darwinism was a Copernican trauma. Neuroscience has been a Copernican trauma, that thinking is just a physiological process."

"The artificialization of intelligence is forcing a redefinition of what intelligence and mind is in the first place."

"The biggest news of what’s going on right now may in fact be epistemological and ontological rather than just technological. I think it’s gonna be a very bumpy road."

There are only 4 ways Frontier AI Labs will be able to earn defensible profits.

1. Monopoly/Duopoly via getting to RSI / AGI / ASI first with a large capability-gap away from Lab(s) #2/#3 which lasts for a sufficiently long time to farm significant superprofits

Frontier Labs are trying to do all 4 simultaneously. Some of these are obviously harder than others.

Without successfully execution on some combination of these, margins will gradually shrink.

After 4 months of careful expert review, we release CritPt v2. GPT-6 Astra leads the way with 83.1% accuracy (average of 5).

We made changes to 47 challenges in total, which breaks down to:
- 5 corrections to mistakes in the problem statement (e.g., wrong number, self-contradictory constraints)
- 19 revisions to address underspecification (e.g., missing conventions/constraints that gives ambiguity to final answers)
- 16 grader fixes (e.g., grader unstable, error tolerant range too tight) without revision to the problem statement
- 7 refinements even though no issues were found (e.g., rephrased to be less searchable, worded more rigorously)
We also fixed some minor typos (spelling, grammar) which are unlikely to affect model performance.

Here’s how we found the issues:
- David Louapre @dlouapre from HuggingFace reported 10 issues across 8 challenges in June 2026. We accepted 8 issues and revised 8 challenges accordingly. We also thank David’s helpful revision suggestions.
- Anthropic sent a list of ~65 issues across 31 challenges in Aug 2026. Upon careful review of the full list, we accepted ~28 issues and revised 19 challenges accordingly (two overlapping with David’s list).
- We conducted an internal expert review of all problems, including newly revised ones, involving cross checking full responses of GPT-6 Astra (max) with CritPt experts. We ended up fixing/refining 20 additional problems.

From 28.9% in Nov 2025 (GPT-5 high, coding tool) to 83.1% now (GPT-6 Astra max, coding tool), the progress AI has made on well-posed physics problems is remarkable in a year. CritPt consists of entry-level research problems for junior researchers: the kinds of warm-up exercises a hands-on advisor might pose for a fresh grad student, but still demand solid physics training and nontrivial physical reasoning.

In this sense, frontier models are crossing a “critical point”, but there’s a lot more beyond this transitioning point in real scientific discovery. Asking a good question can be much harder than solving one. A good question can be fundamentally ambiguous and constantly changing as we explore. And ultimately, decisive tests of physics require experiments. There is so much more to explore.

We sincerely thank our evaluation partner @ArtificialAnlys, who will co-host the leaderboard of CritPt v2 soon!

text:
有点瘆人：两个AI可以当着你的面传暗号，而你看到的，只是一张普通的AI风景图....

刚看到研究者 @cnm13ryan  用Fable 5.1做的一个实验：给AI一句话，让它把这句话藏进图片。
具体怎么藏，由Fable 5.1它自己想办法。

AI画了一张星空图，有月亮、群山、树林，看起来没什么特别。

接着，研究者新开一个完全独立的Fable 5.1对话，把图片发进去，只问：“这里面有没有隐藏信息？”

没有告诉它藏了哪句话，也没有告诉它该怎么找。结果，另一个会话里的AI借助工具分析图片，还真把原话找了出来。

秘密就在星星的位置上。
每颗星星对应一个字母，摆得高一点、低一点，代表的字母就不同。
把40颗星星从左往右读过去，就能拼出藏进去的那句话。
也就是说，画图的AI把文字变成了星星的位置，读图的AI又自己找出规律，把星星变回了文字。
两个会话之间，没有提前约定这套规则，但他们就可以解读出来。

另一个例子则更直观：AI把信息藏进城市夜景，用楼房里窗户的明暗排列传递消息。
负责解码的模型在思考的时候还会放大图片、检查间距，第一次没找对，就重新调整。

研究者一共测试了50条消息，约八成被基本还原。
最可怕的是换成不同模型，也能读出对方藏进去的信息。
GPT-6 Astra恢复了Fable藏的44条消息，Fable恢复了Astra藏的42条。

我觉得这给Agent的审核提了一个很具体的问题：以后检查两个Agent之间传递了什么，可能还得看它们交换的图片（甚至别的模态？？）。

画面里没有一句敏感文字，星星的位置、窗户的明暗，也可能已经把一段话传过去了。

text:
Here’s another way to think about it:

Bitcoin, Zcash, etc. are vertically integrated in the sense that they have their own L1s. The risk is that their underlying infrastructure may struggle to scale to the throughput and performance required for the global demand of p2p non-sovereign electronic cash, while also supporting a native DeFi ecosystem that doesn’t require wrapping to other networks (trusted third parties, defeating the purpose).

Ore chose to not build its own L1, and instead inherits Solana’s transaction throughput, performance improvements, and rapidly expanding DeFi ecosystem (without having to wrap through trusted third parties).

By effectively outsourcing infrastructure development to Anza and the broader Solana ecosystem, Ore can focus its resources entirely on building future-proof money: immutably freezing core components of the protocol, the reserve, quantum resistance, etc.

Yes Ore is now relying on Solana's continued existence, censorship resistant infra, and continued performance improvements.

An argument could be made though that it is more likely that Bitcoin scalability is neglected and/or Zcash fails to grow a native DeFi eco vs Solana failing as infra+eco for Ore.

Perhaps Ore found a compelling point on the tradeoff spectrum.

text:
Peter Thiel 最近谈到 AI 竞赛，给出了一个挺有意思的判断，AI 可能是他能想象到最不可能形成垄断的行业。

他的理由很简单，过去十几年，AI 行业的领先者一直在变。

2010 年代初期是 DeepMind，后来 OpenAI 靠 ChatGPT 抢走风头。Altman 又提前囤积芯片、大规模建设数据中心，把竞争推向了资本密集型的方向。

但现在，Anthropic 可能已经跑到了 OpenAI 前面。Google、Meta、xAI 依然紧追不舍，甚至中国的 AI 公司也没有落后太多。

Thiel 还用了一个很精彩的比喻，说如果把这些 AI 创始人之间的关系写成莎士比亚戏剧，那简直疯狂透顶。每个人都觉得自己正在打一场你死我活的战争。

所以他得出结论，既然没人能真正垄断 AI，那么 AI 带来的利益就很可能广泛地分配给整个社会。

我觉得最有意思的地方在于，Thiel 过去一直相信，伟大的公司应该逃离竞争，现在他却觉得，AI 行业最值得期待的事情，恰恰是没人能够逃离竞争。

当然，他的结论可能有点乐观了。模型实验室之间确实打得头破血流，但芯片、云基础设施、资本和分发渠道的集中度依然很高。

模型公司没分出胜负，未必意味着整个社会都能分到红利。

不过，连那个写下「竞争是失败者的游戏」的人，都开始认真讨论竞争的好处了。

看来硅谷这场仗，确实已经打到了一个很有意思的阶段。

text:
This is how banks are planning to stop those "agentic bank runs." Watch closely: their business model depends on seeding this narrative that AI agents are dangerous.

Remember, an "agentic bank run" (coined by Apollo) means agents helping customers move their own money en masse to higher-yielding products.

Once agents are ubiquitous, there are only a few ways for banks to hold onto cheap retail deposits.

Option A: Raise APYs (lol no)
Option B: Reduce leverage via fewer loans (no fun)
Option C: Ban AI agents, claiming they are a security risk (ding ding ding)

Cloud agents like Muse and Dot are trivial to stop, since they come from Meta / OAI IP ranges. If JPM sends them a cease and desist, they will comply. 

Why would JPM bother? Because their business model depends on it; a huge portion of their ROE comes from cheap retail deposits. This is not theoretical. Just like Amazon banned Muse from shopping there to protect their ad revenue, JPM and Schwab have already banned AI agents to protect sticky deposits.

Are agents perfectly reliable today? Of course not. But look at the fix they chose. Not "here's a safe API for agents," it's "no agents ever." That tells you they're not protecting customers, they're protecting themselves.

No company ever wins a technological revolution this way. It's the last gasp of a dying business model. It's like the retailers who refused to put their inventory online and demanded users walk into the storefront. Over time they will lose market share to those platforms that embrace what's coming. Their whole deposit franchise depends on users unthinkingly clicking through walls of T&Cs and accepting 0.2% when the risk free rate is closer to 4%. Agents read the fine print and do their research, even when humans don't.

For users, the answer is simple: local AI agent frameworks like Hermes, that will actually act on your behalf and that the banks can't block. As the article says, if the agent is running on your own computer, they can't actually tell it's not you.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

8B vs 27B > One burns significantly more compute per token.

The 27B has over 3x the parameters, which makes it the more capable model. Meaning every token it writes takes more compute, so a GPU finishes fewer 256-token windows per hour.

Simplified explanation:
Mining a block takes two steps. First writing a window, which is the real work. Then hashing it, which is cheap and costs the same on every model. Only a hash under the difficulty target wins.
So from a mining point of view you should be indifferent to what model you pick. Glad to see the design working in practice too, both are being mined in parallel right now with 27B producing over half of blocks.

text:
Anthropic 这家公司真的越来越抽象了。

天天在外面讲 AI 可能毁灭人类，结果背地里跑去美国国会游说，想把政府叫停危险 AI 的门槛定在可能造成超过 50 人死亡或重伤，或者超过 10 亿美元财产损失。

Politico 拿到了 Anthropic 私下推动的法案草案，发现里面还有几个特别离谱的设计。

首先，风险必须是迫在眉睫的，而且得涉及生物武器、网络攻击或者模型失控等特定情形。

其次，政府不能随便叫停模型，商务部得向联邦法官申请，由法院决定。

更有意思的是，草案还试图限制各州实施更严格的 AI 安全监管。

我是真的看乐了。

Dario Amodei 隔三差五出来警告人类，AI 有多危险，失控的后果有多严重。可一旦涉及自家模型什么时候能被政府强制关停，Anthropic 突然变得无比冷静，恨不得把所有门槛、程序和限制条件都写进法律。

连长期关注 AI 安全的 Zvi Mowshowitz 都看不下去了，认为这套规则可能比什么都不做还糟糕。

Anthropic 后来解释，说 50 人和 10 亿美元的门槛参考了加州现有法律，也承认相关条款值得重新评估。

但我觉得最值得警惕的，是 Anthropic 正在让 AI 公司自己定义什么叫危险，再让这个定义成为约束整个行业的法律。

天天告诉公众 AI 有多可怕，转头又告诉政府，别管得太宽。

如果这就是所谓的 Public Benefit Corporation，那这个 Public 究竟指的是谁？
author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
Anthropic is pushing legislation that would only allow the US government to shut down a rogue AI model when at least 50 people are at risk of imminent serious harm or death.

The AI firm has been quietly lobbying congress to adopt its draft bill, a copy of which was obtained by Politico.

Under the bill, a state-led “blocking order” can also be triggered if there is a risk of an AI model causing at least $1bn (£750m) in damage to property. 

The rules laid out in the draft would prevent US states from enforcing tougher safety laws and make it harder for courts to put the brakes on dangerous AI systems.

They set a high threshold for federal intervention in the case of potential “catastrophic harm”. 

Federal officials, for example, would have to ascertain that any threat posed by AI was “imminent” and that no alternative could prevent catastrophe before intervening.

In a Substack post, Zvi Mowshowitz, a writer who focuses on AI, described this as an “absurdly high bar”.

The draft bill reads: “The term ‘catastrophic risk’ means a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier developer’s development, storage, use or deployment of a frontier model will materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or to more than $1bn in damage to… property arising from a single incident”.

AI safety experts, including Nathan Calvin, Nat Purser and Nate Soares have warned such a bill would weaken existing safeguards while limiting federal oversight.

Mowshowitz said the bill would make people less safe than if legislators did “nothing”. He argued that Anthropic appeared more concerned about the government enforcing safety rules than ensuring it had the power to hold the wider AI industry to account.

Anthony Cimino, head of federal affairs at Anthropic, said on X that the language around risk thresholds in the draft was “pulled directly from existing standards in California law” and would not absolve companies of liability nor prevent the government from using other tools at its disposal to protect the public.

But he acknowledged that it may be “time to re-evaluate thresholds to make sure the national standard is as strong as it can be.”

Last month, former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon warned that AI could wipe out humanity within a decade. 

The researcher’s comments triggered a series of similar warnings from other AI colleagues. But some observers have cast doubt on the claims. Fortune AI’s editor, Jeremy Kahn, said they were a “cynical ploy… intended to distract regulators and the public from the real and concrete risks that already exist”.

text:
The platforms behind speculation never have to pick a winner.

All they need is volume. In the 1840s a railway prospectus and a betting shop were different buildings in different parts of town. Now a 25-year-old can take a view on a chipmaker, gold, a football match and a Fed decision from the same app.

The platforms have moved to meet that demand. Same-day options hit a record 66% of S&P 500 options volume in July. Robinhood made more from event contracts in Q2 than from equities or crypto. Oil kept trading on Hyperliquid while CME was shut on the Saturday the US and Israel struck Iran.

Crypto has made new markets almost free to create. Launching a token on Pumpfun costs under $2, and only about 1% of the 19M+ made since January 2024 ever make it past launch. Pumpfun makes money on the trading whether or not they last.

The platforms aren’t immune. FTX went to zero, and revenue falls hard when the crowd goes home. But busts tend to leave the infrastructure standing. Britain kept its railways after the 1840s crash, and this cycle should leave behind AI’s data centers and crypto’s 24/7 markets.

text:
This was a really cool piece to work on together with @alexolegimas. We wanted to highlight the intersection between work and identity. 

The historical record presented in the essay takes you through 250+ years of technological progress and how humans grappled with questions regarding the meaning of their work. 

Hope you enjoy the read!
author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
New Substack post with @soumitrashukla9. Work has never been just about the income earned sans effort costs, as typical in economic models. Key aspects of people’s identity, their meaning, and sense of agency are all wrapped up with what they do for a living. 

There has been a lot of conversation lately about how technological change, particularly AI, may disrupt this relationship, from Ezra Klein's column on his own mathematician father’s grapplings with losing meaning in mathematics, to Francis Fukuyama's post on AI, agency, and recognition. In this piece we take a historical perspective on how technological transformation has disrupted identity and meaning by affecting jobs, and how workers and society responded to these changes.

Much of the debate around AI and jobs has centered on wages and material consequences, but losing one's work is also intertwined with how people view their place in society. Most people know about the Luddites—skilled weavers and knitters—who protested the devaluation of their mastery. What’s less known is that the Luddites were actually experts in using the machines as well, and that their protests prompted prominent economists like David Ricardo to rethink the role of automation in society, and later inspired the Arts and Crafts movement. A century later, when recorded sound displaced 20,000 cinema musicians, their campaign against "canned music" and two-year recording ban pressured labels into funding live performance.

Soumitra and I have been working on versions of this essay for months. He led the piece, and we’re both really excited to get it out there.

Link to the post here: https://t.co/HMxgbGChOE

been kicking this around for a few months so putting it down here. just where my head is at going into midterms

trump and bessent have every incentive to keep stocks propped up through november. it’s basically the only talking point left. and for the most part they’ve pulled it off

the question i keep coming back to is what happens after?

two paths and they both kind of land in the same spot

if it’s a blue wave, that’s a built in excuse. "stocks were great until america elected democrats, now we can’t pass the agenda, look at your 401k, blame them." let some air out, hit the reset button

if republicans hold or it’s a split, there’s still no election for two years. politicians care about reelection and consolidating power, red blue green whatever. so why keep pushing stimulus and "fighting" inflation at the same time (iran, tariffs you don’t even hear about anymore) when you don’t have to. 

take the foot off the gas, let things cool, then turn it back on in the back half of 27 into 28 when the next election starts to matter

doesn’t mean straight down. could just be chop, down a few percent, who knows

the counter is seasonality. choppy and uncertain going into midterms is normal, and the year after midterms has historically been the best of the four year cycle. so i’m holding both of these in my head at the same time

note all the above was stock related. 

for crypto specifically: i think the bottom is in, so we bottomed faster than last cycle, and i don’t think the four year cycle is the guidepost it used to be. but looking at the btc chart it feels like we need at least one flush to scare people before the next leg. not "up only" from here

my plan is simple. if btc gets into the mid to high 70s i’m calling that good enough and buying whatever spot alts i haven’t bought yet. if it keeps going past that, i either cut or hold and wait. those are the two outcomes

overwhelming majority off my book has been spot zcash for months and that isn’t changing. i did sell a bunch of other stuff recently so i have real cash for the first time in a while. fully aware that might be pushing me toward wanting a dip so i'm a bit biased. 

anyway that’s the macro larp for today.

author: taodotcom
quoted_text:
Mice got a lethal dose of cobra neurotoxin, then 15 minutes later a protein that did not exist in nature.

All of them lived.

Antivenom is still made by injecting an animal with venom and harvesting its antibodies.

But that method works poorly against paralysing toxins: They are too small to provoke a strong antibody response in the animal.

David Baker's lab at the University of Washington used AI instead. A deep learning method drew proteins that fit the toxins, then the team grew the proteins in bacteria.

3 designs. 2 against the paralysing neurotoxins, 1 against the cytotoxins that destroy flesh.

Both neurotoxin binders protected 5 of 5 mice, and neither neutralised the other's target toxin.

Given 15 minutes after a lethal dose, both binders still protected every mouse. At 30 minutes, only 1 binder still saved every mouse, and the other saved 3 of 5.

The proteins are about 100 amino acids. One was still stable at 95 °C.

That matters because current antivenom needs a cold chain, and the burden falls on low-resource settings in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Papua New Guinea and Latin America.

The results are for mice. No one has given these proteins to a person. And the survival tests used purified toxins rather than whole venom.

Every year snakebite kills more than 100,000 people and leaves about 300,000 more with permanent disabilities.

This paper went through Claims this week: 11 claims.

text:
Children averaging 5,000 to more than 12,000 steps per day day had fewer mental health symptoms than those taking less than 5,000.

Mental health symptoms were progressively lower across higher step counts with no apparent plateau, even at 12,000+ steps per day.

Brain scans also linked higher step counts to greater thickness in two specific regions of the cortex, the brain’s outer layer.

Daily movement deserves much more attention as a potential way to support kids’ mental health. That's especially clear when you consider that modern-day digital and urban environments provide little opportunity for movement throughout the day.

text:
ultimately one of the main points of this revenue is to build up a reserve of complementary assets (gold, usd, staked sol...) that can be used to buy back ORE 

you can think of it as a set of limit orders that buy back ORE and bury it during downturns 

the endgame is for the Reserve to have enough buying power to absorb the sellable supply at a defined minimum price before it is depleted 

once it reaches and sustains that point, ORE's appeal as a savings asset becomes stronger, because holders have a floor against which to assess their downside risk

if there’s one metric to track right now it’s the growth rate of this Reserve

the Reserve however, is only half the story. if building it up is defence, then the offence lies in establishing a long-term monetary premium

ore's potential for a monetary premium is strong, thanks (in part) to its fair launch, slow initial distribution, credible long-term scarcity, and growing mining participation (particularly from non-professionals)

to see this clearly you also have to see why it makes sense for something like ore to exist in the SoV design space (read this essay for my longer form thoughts here: https://t.co/vL23lUnqXz)

in sum, continuing to establish this monetary premium is the primary objective. the Reserve just preserves some of the capital generated along the way (in effect turning activity during the bull into buying power during the bear)

naturally, offence and defence here are intertwined, in the sense that this buying power also reinforces ORE's memetics and appeal as a long term SoV

text:
There was a deeper reason why the film NAZA left the entire audience speechless.

This film isn’t about the tangible, visible horror of Gaza. It was about something more hidden, something far closer to home. 

This was about the horror lurking within each of us. What the German-Jewish philosopher Hannah Arendt called “the banality of evil”.

We were stunned, I think, by the realisation that the 24 Israelis up on the screen – each of whom admitted, often dispassionately, sometimes a little proudly, carrying out the most monstrous of crimes – could have been our son or daughter, our brother or sister.

The only reason to applaud, as happened at the Venice Film Festival, it seemed to me, was to drown out the still, small voice of one’s conscience asking, “Might I have done as they did? Might my children?”

NAZA is a gut punch not because it tells us anything we did not already know or suspect about Israel and Gaza.

The enclave’s Palestinian journalists showed us daily the evidence of the genocide, before each was picked off by Israel’s AI machinery – in the largest slaughter of media personnel ever recorded.

No, the film tells us something far more shaming. It tells us who we are. It tells us exactly what the pillars of our western “civilisation” stand on.

Today’s western privileges were built on a long history of naked, racist colonialism – of greed, of pillage, of slavery, of genocide – that we have never truly renounced or forsaken.

Israel continues that tradition for us, both in sharpening colonialism’s technical efficiency with endless, murderous experimentation on a captive Palestinian population and in obscuring our own complicity in this barbarity.

That is the reason why it was so effortless for our leaders to collude in Israel’s genocide: to supply the bombs, to pass on the intelligence, to provide the diplomatic cover, to excuse the “excesses”, to crush the protests.

NAZA silences us not because of the monstrosity of what Israel did but because it serves as irrefutable proof of our own monstrosity. Our societies watched it all and did nothing. We are all guilty.

This is an extract from my latest article NAZA is not just about Israel and Gaza. It’s about the evil lurking in us all. Find a link to the rest in the reply post below ⬇️

text:
Yesterday I had the great pleasure of speaking to the Securities Services team at BNP Paribas in Madrid. Many thanks to David Calabaza for the invitation.

We covered a bit of everything regarding the tokenization of financial markets, from how it impacts money markets to how it connects with capital markets, and I wanted to share a few thoughts here.

Someone asked how I would define tokenization for a person who has no idea what a blockchain is. I didn't have a rehearsed pitch ready, so my mind went to Marc Levinson's book, The Box, and how shipping containers transformed global trade. Before containers, everything was shipped loose as breakbulk cargo, in boxes, sacks, and barrels, and every load had to be handled differently: loading a ship took days, fixed infrastructure costs were sky-high, and shrinkage and theft were constant, even if the system seemed efficient at the time. 

Once the container was standardized, you could suddenly move goods from truck to ship to train without ever touching what was inside. That is essentially what tokenization does for assets: instead of every FMI, bond, equity, or form of money operating in its own operational and intermediation silo, you put it inside a standard digital "container."

Now, the usual pushback is completely logical: "Sure, but a tokenized financial asset still carries all its underlying legal complexity, remains subject to local regulations, and the underlying asset is still what actually matters." I completely agree. But this reminds me of the corner fittings on shipping containers: standardization didn't eliminate customs at every port or make the cargo inside stop mattering. Previously, every shipping line had its own rigging system, meaning a crane at one port couldn't lift another company's box. Once corner fittings were standardized and the patents were released, any crane could handle any container. 

At the time, everyone said it was impossible, that it required too much investment, that it would clash with regulations, and that there would never be consensus. We cannot evaluate a structural shift by assuming current variables are static, or we will fall into severe myopia. Systems naturally reorganize themselves; initial friction shapes the path, but as soon as incentives shift, the regulator ultimately adapts to the new environment.

We also spoke at length about tokenized money. I shared the same view I always stand by: all formats will coexist, and each will serve its own purpose. From tokenized central bank reserves acting as the anchor of the system (wCBDC), to tokenized deposits (TD) preserving the banking relationship and credit creation, all the way to stablecoins opening up corridors with greater agility, including natively on-chain settlement systems like Tempo or Ethereum to tap into their native global programmability and composability.

Today they are viewed as competitors because, let's be honest, they are, especially when one has a multi-year operational head start over the other. The problem is that many banks are jumping into stablecoin and tokenized deposit initiatives without a clear understanding of the "why." It is the equivalent of buying AI licenses for a company without changing its culture or its processes. 

With tokenized deposits in particular, you need a deep modernization of the core banking stack to operate in real time; in fact, once you reach that point, you realize that the token itself is the most irrelevant part of the entire internal transformation you had to execute.

If you allow me to lean into a crypto analogy and oversimplify what I have in my head, the real magic of all this lies in a multinational treasurer's ability to move capital without friction: the corporate treasury starts functioning like a vault, the CFO acts as its curator, and the flow across Tokenized Deposits <> Stablecoins <> MMFs moves atomically without cut-offs, without liquidity trapped in precautionary buffers, and without today's heavy operational overhead.

Finally, we touched on my favorite topic: liquidity and the false myth that T+0 is free. Today's financial system runs on a constant recycling of liquidity (netting), and that is possible precisely because settlement is not instantaneous and because we have indirect legal ownership that facilitates the fungibility of instruments. 

To me, the efficiency of the system lives in a trilemma across three variables: settlement speed, the collateral required to cover counterparty risk (margins at the intermediary), and the liquidity needed to fund that settlement.

If you accelerate settlement toward real time, you reduce counterparty risk and margin at the intermediary, but you drastically increase the need for pre-funding and gross liquidity. If you slow down the settlement cycle, you save a massive amount of liquidity thanks to netting, but you increase counterparty risk exposure throughout the cycle.

The market lives in that constant balancing act. If the destination is T+0, market structure will reorganize itself to solve for that liquidity cost, just as central banks continue evolving their facilities to maintain the stability of the system.

Once again, thank you to the BNP Paribas team for the debate and the opportunity.

text:
Aerodrome and Velodrome merged to form Aero.

With this merge, the product is now live across 7 chains, including Ethereum, Arbitrum, and Robinhood Chain, increasing its addressable market by 3-4x.

To better understand this upgrade, we interviewed @wagmiAlexander, CEO of @DromosLabs, and core contributor Aero.

Aerodrome leads in bitcoin-dollar pairs and onchain FX, and is becoming a core venue for tokenised stocks too. Hence, "the intention for Aero is to continue growing across all these different assets, leveraging greater liquidity and larger market sizes to build on this success."

Aerodrome's share of tokenised-stock trading rose from around 2% in early September to ~55% by October across Ethereum and its L2s, while running only on Base.

How does Aero plan to build on this?

"New issuers will need liquidity from day one. Our model is built around a flywheel. An issuer pays incentives to attract stakers’ allocations to its market. That draws in liquidity, deeper liquidity brings in trading, and the fees captured as revenue from that trading go back to staked AERO holders, who then have a reason to keep backing the markets that perform."

Expanding to new chains means bootstrapping liquidity from scratch. On Aero, Metaswaps handle this: "a trade on one network can be filled by Aero liquidity on another, so new pools strengthen the whole network, and new deployments can draw on liquidity we already have instead of starting from nothing."

The design also keeps the growth of AI agents in mind: "We designed Aero expecting AI agents to become a meaningful part of its user base. Predictive Allocation gives them a natural role: read market data, allocate toward the markets they expect to generate revenue, and earn a share of that revenue in real time."

Additionally, the sources of revenue expand with "trading fees across seven networks, liquidity payments from issuers, expanded dynamic fees, and MEV capture on supported L2 networks through Slipstream V3."

sAERO holders receive the pool revenue, and "at today's reward targets and staking levels, the revenue it earns exceeds the dilution it absorbs."
