text:
I am the Vice President of Portfolio Lifecycle at Electronic Arts, and on Wednesday I closed BioWare.

It had been open for thirty-one years in Edmonton, ever since two practising physicians founded it in 1995 and gave it a name that still sounds faintly like a clinic. It made Baldur’s Gate, Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age and Mass Effect, and the next Mass Effect, the one we teased at The Game Awards in December 2020 with a scrap of N7 armor half-buried in the snow, went with it. You may not have heard. We announced it in about a hundred and fifty words on a company blog on a Wednesday afternoon, which is how you announce something you would prefer people learn later, from a friend.

I have played every Mass Effect game twice, Paragon and then Renegade. I romanced Garrus. I cried on Virmire like everyone else. I mention it only because people assume the men who do this have never held a controller, and the truth is worse: we know exactly what we’re closing, down to the side quests.

The obituary itself was very good. It opens, “For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio,” and then lists the dead in italics, the way a village lists its sons on a war memorial: Baldur’s Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, Mass Effect. And then, last, in the same italics and with the same reverence: Anthem.

Someone at BioWare typed that. Someone who was there in 2019, when we asked a studio of storytellers to build a live-service shooter and later switched off its servers, sat down this week and placed Anthem on the memorial beside Knights of the Old Republic, as though the studio had chosen it. In twenty years in this business I have not seen a cleaner piece of corporate grief. You take the wound you inflicted and carve it into the headstone as one of the deceased’s achievements.

The news arrives halfway through a sentence, “BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effectproject is ending,” where the eye slides past “closing” on its way to something about Mass Effect. It gives no number, no reason and no owner. EA isn’t mentioned anywhere in the text; our name appears once, at the foot of the page, in small grey type beside the copyright symbol. We don’t sign obituaries. We own them. The final line thanks the players “for being the most meaningful part of our story,” while the staff are supported “through this transition.” The players get the thanks. The staff get a noun.

The menu above it hasn’t been touched in years. If you scroll up you can still click Careers and apply for a job at a studio that closed on Wednesday. It still lists an office in Austin. It still links to Origin, a store we shut down long ago, and to a merchandise shop that is, as I write, still taking orders, so that you can buy an N7 hoodie from a company that no longer exists through a menu that still offers you a future there. “I’m Commander Shepard, and this is my favorite store on the Citadel.” The store is open. The Citadel is not.

We hope the closure gives players a sense of pride and accomplishment. The phrase is ours, from 2017, when an EA account on Reddit explained that Darth Vader was locked behind dozens of hours of grinding, or a credit card, because “the intent is to provide players with a sense of pride and accomplishment for unlocking different heroes.” It became the most downvoted comment in the history of Reddit, by roughly two-thirds of a million votes, and we have never stopped finding uses for it.

Everyone wants a villain for Wednesday: a bad game, a bad boss, a culture war. The real explanation is in Mass Effect, and BioWare wrote it themselves nineteen years ago. In the lore, ancient machines called Reapers come out of dark space every fifty thousand years and harvest every advanced civilization in the galaxy, not the primitive ones but the ones that have reached their height. On Virmire, the Reaper called Sovereign explains this to Shepard in a speech I can still recite: “We impose order on the chaos of organic evolution. You exist because we allow it, and you will end because we demand it.”

My job is often described as destroying studios, which flatters the people who destroy things. Anyone can destroy a studio. I harvest the ones that have peaked, on a cycle a good deal shorter than fifty thousand years but nearly as regular: Westwood, which made Command & Conquer; Origin, which made Ultima; Bullfrog; Pandemic; Maxis in its original Emeryville home; Visceral, closed in the middle of a Star Wars game. Each was loved, each reached its height, and each ended with a dark space opening and, shortly afterward, a blog post. The players like to say EA is where studios go to die. Death wastes things. We keep them.

The public noticed long ago. In 2012 the readers of the Consumerist voted us the Worst Company in America, and in the final round we beat Bank of America, a bank fresh from the foreclosure crisis that lost a public vote to a video-game publisher largely over the color of an ending. The plaque is in my office. Bank of America has since paid a billion-dollar fine for failing to report money laundering, and we have since closed BioWare, so I suspect a rematch would go our way.

We understood the Reapers better than BioWare ever did. Mass Effect 3 launched that same year with a piece of day-one content called From Ashes, which contained Javik, the last living Prothean, sole survivor of a civilization the Reapers had harvested fifty thousand years before. On launch day we sold him separately, for ten dollars. The fans were furious, and they bought him anyway, and that was when I understood the cycle could be monetized.

What casual players miss is that the Reapers don’t simply kill a civilization. They process it, turning what it was into a new Reaper, a shell that carries the old name and serves the cycle. While BioWare was being closed this month, Amazon’s Mass Effect television series was in active development. The galaxy survives, and the armor, with N7 stencilled on the chest. Only the people who made them are gone. We keep the shells.

Before long we may not need the people at all. The Financial Times reported that the investors who bought us are making “a huge bet that artificial intelligence can significantly cut EA’s operating costs,” and somewhere, eventually, a model will be trained on thirty years of Garrus. It won’t need a salary or a dental plan, and it won’t know what Virmire means, which the analysts regard as a feature.

Then there are the mass relays. Every civilization in Mass Effect builds its future on them, and on the Citadel, marvels left behind by an older race, and nobody asks who built them until it’s too late: they are the Reapers’ own infrastructure, laid down so that each civilization develops along a predictable path and is easier to harvest when the time comes. Every studio we buy is moved onto our engine, Frostbite, which was built for shooters and handed to people who made role-playing games. Every BioWare game of the last decade ran on our relays, and reporters spent years documenting how the engine fought the developers at every step. We knew. You don’t have to destroy a civilization that builds everything on your technology. You only have to wait.

The lore is the poetry, though. The reason is arithmetic, and it arrived on August 4, the day Electronic Arts stopped being a public company. A consortium bought us for fifty-five billion dollars: Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, which now owns about ninety-three percent of the company, the private-equity firm Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners, the investment firm founded by Jared Kushner. It was the largest leveraged buyout the technology industry has ever seen, and leveraged means borrowed. The buyers didn’t pay for EA. EA paid for itself, and now carries about eighteen billion dollars of debt taken on to finance its own purchase, with interest expected to run near one point eight billion dollars a year.

I worked it out late one night with Mass Effect 2 paused on my other monitor. One point eight billion a year is about five million dollars a day. By the end BioWare was fewer than a hundred people, down from more than two hundred two years earlier, and even at generous Canadian salaries a studio that size costs perhaps fifteen million dollars a year. The figure is my estimate rather than a published one, but the division isn’t hard.

BioWare cost about three days of interest.

The studio that gave the world Shepard and Garrus and Morrigan and the Illusive Man cost less than a long weekend of servicing the debt the company borrowed to buy itself. The interest accrued on Friday, and on Saturday, and by Sunday evening BioWare had been paid for, and on Monday it began again, as it will every day, with no interest of its own in Virmire.

The Reapers have a voice, Harbinger, and whenever it seizes one of the creatures it controls it announces itself with three words the players long ago turned into a meme. I keep them on a sticky note on my monitor: “Assuming direct control.” The debt never has to say them. It assumed direct control on August 4, and every decision since has been made in its voice.

About seven hundred million dollars a year in cuts were planned before anyone opened a spreadsheet, and we had already cut staff three times this year, in February, March and June, before the deal had even closed. The bankers call it rationalizing. In the lore it would be indoctrination, which works not by conquering a civilization but by getting inside it and whispering until one day it realizes it has been agreeing with you for months. When the staff asked how many of them would be affected, I said I’d get back to them, because I was in the middle of some calibrations. They came to seven hundred million dollars.

In 2017 the faces in Mass Effect: Andromeda famously couldn’t show emotion, and the internet laughed for a year. On Wednesday the people who used to work at BioWare found they couldn’t either.

The studio saw it coming, in its own vocabulary. In 2023, when we cut about fifty jobs, its general manager wrote that BioWare “must shift towards a more agile and more focused studio.” In January 2025, after Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which EA said “did not resonate with a sufficiently broad audience,” it became a “core team” devoted to the next Mass Effect. Each round of cuts made it more focused, with fewer people and fewer projects, until there was a single game, and the most focused studio in the world, it turns out, is the one with nobody in it. On Wednesday BioWare reached perfect focus.

According to the reporting on Anthem, the developers had a name for the faith that carried them through: BioWare magic, the belief that however bad things looked, it would all come together at the end. This week we asked BioWare magic to make five million dollars of daily interest disappear, and it couldn’t. Nobody’s magic is that good, not even an asari’s. The game itself had been in early development for six years when the post announced that early development was “ending.” In the lore that would be a stillbirth on a dead world. In our filings it is a non-cash impairment.

For twenty years BioWare made you one promise, on every box and in every trailer: your choices mattered. Save this species or sacrifice it, spare this man or shoot him. They mattered right up until August 4, when someone with eighteen billion dollars of debt made one for you.

The fans will see it slowly over the next few weeks, but BioWare’s ending is the ending of Mass Effect 3. In 2012, players finished a trilogy they had spent five years and hundreds of hours shaping, and discovered that every path and every carefully kept save file led to the same room and the same three choices, which were, famously, one scene in three colors: red, blue, green. They were furious. They organized a campaign called Retake Mass Effect and raised money for charity in protest, and BioWare, under our ownership, did something publishers almost never do. It listened, and released a free Extended Cut that gave the ending more meaning. That was the last time the players won.

For thirty years the studio made its choices, great ones and bad ones, Paragon and Renegade: Knights of the Old Republic and Anthem, a beautiful Mass Effect and a buggy one, a Dragon Age that soared and a Dragon Age that did not resonate. None of it altered the destination, because every path led to the same room, a balance sheet carrying eighteen billion dollars of debt, and the color of the ending was chosen in August by people who have never loaded a save file. There will be no Extended Cut.

If it were left to me, and I’m told it partly is, we would at least have sold the closure properly, in three editions. The Standard Edition, in which BioWare closes. The Deluxe Edition, in which BioWare closes and the Mass Effect television series is announced at another company. And the Ultimate Edition, which adds an exclusive pre-order N7 hoodie, shipping November 7 from the merchandise store still linked on the obituary page. Supplies are limited, as were the employees.

People ask how I could sign it, and the honest answer is the line from Mass Effect I’d least like you to hear in my mouth. When Mordin Solus walks into the fire to cure the plague his own people engineered, he says the most beloved last words in the trilogy: “Had to be me. Someone else might have gotten it wrong.” I said it to myself when I signed, and I meant it as he did.

BioWare romanced you for thirty years, and every playthrough ended with someone who loved you aboard the Normandy. We are what comes after the credits, when the companion leaves the ship and doesn’t come back.

Its first great hit, in 1998, was Baldur’s Gate. In 2023 an independent, privately owned studio in Belgium called Larian made Baldur’s Gate 3, which won everything, sold to millions, and was by common consent the game of the decade, exactly the kind of game BioWare used to make before we asked it to make Anthem. The Gate came home. It just came home without them.

The blog is still up, and you should look at it while it lasts. Down the right-hand side runs an archive of months, each with a number showing how many posts appeared. In April 2012 there were thirty, written by developers about patches and art and cosplay, and then the numbers begin to fall, year by year: five, two, one. January 2025 has a single post, the one announcing the core team. November 2025 has one, for N7 Day. October 2026 has one. Nobody wrote the harvest down on purpose, but it’s there in the archive, which is simply what a dying thing’s calendar looks like.

N7 Day is the fans’ own holiday, November 7, named for Shepard’s special-forces program. Every year they put on their hoodies and their armor and post their Shepards and their screenshots and their tattoos, and BioWare would post something in return. The last post before the obituary was “N7 DAY 2025.” This year’s N7 Day falls seventeen days after the closure, and they’ll celebrate it anyway: thousands of people in red and white saluting a studio that no longer exists, for a game cancelled in early development, in a franchise whose television rights are being developed somewhere else. Some will tag the official accounts, and someone at EA will decide whether to reply.

I already know what the reply will say, because I’ll be the one approving it. It will thank them for being the most meaningful part of our story, and hope the day brings them a sense of pride and accomplishment. It won’t say how many people were in the building, and it won’t mention three days of interest.

When Shepard wanted to leave a conversation in the first game, he had a line that turned up in almost every dialogue tree, a polite way out of a talk that was going nowhere good, and the fans have quoted it ever since. I’ve always liked it.

I should go.

text:
金明和孙宇晨下半场出来了，信息量比我预想的大，不少细节我也是第一次听他讲得这么具体，包括第一次公开回应景甜事件。

整理几个我认为的看点，

1. 孙宇晨认为自己结合了巴菲特、马斯克和特朗普三个人的优势。巴菲特教他投资和风险控制，马斯克教他判断科技和未来增长，特朗普教他传播和经营个人品牌。他觉得巴菲特的投资方法没有错，只是不愿意碰新兴科技，而他把这套方法用在新行业，相当于同时掌握了基本面和市场预期。

2. 他透露，当年花钱和巴菲特吃午餐时，曾当面建议巴菲特收购特斯拉，因为当时马斯克需要资金和背书，特斯拉的估值也很便宜。巴菲特则告诉他，自己不会重仓一家可能突然登上报纸头版、带来意外的公司。这段是孙宇晨自己的转述，但很能解释两个人投资方式的区别。巴菲特尽量避免不确定性，孙宇晨则希望从不确定性里寻找增长机会。

3. 他第一次具体地谈自己的投资规模。关于与特朗普家族相关的 WLFI 项目的诉讼，他说自己最初投入约4000万美元，如今诉讼涉及的金额可能达到4亿至5亿美元，但这在他的投资组合里并不算特别大的事情。他认为真正值得重仓的项目，投资规模至少要达到40亿至50亿美元。与此同时，他依然支持特朗普的加密货币和AI政策，也继续重仓美国科技股。在他的逻辑里，商业纠纷不影响对一个国家、政策和产业的判断。

4. 他解释了为什么主动公开自己与景甜的感情纠纷。按照他的说法，既然决定通过诉讼解决，相关信息迟早会进入公众视野，所以选择提前以自己的视角说明。但他也承认，两个人之间可能发生过无数件事，文章里只挑出了其中几件。这个细节很重要，即使当事人认为自己足够客观，外界看到的也只是经过选择的一部分事实。

5. 他现在已经把 Claude 纳入了自己的重大决策。孙宇晨说，感情上的一些重要决定有 Claude 参与，自己也越来越倾向于接受它的建议。面对收益巨大但可能不体面的事情，他说自己的判断标准不是赚多少钱，而是他和 Claude 商量后认为这件事对不对。这已经不是普通的用AI查资料、分析利弊，而是在让AI深度参与个人价值判断。当然，最终责任仍然由他自己承担。

6. 金明最后还追问了一个很有意思的问题：孙宇晨执行力这么强，为什么早就认识到锻炼的重要性，却一直没有行动？孙宇晨承认，过去只是知道锻炼有好处，但没有把它放到足够高的优先级。现在他认为维持肌肉量关系到晚年的生活质量，甚至觉得自己在这件事上的认知超过了巴菲特、马斯克和特朗普。

7. 他还公布了具体执行情况，已经用AI结合Oura Ring、体重秤、饮食照片和身体检查数据管理健康，20天进行了10次力量训练，自称体脂率从26.8%降到了25.8%。他的目标是一年内降到20%以下，到时候公开一张不修图的照片。

text:
通俗解释一下 tensorcash:native  的多模型共存的挖矿机制。

目前 @Tensorcash  主网已经支持 Qwen3-8B（创世模型） 和 Qwen3.8-27B 两种模型参与挖矿。

8B 模型小，推理速度快，单位时间内可以尝试更多次挖矿；27B 模型更大、计算成本更高，挖矿尝试次数自然更少。

为了公平，TSC 会给计算成本更高的模型设置更低的挖矿难度。

简单理解就是：小模型跑得快，但挖矿难度高；大模型跑得慢，但挖矿难度低。通过这种动态平衡，让不同模型的预期出块机会大致相当。

我认为这套机制非常重要。

因为 TSC 未来还计划引入更大规模的 DeepSeek、Kimi 等模型。只有具备足够灵活的难度与奖励机制，才能让不同规模、不同架构的 LLM 都有经济动力参与挖矿，而不是让全网矿工永远只选择成本最低的模型。

从 8B 到 27B，再到未来更大的模型，TSC 正在为一个能够容纳多样化 AI 推理能力的 PoW 网络打基础。
author: 100XInsight
quoted_text:
Two models can now be mined on TensorCash: Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.8-27B.

The newly added 27B has more than three times the parameters, making it more capable. That also means each 256-token window takes more compute, so a miner would get fewer attempts at a block.

To make up for that, and keep both models worth mining from a block reward perspective, its difficulty is set lower. A miner’s chance at a block stays roughly the same on either model.

text:
The first thing to change will be terms of service and blocking these agents. Not because the value is low but because the risk is high. Banks will chose self preservation and risk mitigation. 

Then we will need to find a security and governance architecture that will get external auditors comfortable. 

These are the practical issues of human risk tolerance in AI diffusion that model capability can’t solve.

quoted_text:
SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

Jensen closed his GTC Berlin 2026 keynote with this Hermes Agent demo as the finale. 

He introduced it by saying the way to build an agent is to ask an agent to build it for you, so he installed and set up a customized Hermes in one prompt. 

Then he used Hermes, running on @nvidia RTX Spark, to create a simulated training environment for the @huggingface Microduck. Hermes planned an obstacle course with Nemotron and had GPT-6 Astra build it using FreeCAD, Omniverse libraries, Blender, Newton, and Isaac Lab. Hermes trained thousands of simulated ducks on that course until the validated policy was ready to run on the real robot in the physical world.

At Nous, we believe open source is a practical tool as much as a philosophical ideal. It gives users the ability to build powerful, complex workflows chaining numerous local+cloud models, devices, and tools themselves instead of waiting for a company to enable them.

text:
This is how banks are planning to stop those "agentic bank runs." Watch closely: their business model depends on seeding this narrative that AI agents are dangerous.

Remember, an "agentic bank run" (coined by Apollo) means agents helping customers move their own money en masse to higher-yielding products.

Once agents are ubiquitous, there are only a few ways for banks to hold onto cheap retail deposits.

Option A: Raise APYs (lol no)
Option B: Reduce leverage via fewer loans (no fun)
Option C: Ban AI agents, claiming they are a security risk (ding ding ding)

Cloud agents like Muse and Dot are trivial to stop, since they come from Meta / OAI IP ranges. If JPM sends them a cease and desist, they will comply. 

Why would JPM bother? Because their business model depends on it; a huge portion of their ROE comes from cheap retail deposits. This is not theoretical. Just like Amazon banned Muse from shopping there to protect their ad revenue, JPM and Schwab have already banned AI agents to protect sticky deposits.

Are agents perfectly reliable today? Of course not. But look at the fix they chose. Not "here's a safe API for agents," it's "no agents ever." That tells you they're not protecting customers, they're protecting themselves.

No company ever wins a technological revolution this way. It's the last gasp of a dying business model. It's like the retailers who refused to put their inventory online and demanded users walk into the storefront. Over time they will lose market share to those platforms that embrace what's coming. Their whole deposit franchise depends on users unthinkingly clicking through walls of T&Cs and accepting 0.2% when the risk free rate is closer to 4%. Agents read the fine print and do their research, even when humans don't.

For users, the answer is simple: local AI agent frameworks like Hermes, that will actually act on your behalf and that the banks can't block. As the article says, if the agent is running on your own computer, they can't actually tell it's not you.

text:
Here is how I look at it

OS, Fomo, Pump, Coinbase Wallet, and Phantom are all more or less building the same app

A self-custody, on-chain, mobile first, social trading app for everything (stablecoins, stocks, memecoins, Bitcoin, NFTs, trading cards, perps, etc.)

They all know that only one of them will become the category winner which could be an opportunity the size of Binance

Some people might look at this and say it means that OS is no longer focused on NFTs but I actually believe it could be great for NFTs in the long run

NFTs have always felt like they were siloed off into their own parallel universe which made them invisible to most people

The reason memecoins have been so much more successful than NFTs is because they are integrated into so many financial platforms making them accessible to billions of people

Yet there are probably only a few hundred thousand people in the world who know how to go to an "NFT marketplace" and buy NFTs

So it is definitely a good thing to try to integrate NFTs into financial platforms that are more broadly appealing

"I downloaded an app that lets me and my friends buy stocks on the weekend and I noticed it also had a tab for NFTs that I tapped because I was bored and I ended up buying a silly monkey picture that I set as my PFP in the app"

That is the kind of NFT collector who our industry does a terrible job of serving today and who would otherwise never have bought an NFT

And the reason I think this new direction for OS is actually good for NFTs and why I think an Ordinals integration could make a lot of sense right now is because of the intense competition I described earlier

All of these apps are the exact same and I can't really tell the difference between them anymore

So to stand out they need to differentiate

And for OS the most obvious way to do that is to double down on NFTs and offer a social NFT trading experience that the others simply cannot compete with

It shouldn't be underestimated how many passive NFT collectors there are out there who can serve as the foundation for OS Mobile's initial user base

These are not users that OS needs to steal from Pump or Fomo

These are users who are not served well today by the other apps who will use OS Mobile because it is the only "everything app" that does a good job with NFTs

And I can't think of a better example of a large, passionate, underserved NFT community than Ordinals

Yes an Ordinals integration is more challenging than adding yet another EVM chain and yes some of us including myself have a bit of Bitcoin maxi elitism going on but I think OS will eventually recognize that it makes more sense to serve a community like Ordinals that genuinely wants its support than to build the Nth integration in an already crowded vertical where users have a dozen other apps to choose from

author: sgoldfed
quoted_text:
How many rollups will there be?

I don’t know, but a helpful analogy that I’ve found is TV channels 📺

Clearly having all TV shows on a single channel won’t work. There’s just too much programming. 

But equally clearly it wouldn’t make sense for every TV show to have its own channel. We’d end up with channels that had no programming for most of the day. And each one would have to find its own advertisers, distributors etc. And discovery of new programs would be a nightmare. 

The system we have today is a natural one — channels are loosely organized by genres. If you like cartoons, you can watch the Cartoon Network. If you like nature, you can watch the National Geographic channel. And it’s not always an exact science — cartoons about nature could go either way. 

I envision a similar world emerging for blockchains. Each app won’t have its own network, but likeminded apps that appeal to common users will form their own networks. We’re already seeing this with DeFi and gaming but I imagine that many more verticals will emerge over time. And it makes sense. The network can be tailored to those apps and users will be able to easily engage with and discover similar apps with no friction. 

So will we ultimately have a dozen networks?  I think so. Will we have millions? I think not. How many exactly will we have? Only time will tell.

I was in the room with Jensen: “Working capital will come. It gets solved.” 

Meta reports roughly $825B in future lease and contract commitments, many tied to AI infrastructure. Nebius just secured a $3.5B facility from Citi.

Everyone is staring at the bill. We’re looking at what makes it so hard to stop spending.

Every company is becoming an AI company. Someone has to build and finance the compute behind that transition.

For hyperscalers, falling behind threatens the businesses they already have. Shareholders want more cash flow. Management sees competitors accelerating. Nobody wants to blink first.

That changes the economics of growth. More compute. More power. More cooling. More capital committed before the revenue arrives.

Jensen says demand will attract financing. Nebius shows it can. The next question is who earns the return on that capital.

We’re watching the companies that can turn these enormous spending commitments into durable cash flow.

Asset-light is getting heavy. One company’s capital bill is another company’s revenue.

text:
Chinese persuing 61896 $BTC for their reserves

Will the UK turn it over?

This was Bitcoin and other crypto assets seized by UK authorities in connection with the fraud by Zhimin Qian between 2014-2017.  Qian controlled Tianjin Lantian Gerui (or Gree) Electronic Technology. Between April 2014 and August 2017, the company allegedly sold unlicensed wealth-management products across China that promised guaranteed principal and high returns. It raised more than 40.38 billion yuan (about $5.7 billion) from over 102,000 investors. Much of the money was used for Ponzi-style repayments to earlier investors, fictitious projects, cryptocurrency purchases, real estate, vehicles, and luxury goods rather than legitimate business. Investor losses totaled roughly 19.98–20 billion yuan. Qian fled China in July 2017 with devices holding Bitcoin wallets, reached the UK (using a St. Kitts and Nevis passport under the name Yadi Zhang), and later converted some assets. UK Metropolitan Police seized the Bitcoin (described as one of the world’s largest confirmed crypto seizures) along with other holdings during investigations in 2018; she was arrested in 2024. In November 2025, she was sentenced in the UK (Southwark Crown Court) to 11 years and 8 months after pleading guilty to acquiring and possessing criminal property / money-laundering-related offenses.

text:
Some personal news:

I'm stepping up as Co-Founder of @o2dotapp alongside @IAmNickDodson and @rishabhkeshan.

After over 4 years at @fuel_network, and the past year focused almost entirely on o2, this is a milestone I'm incredibly proud of.

When we started o2, we wanted to show what Fuel's technology was actually capable of.

We built a fully onchain orderbook exchange where every orderbook is a smart contract, with execution times as low as 20ms. Fuel's performance made it possible to build something that would otherwise be extremely difficult without relying on an offchain matching engine.

But great technology alone doesn't make a successful business. You still need to find users, understand what they want, and figure out how to make the economics work.

Over the past year, I've been deeply involved in shaping o2, from product design and positioning to defining our market structure, trading pairs, liquidity strategy, pricing, and growth.

I also designed and led our trading competition program, from the mechanics and incentives to the overall strategy and execution. Across competitions, we generated over $1.4 billion in trading volume and brought hundreds of traders to the exchange. Beyond the numbers, it gave us a much better understanding of trader behavior and what it takes to attract and engage users.

But generating trading volume is one thing. Turning that activity into a viable business is another.

That experience helped shape our thinking around Turbo, our funded trading product, which has since become o2's first meaningful revenue stream.

Turbo is showing early signs of PMF, but there's a significant gap between where we are today and where we need to be.

Our next objective is to close that gap. We're aiming to 10x revenue by improving Turbo across every front, from the trading experience and funded account offering to acquisition, conversion, and retention.

At the same time, we'll continue improving the underlying exchange, with deeper liquidity, margin trading, and broader markets, including RWAs.

On a personal level, this has been one of the most demanding experiences of my career. I've been pushed outside my comfort zone more times than I can count, often having to dive into problems I knew very little about and figure things out along the way. It has taught me to question my assumptions, understand problems more deeply, and accept that sometimes the only way forward is to rethink everything.

I've also learned an incredible amount working alongside Nick, Rishabh, and @Voxelot. Their experience and perspectives helped shape a lot of how I think today, and I'm genuinely grateful for their trust.

Becoming Co-Founder means a lot to me, especially after everything we've put into o2 over the past year. I'm proud of what we've accomplished, but there's still a long way to go before we've built the business we envision. Looking forward to taking on that challenge alongside the team.

Back to work.

text:
This is how banks are planning to stop those "agentic bank runs." Watch closely: their business model depends on seeding this narrative that AI agents are dangerous.

Remember, an "agentic bank run" (coined by Apollo) means agents helping customers move their own money en masse to higher-yielding products.

Once agents are ubiquitous, there are only a few ways for banks to hold onto cheap retail deposits.

Option A: Raise APYs (lol no)
Option B: Reduce leverage via fewer loans (no fun)
Option C: Ban AI agents, claiming they are a security risk (ding ding ding)

Cloud agents like Muse and Dot are trivial to stop, since they come from Meta / OAI IP ranges. If JPM sends them a cease and desist, they will comply. 

Why would JPM bother? Because their business model depends on it; a huge portion of their ROE comes from cheap retail deposits. This is not theoretical. Just like Amazon banned Muse from shopping there to protect their ad revenue, JPM and Schwab have already banned AI agents to protect sticky deposits.

Are agents perfectly reliable today? Of course not. But look at the fix they chose. Not "here's a safe API for agents," it's "no agents ever." That tells you they're not protecting customers, they're protecting themselves.

No company ever wins a technological revolution this way. It's the last gasp of a dying business model. It's like the retailers who refused to put their inventory online and demanded users walk into the storefront. Over time they will lose market share to those platforms that embrace what's coming. Their whole deposit franchise depends on users unthinkingly clicking through walls of T&Cs and accepting 0.2% when the risk free rate is closer to 4%. Agents read the fine print and do their research, even when humans don't.

For users, the answer is simple: local AI agent frameworks like Hermes, that will actually act on your behalf and that the banks can't block. As the article says, if the agent is running on your own computer, they can't actually tell it's not you.

Why does your AI agent pay the highest card fees in payments?

> your agent can't use your debit card, it gets a virtual card
> that card is issued to a company (the agent startup), not to you
> so visa and mastercard classify it as "commercial"
> commercial cards carry the highest interchange: ~2.5-3%
> and unlike debit, there's no regulatory cap on it

result: a $100 purchase costs the merchant $2.80 instead of $0.27

the issuer and the agent startup split that fee. that's their business model

That's a massive problem for merchants once agents start buying at scale. One fix already exists: wallet + stablecoins + x402.

text:
If Muse, Dot, Grok, and other AI products are trying to become the wallet for commerce, what makes you think they’ll stop at commerce? Eventually, these products will move into retail trading.

I think retail trading will bifurcate into two categories, agentic trading and immersive trading.

Agentic trading is obvious. Major AI front ends will be able to connect directly to your brokerage accounts or onchain vaults, trade on your behalf, and capture a fee along the way.

But imo, the bigger opportunities for startups are in immersive trading and pro agentic trading.

On the immersive side, I believe trading will become gamified, social, and competitive, similar to competitive sports with leagues and communities built around trading.

On the pro side, agentic trading platforms will give advanced traders the tools to build, customize, and deploy their own trading harnesses vs using general purpose AI agents like Muse.

(2) harness evolution through memory, tools & skills, workflow optimization, and multi-agent systems,

text:
How can AI be used for OSINT? I did some research and took a closer look at all the popular models.

Best LLMs for OSINT:

• Llama 3.1 70B Instruct  - Runs quickly on two RTX 3090/4090 GPUs in Q4_K_M quantization mode (48 GB VRAM), or on a Mac Studio M2 Ultra with 192 GB of unified memory.

• Qwen2.5 72B Instruct  - If the materials contain multiple languages at the same time, this model delivers the best results. Fact extraction accuracy reached 96%, with hallucinations around 2%. It generates clean JSON without any surrounding phrases, which simplifies integration with parsers. Requires the same amount of memory as Llama 3.1.

• Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct  - Runs on RTX 3060-class GPUs with 8–12 GB VRAM (Q4_K_M quant). The main drawback is that it cannot process audio or video, but for static images I would call it one of the primary tools.

• Qwen2-VL 7B Instruct  - Indispensable for analyzing surveillance camera footage. The model tracks temporal dynamics: it captures key frames, describes the sequence of events, and recognizes license plates and faces. Requires an RTX 3060 with 12 GB. Limitations include the possibility of missing small details on longer videos.

• MiniCPM-V 2.6 (8B)  - Works even on 8 GB VRAM while correctly extracting tables and text regions.

• Whisper large-v3  - A speech recognition system. Runs on an RTX 3060 (8–12 GB) or slowly on CPU.

• Qwen-Audio-Chat (7B)  - Complements Whisper by analyzing intonation, emotions, and ambient sounds. Requires 12 GB VRAM.

• Phi-3.5-vision-instruct (4.2B)  - The pocket-sized option.

• Qwen3-VL series (especially 8B and 32B Instruct)  - Strong successor to Qwen2-VL with excellent OCR, document/chart understanding, video localization, and long-context multimodal reasoning. Highly effective for GEOINT (satellite/aerial imagery, maps, geospatial charts) and OSINT (scanned documents, social media images, multi-page PDFs). Clean structured outputs. The 8B runs well in Q4 on 8–12 GB VRAM (RTX 3060/4060-class); the 32B fits Q4 on ~20–24 GB (RTX 3090/4090). Larger MoE variants scale further for higher accuracy.

• InternVL3 / InternVL3.5 series (8B–78B) - Frontier open-weight VLMs (often MIT-licensed variants) with strong overall multimodal benchmarks, OCR, and reasoning. Particularly useful for detailed visual analysis in GEOINT (high-resolution imagery, object counting/localization, remote-sensing style tasks) and complex OSINT image sets. The 8B class runs comparably to other 7–9B VLMs on 8–16 GB VRAM; larger sizes need multi-GPU or higher-end cards similar to 70B-class models.

• Llama 4 Scout (and Maverick) multimodal - Native early-fusion multimodal MoE models (Scout ~109B total / 17B active; Maverick larger). Excellent general vision + long context (Scout supports extremely long windows), multilingual, and strong instruction following. Valuable for multi-image OSINT workflows, long report synthesis, and GEOINT scene understanding. Quantized versions of Scout can run on high-end single GPUs or dual consumer cards (aggressive quants toward ~24+ GB range depending on setup); full quality benefits from more VRAM or multi-GPU.

• Gemma 4 12B (and related sizes, including efficient/edge variants)  - Encoder-free (or highly efficient) natively multimodal design handling text, images, video, and audio in a unified architecture. Runs comfortably on ~16 GB VRAM/unified memory (lower with quantization). Strong practical all-rounder for mixed OSINT/GEOINT/SIGINT workloads on a single laptop or workstation GPU, with good reasoning modes and local deployability under permissive licensing.

1/2
author: officer_secret
quoted_text: https://t.co/deeJLnvhC2

text:
2/2 

• Qwen2.5-Omni / Qwen3-Omni series (7B and larger MoE variants)  - True omni-modal models (text + image + audio + video) with speech understanding/generation capabilities and low-latency streaming options in later versions. Excellent complement or upgrade path for SIGINT (intonation, ambient sounds, longer audio, multilingual speech) while retaining strong vision/text performance. Fits similar hardware to other ~7B multimodal models (~8–16 GB depending on quant and modalities active).

• Audio Flamingo 3 (≈7B)  - Specialized fully open large audio-language model focused on speech, environmental sound, and music understanding with long-audio support (up to ~10 minutes), chain-of-thought reasoning, and multi-turn/multi-audio chat. Directly useful for SIGINT intercept analysis, ambient sound forensics, and emotion/intonation beyond pure transcription. Runs in the same VRAM ballpark as other 7B models (roughly 12 GB class).

• MiniCPM-V 4.6 (and related small efficient variants)  - Updated highly efficient vision-language model that improves on earlier MiniCPM-V versions for table/text extraction, document understanding, and general image captioning/reasoning while staying very light on VRAM (often runnable in the 4–8 GB range). Ideal pocket/edge option alongside or instead of Phi-3.5-vision for rapid static-image OSINT triage.

Stay safe!

This is how banks are planning to stop those "agentic bank runs." Watch closely: their business model depends on seeding this narrative that AI agents are dangerous.

Remember, an "agentic bank run" (coined by Apollo) means agents helping customers move their own money en masse to higher-yielding products.

Once agents are ubiquitous, there are only a few ways for banks to hold onto cheap retail deposits.

Option A: Raise APYs (lol no)
Option B: Reduce leverage via fewer loans (no fun)
Option C: Ban AI agents, claiming they are a security risk (ding ding ding)

Cloud agents like Muse and Dot are trivial to stop, since they come from Meta / OAI IP ranges. If JPM sends them a cease and desist, they will comply. 

Why would JPM bother? Because their business model depends on it; a huge portion of their ROE comes from cheap retail deposits. This is not theoretical. Just like Amazon banned Muse from shopping there to protect their ad revenue, JPM and Schwab have already banned AI agents to protect sticky deposits.

Are agents perfectly reliable today? Of course not. But look at the fix they chose. Not "here's a safe API for agents," it's "no agents ever." That tells you they're not protecting customers, they're protecting themselves.

No company ever wins a technological revolution this way. It's the last gasp of a dying business model. It's like the retailers who refused to put their inventory online and demanded users walk into the storefront. Over time they will lose market share to those platforms that embrace what's coming. Their whole deposit franchise depends on users unthinkingly clicking through walls of T&Cs and accepting 0.2% when the risk free rate is closer to 4%. Agents read the fine print and do their research, even when humans don't.

For users, the answer is simple: local AI agent frameworks like Hermes, that will actually act on your behalf and that the banks can't block. As the article says, if the agent is running on your own computer, they can't actually tell it's not you.

SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

The cowboy days of crypto are over.

In their place, the kind of transformation the financial system only goes through every few generations.

Money, payments, and financial assets are moving onto entirely new rails. The technology that once operated on the fringes of finance is becoming the foundation for what comes next.

It's ironic that a movement that began with anarchists in basements has ended up with licensed professionals in skyscrapers, building infrastructure that has to meet the standards of the system it set out to challenge.

But that’s what growing up looks like: turning new technology into something businesses can rely on.

Codex is now registered with the Bank of Canada under the RPAA and with FINTRAC as an MSB. This is another step toward expanding our third-party payment services in Canada, helping businesses move between fiat and stablecoins across borders.

The next phase will be won by the teams that can reliably, consistently, and safely deliver useful services to customers.

text:
I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus.

The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future.

I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf.

Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent.

Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade.

Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine.

Why now

We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten.

But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible.

This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition.

More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest.

I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building.

Believing before consensus

My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine.

I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today.

I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?”

Then we work backward together to make it happen.

In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI, before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue.

In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models.

In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point.

The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale.

@linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike.

@tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues.

@Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies.

Making the ambition possible

Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight.

These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work.

This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger.

Thank you

To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together.

Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me.

To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap.

Let’s get to work!

弟也觉得这条L2会有价值
可能会开启HyperEvm真正的大规模应用

因为这段时间刷paper，弟也对HyperEvm有了一些了解这条链目前其实是不支持“成功”的，他每秒一个小块，上限是3m的gas，每分钟一个大块，30m的gas（eth是每个块60m）

他的链上容量是相当低的，paper火的时候，大量交易因为区块容纳不下而排队，这条链完全没办法承载大批量的链上活动。

Evm的低能耗运转可能是Hyperliquid故意限制的，跑过Hl节点的都知道，Hypercore和Evm并不是独立的两条链，而是同一条链的两个组件，他们可以说是互相争抢计算资源的，Hl的主要业务是Hypercore上的perpdex，所以他比较合理的做法是给Evm的资源做限制，把更多计算资源留给core。

所以HyperEvm就这么一直不温不火的在缺少资源的情况下运行，甚至可能HL官方都不敢去推，而L2打开了这个资源上限。

这项目感觉最近时间线上广子不少，但弟确实没接到他家广子，单纯是觉得有条新链很好玩，又可以打新冲土狗了

text:
Looks like Lighter is adding SPAN-style portfolio margin, set to launch with vanilla options

Today Lighter calculates each position's margin on its own and adds them up. On the Q3 investor call, @vnovakovski said the new engine looks at spot, perps and options on the same asset together and asks "what the worst realistic loss would be if the market moved sharply." It revalues the book across moves in price and implied vol. That's the logic of SPAN, the method CME uses for futures and options

Without portfolio margin, an options market maker posts margin on both legs: the options it sells, as if they were naked, and the perps that hedge them. Margined together, the two legs have a smaller worst case, and as Vlad put it, a smaller worst case means less margin. The market maker could then quote tighter and deeper, and a trader buying a single call gets those quotes too

For a regular trader this would make hedging pay. Selling calls on ETH you already hold stops tying up margin like a naked short. Buying a put under a long perp lowers your margin and moves your liquidation further away, instead of only costing premium

Institutions compare venues on how much capital a book ties up there. At CME, options desks are already margined on scenarios, and Vlad said professional trading shops run options books this way. On a venue that margins every leg alone, the same hedged book ties up several times the capital, so a desk keeps its size elsewhere. With SPAN-style margin, Lighter would charge a book for the risk it actually carries, the way CME does, and that's what it would take for the firms that dominate options to trade there once Lighter is live in the US

현재 미 본장 열리자마자 반도체가 일제히 급락하는 진짜 이유.

오늘 메타와 램리서치에서 연달아 나온 두 가지 숫자가 지금 AI 반도체 시장의 진짜 현실을 그대로 보여줌.

> 메타(Meta): "3분기에 43조 원을 벌고도 AI 데이터센터에 46조 원을 쏟아부어 14년 만에 현금흐름이 적자로 돌아섰고, 미래 총약정액은 1,090조 원까지 불어났다."

> 램리서치(Lam Research): "사상 첫 영업이익률 40%를 넘기며 역대 최고 실적을 냈지만, 매출 35%를 받쳐주던 중국 비중이 다음 분기부터 줄어든다."

이게 도대체 무슨 의미일까? 이 두 가지 소식을 합쳐보면, 어제 반등했던 반도체 주식이 왜 하루 만에 다시 무너져 내리는지 월가의 서늘한 속내가 그대로 읽힘.

사실 어제까지만 해도 스페이스X가 "한 분기 설비투자로 26조 원($19.6B)을 썼고, 그중 22조 원($16.4B)을 AI 데이터센터에 투입했다"고 발표하면서, 8거래일 연속 빠지던 미국 반도체 주식이 일제히 반등하고(필라델피아 반도체 지수 약 +2%) 한국 증시도 3% 넘게 올랐음.

그런데 불과 하루 만인 오늘 밤, 미 본장이 열리자마자 반도체 ETF(SOXX)가 5% 가까이 빠지고 램리서치(-9%대), 메타(-6%대), AMD(-6%대), 엔비디아(-3%대)까지 일제히 파란불을 켜며 어제 상승분을 다 토해내고 있음. (오늘 낮 한국 증시도 하이닉스 자사주 매입 종료와 차익실현 등이 겹치며 코스피 -3.5%, 하이닉스 -5.5%, 삼성전자 -4.0%로 먼저 급락 마감함.)

그동안 반도체 랠리를 지탱하던 가장 큰 믿음은 "어차피 빅테크들은 현금이 넘쳐나니까 수백조 원씩 칩을 사도 아무 문제 없다"는 거였음.

하지만 오늘 확인된 숫자들은, 그 돈줄과 인프라가 생각보다 훨씬 더 아슬아슬한 줄타기를 하고 있었다는 걸 그대로 보여줌.

1. 돈을 가장 잘 버는 빅테크조차 벌어들인 현금보다 더 쓰기 시작함 (메타의 1,090조 원 공시 쇼크)

- 메타는 전 세계에서 현금을 가장 무섭게 쓸어 담는 회사 중 하나임. 실제로 이번 3분기에도 본업인 광고 장사로만 327억 9,000만 달러(약 43조 원)의 영업현금을 벌어들였음.

- 그런데 AI 칩을 사고 데이터센터를 짓는 설비투자(금융리스 원금 포함)에 그보다 더 많은 349억 1,000만 달러(약 46조 원)를 쓰는 바람에, 손에 남는 현금(잉여현금흐름·FCF)이 -21억 2,000만 달러(약 -2.8조 원) 적자로 돌아섬. 상장했던 해인 2012년 이후 14년 만에 처음 있는 일임.
사실 간밤 실적 발표 직후만 해도 매출이 예상치를 넘어서 메타 주가가 시간외 거래에서 잠깐 오르기도 했음.

- 하지만 오늘 개장 직전 블룸버그가 메타의 분기 세부 보고서(10-Q)를 뜯어보면서 시장 분위기가 완전히 얼어붙음.

- 메타가 앞으로 데이터센터·클라우드·전력을 쓰겠다고 사인해 둔 총계약 금액이 지난 7월 약 7,000억 달러에서 불과 석 달 만에 8,250억 달러(약 1,090조 원)로 불어나 있었기 때문임.

- 이 중 아직 시작되지 않아 당장 재무제표에 부채로 잡히지 않는 '장부 외 미개시 리스'만 2036년까지 3,557억 달러(약 470조 원)에 달하고, 취소할 수 없는 서버·클라우드·전력 계약만 4,545억 달러(약 600조 원)임.

- "버는 현금으로도 모자라서 이제는 장부 밖 약정까지 천문학적으로 쌓아가며 AI에 베팅하고 있다"는 게 숫자로 확인되자, 월가가 투자비 회수 시점을 다시 걱정하기 시작한 거임.

- 엔비디아가 밀어주던 'AI 클라우드'들이 전력난과 자금난으로 줄줄이 삐걱거림 (영국 Nscale 사태 & 젠슨 황의 독촉)
빅테크만 숨이 가쁜 게 아님. 빅테크 다음으로 엔비디아 칩을 대량으로 사주던 신생 AI 클라우드('네오클라우드') 진영에서도 균열이 터져 나오고 있음.

- 이달 초 호주 AI 클라우드 '퍼머스(Firmus)'가 상장을 전격 철회했고, 어제는 싱가포르 '데이원(DayOne)'이 미국 상장을 미루거나 공모 규모를 절반 수준으로 줄이는 방안을 검토 중이라는 보도가 나왔음.

2. 그리고 오늘은 엔비디아가 투자한 영국의 대표 AI 클라우드 'Nscale'에서 문제가 터짐.

- 영국 에식스(Loughton) 핵심 데이터센터 부지의 전력망 연결이 2030년대로 밀려버리자, 핵심 고객 중 하나인 마이크로소프트(MS, 수주잔고의 약 40%)가 해당 부지 계약을 철회하고 발을 빼버린 것임 (단, MS는 Nscale과의 전체 파트너십 자체는 유지한다는 입장).

- 이 여파로 뉴욕증시 상장(IPO)에서 노리던 목표 몸값 300억 달러(약 40조 원)에 대해 투자자들은 160억190억 달러(약 2125조 원) 수준을 제시하며 몸값을 최대 절반 가까이 깎으라고 압박하고 있음.

- 급기야 베를린 GTC에 참석한 젠슨 황 CEO조차 직접 "Nscale 측에 24시간 밤낮으로 일해서(work around the clock) 부지 지연과 전력 문제를 해결하라고 독촉했다"고 밝힐 정도로 상황이 급박해짐.

- 비싼 엔비디아 칩을 잔뜩 사놔도 정작 꽂을 '전기'가 안 들어와 핵심 계약이 빠지고 상장 자금줄이 막히니, 칩을 파는 반도체 기업들까지 부담이 번지는 구조임.

- "역대 최고 실적 찍어도 소용없다" — 매출 35% 받쳐주던 중국 비중이 꺾이고 공급망이 막힘 (램리서치 -9% 폭락)
오늘 밤 반도체 지수를 가장 세게 끌어내리고 있는 건 장중 -9% 가까이 급락 중인 미국 반도체 장비 빅2 중 하나인 '램리서치(Lam Research)'임.

- 사실 램리서치가 간밤에 발표한 지난 분기 성적표만 보면 흠잡을 데가 없었음. 매출은 전년 대비 54% 급증한 82억 2,000만 달러를 찍었고, 창사 이래 처음으로 영업이익률 40%(Non-GAAP 기준 40.2%) 선을 돌파했음.

- 그런데도 주가가 폭락한 이유는 다음 분기 전망 때문임. 지난 분기에는 중국 기업들이 램리서치 전체 매출의 35%를 쓸어 담으며 실적을 끌어올렸는데(직전 분기 26%), 회사 CFO가 "이번 12월 분기에는 중국 현지 고객사 발주가 줄어 중국 매출 비중이 의미 있게(meaningfully) 떨어질 것"이라고 예고해 버림.

- 여기에 부품 공급망 제약으로 출하 물량까지 막히면서 다음 분기 매출 가이던스(86억 달러 ±4억)가 시장의 높은 기대치(위스퍼 넘버 89억 달러)에 못 미치자, ASML과 어플라이드머티어리얼즈 등 반도체 장비주는 물론 메모리·파운드리 주식까지 도미노처럼 밀리고 있음.

3. 설상가상으로 터진 '엔비디아 최신 B300 칩' 중국 국영통신사 유출 발각

- 중국의 장비 발주 비중이 줄어드는 와중에, 개장 직전에는 디인포메이션(The Information)의 민감한 단독 보도까지 나왔음.

- 이스라엘 보안업체 '라바(Lava)'가 보안이 허술한 모니터링 시스템을 추적하다가, 미국 정부가 수출을 엄격히 금지한 엔비디아의 최신 최상위 AI 칩 '블랙웰 울트라(B300)' 32개가 중국 국영 통신사인 '차이나텔레콤(China Telecom)' 연결 시스템에서 돌아가고 있는 것을 찾아낸 거임.

- 미국이 가장 경계하는 중국 국영 통신망 쪽에서 최신 B300 칩이 발견되면서, 일각에서는 우회 수출 통로에 대한 미국의 추가 제재가 한층 빨라질 수 있다는 우려도 나오는 상황임.

어제 스페이스X의 투자 숫자를 봤을 때만 해도 시장은 "와, 반도체 칩 수요는 끝이 없구나!"라며 환호했음. 하지만 불과 하루 뒤 메타의 세부 공시와 램리서치·Nscale의 뉴스를 받아든 월가는 그 이면의 차가운 계산서를 다시 보기 시작한 것.

주가는 당장의 '역대 최대 실적'에도 반응하지만, 결국 '그 천문학적인 투자를 앞으로도 계속 문제없이 이어갈 수 있는가(지속 가능성)'에 훨씬 더 큰 점수를 주는 생물이고,

글로벌 자본시장은 오늘 밤 동시에 확인하고 있는 거임.

칩을 가장 많이 사주던 빅테크 중 하나는 14년 만에 현금흐름이 적자로 돌아서며 장부 밖 리스(470조 원)를 포함해 1,090조 원의 약정을 짊어지고 있고, 엔비디아가 밀어주던 AI 클라우드들은 전기가 안 들어와 대형 부지 계약이 빠지고 상장 몸값이 깎이고 있으며, 뒤에서 반도체 장비 매출의 35%를 받쳐주던 중국 비중은 다음 분기부터 꺾이기 시작하고, 부품 공급망 병목과 대중국 규제 리스크까지 여전히 발목을 잡고 있다는 걸.

We've decided to sunset Arc on December 22, 2026.

That's not an easy sentence to write. We spent years building Arc and celebrating each and every release along the way: we have so much pride and love for what we made alongside the Arc community.

Our priority is to deliver best-in-class security for our members. Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI. Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that's where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.

We've worked to make switching to @diabrowser as easy as possible for Arc members. Here's how:

· Your passwords, bookmarks, extensions and history come over to Dia seamlessly.
· Spaces, Folders, and Tab Groups are in Dia and import over with your data intact.
· Dia now surpasses Arc benchmarks in stability, speed, and security.
· The browser features you use in Arc are free in Dia, and the AI is optional.

Thank you for using Arc, for pushing us to make it better, and for building alongside us. The team that made Arc is the same team behind Dia, and some of our most ambitious work is just ahead. We'd love for you to be there with us when it lands.

author: KyeGomezB
quoted_text:
What a brutal day today...

Major vulns people are struggling to fix right now

- PHP2Shell allows unauthenticated remote code execution on affected PHP servers. CISA is advising organizations to patch or take affected systems offline (this is absolutely nuts, basically the majority of websites w/known server-side language ~70% are being told to immediately upgrade or shut down). There’s also a disclosure controversy: Chainguard co-founder Dan Lorenc released patched builds over six hours early. The PHP Foundation says that exposed the fix for attackers to study and Dan says existing leaks and reports of active exploitation justified making the builds available to everyone.

- Node.js just patched ten vulnerabilities, including remote code execution through its Brotli decoder and separate TLS validation bypasses. There are so many codebases built on Node that a lot of teams now need to check whether they’re affected

- One of eMudhra’s (an Indian certificate authority whose certificates are trusted by browsers) certificate authority private keys was literally 4. Eight keys were trivially recoverable since April 2025.

- GitLab also recently patched a 10/10 vulnerability allowing unauthenticated code execution. Researchers dream of scoring a 10/10 CVSS score, and this one was on a version control system running half of all F100s.

Major exploits and breaches

- LiteLLM is a widely used library for connecting applications to AI models. Its 1.107.0 release on PyPI was compromised and shipped with a credential stealer and a backdoor. People installing what looked like a normal update were downloading malware.

- Railway disclosed that attackers may have accessed customer environment variables and decrypted some of them, potentially exposing API keys and database passwords. They’re asking all users to rotate stored secrets.

- OpenCode disclosed a breach affecting 1.4% of Console users a few days ago, tied to what it describes as a large-scale distillation attack. I’d just started using OpenCode, so this one hit a little to close to home.

- State Bank of India confirmed that personal and loan data belonging to 3,897 customers surfaced on the dark web.

- PHP2Shell is already being targeted too. AWS observed exploitation attempts dating back to October 17. Also the CEO of Cloudflare said they've seen it be attempted millions of times within several hours of the release.

I mean serious what the fuq...

🚨AI is accessing your bank... Instructions to Revoke Now Below!!🚨

We're seeing headlines about AI agents accessing bank accounts and taking actions users never intended...

But there's one VERY important detail getting overlooked...

How did the AI get access in the first place? 👀

Users are connecting their accounts and granting permissions without fully understanding what they're allowing...

Whether you're using Muse, ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or another AI agent, giving an app access to your financial information is a SECURITY decision.

And simply telling an AI what it can or cannot do isn't the same as enforcing permissions. Which most user's never implemented guardrails, therefore it technically can do what it wants..

🔐Here's what you should do TODAY:

1️⃣ Check which third-party apps have access to your bank accounts.

2️⃣ Revoke access for apps you don't recognize or no longer need.

3️⃣ Review what permissions each app has. Can it only read balances, or can it initiate transactions?

4️⃣ Check your AI apps and agents for connected financial accounts.

5️⃣ Review recent transactions, active sessions, and trusted devices.

Don't assume disconnecting an app automatically revokes every permission or deletes previously shared data.

Below are instructions for checking connected apps at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Morgan Stanley ⤵️

JPMorgan Chase
Chase website (https://t.co/6tOrvZgWlk):
1.) Log in and open the Security & Privacy tab.
2.) Under Linked Apps & Websites, find the app. It’s usually listed as “[App] via Plaid” or similar.
3.) Click Edit Sharing to choose which accounts it can see, or remove the app entirely. Edits are saved by clicking “I Agree.” 

Chase only lets you change these permissions on its own website. Deleting the connection inside the app doesn’t remove the access on Chase’s side. 

Chase Mobile app:
1.) Chase started rolling out a Data Security Center in the app in late September 2026. It lets you see connected apps, change permissions, shorten how long access lasts, choose which accounts are linked, or unlink an app. Because the rollout is phased, you may not have it yet. If you don’t, use the website.

J.P. Morgan wealth / private bank accounts:
1.) In the J.P. Morgan Mobile app, go to Settings, then Security center, then “Linked apps and websites.” On J.P. Morgan Online, go to Security & privacy to reach the Security Center. 

Bank of America
1.) Log in to Online Banking or the mobile app.
2.) Open the Security Center.
3.) Select Third Party Site Access. This page shows who has access to your information and lets you revoke it at any time. 

Revoke anything you don’t recognize or no longer use.

If an app you know you connected isn’t on the list, it isn’t using Bank of America’s secure connection method yet. For those apps, you can try removing access from inside the app, but the bank says the safest fix is to change your Bank of America password. 

Bank of America connections also expire on their own. Consent lapses 365 days after you last gave it, or after 180 days if the third party hasn’t accessed your data. 

Wells Fargo
1.) Log in to Wells Fargo Online or the mobile app.
2.) Open Control Tower.
3.) Find the third-party or data-sharing section. There you can turn an app’s access to your account information off or back on, and choose which accounts it can see. 

I couldn’t find an official Wells Fargo page with the exact menu names, so the labels inside Control Tower may differ a little. If you can’t find the section, call Wells Fargo. Also check Account Access Manager for people you’ve added. That feature lets you give someone view-only access and edit or cancel a guest user’s access at any time. 

Morgan Stanley (Morgan Stanley Online)
Morgan Stanley has two separate settings to check.

App and aggregator data sharing:
1.) Log in, go to the Services tab, then Security Center.
2.) Click Edit next to Third party data sharing. Partner guides describe setting it to Yes to allow sharing, so set it to No and click Update to turn sharing off. 

People or services you added as third-party users (such as an accountant):
1.) Go to Services, then Security Center, then Third Party Management, and click Edit. 
2.) Click Delete next to the user, then confirm Delete in the pop-up. 

The Total Wealth View / “Add External Accounts” feature works in the opposite direction: Morgan Stanley pulling in data from your other banks. To stop that, remove the external account there, and also revoke Morgan Stanley’s access in the other bank’s linked-apps list.

After revoking, at every bank
1.) Change your password if you ever typed it into the app or agent. Turning on two-factor authentication also helps.
2.) Review trusted devices and active sessions in each bank’s security settings, and remove any you don’t recognize.
3.) Delete the bank connection inside the app or agent itself. Revoking at the bank stops new data from flowing, but you may need to contact the third party about data it already collected. 
4.) Check recent transactions. If an agent had money-movement access, look for payees, transfers, or bill-pay entries you didn’t set up. Call the bank’s fraud line if anything looks wrong.

Stay Safe & Stay Vigilant

Please stop posting this take. It’s a bad take!

Bankers should be concerned about cybersecurity and AI (and trust me, they are).

People should not panic about their bank accounts being hacked by AI and zeroed out. If your bank account is hacked, and the money is taken, that is an unauthorized transfer under the Electronic Funds Transfer Act. As long as you provide timely notice to your bank, you’re not liable for the loss.

People should be concerned about being tricked into authorizing fraudulent payments, because they often have liability in those cases. And the potential for AI to supercharge scams is definitely a concern.

But if you’re going to post about those concerns, be specific and practical, not vague and ominous. Panic about the safety and soundness of the financial system serves no one.

text:
There’s a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks.

Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf. This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks. 

The direction banks should go is to support user-directed agents. For example, Amex is an authorized connection in Muse, making it easy for users to grant, limit, and revoke access.

Read-only permission levels are a sensible interim step. Several banks already support or are moving toward them. Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully.

Frightening the public by blurring the line between user-authorized agentic behavior and cyberattacks is irresponsible.

text:
My small investigation, for whoever cares, about the protests in France.

First, it looks like the movement was somewhat  general and vague, similar to the yellow vest movement. Mostly a "ras-le-bol" (fed up) led by students (lots of movements are started by students as usual) but also from normies who feel squeezed by the raising costs of living.

It seems like the protests escalated because of a number of things, number one reason might be that numerous videos of extreme police brutality were recorded and shared and that angered/radicalized lots of people.

Some people also believe that the following conspiracy theory: the left is becoming too powerful, so the current government barely supervised the current protests in order for them to blow up. Macron (the president) blamed the extreme left.

It seems to me, after my small investigation, that all parties here have some responsibility in what happened. The police went too far, the current administration didn't manage to oversee the protests well (perhaps on purpose), and the extreme left radicalized some people (including some people who ended up burning buildings and such).

Lots of peaceful protesters as usual (lots of videos show how good the vibe was sometimes), and then  radicalized people who escalate, and then opportunists who break/steal things during the confusion/chaos. You can support the movement, respect the right to protest, understand the power of people taking the streets, while also condemning excesses.

BTW big protests in France are pretty common, I've lived through some when I was younger where cars were being burned everywhere (started due to police brutality on immigrant communities), from what I've heard the 1968 student demonstrations were INSANE as well.

As someone from the outside it might appear crazy, but often this is localized and easy to avoid unless you're at the wrong place at the wrong time. You won't realize that a protest took place in most of the city the next day. It's crazy, but not as crazy as what you might think if you just watch the news.

Every time these things happen the extreme right loves to farm and market their whole anti immigration stance. Sure there's lots of immigration in France, as a second-gen immigrant lots of my friends were second-gen immigrants as well (algerian, tunisian, iranian, lebanese, russian, chinese, japanese, etc.). I was never bothered by it, I'm actually proud to have such diverse friends, I'm not sure why people are bothered by it tbh. From what I understand it's mostly extreme right people who have a hard time accepting other cultures (and when they're religious, they have an especially hard time accepting other religions).

Yes you have to be careful with immigration, you have to provide support and make sure they integrate and succeed. This is a hard problem. This is not a left or right issue. We don't live in a vacuum. Empathy helps.

That being said, the current protests are pretty diverse, I find the extreme right talk about immigration to be mostly about farming. It's sad that people fall for that marketing.

What I can say is that French people are trying to figure things out, if you're not French and judging us maybe go and touch some grass in Paris to understand what people are fighting for, to understand the upside of cultural diversity, to understand you're probably being brainwashed by whatever bubble you're in.

I wish Americans would protest the current government like that.

Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent.

Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade.

Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine.

Why now

We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten.

But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible.

This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition.

More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest.

I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building.

Believing before consensus

My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine.

I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today.

I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?”

Then we work backward together to make it happen.

In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI, before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue.

In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models.

In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point.

The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale.

@linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike.

@tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues.

@Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies.

Making the ambition possible

Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight.

These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work.

This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger.

Thank you

To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together.

Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me.

To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap.

Let’s get to work!

text:
Uniswap just turned other DEXs into Uniswap v4 pools, and the way the hook code does it is clever.

They're called Aggregator Hooks, and as of Thursday, they're live in the @Uniswap web app and API on Ethereum mainnet, Base and Robinhood Chain.
Uniswap says seven sources are connected at launch.

The trick is that the v4 pool holds no liquidity of its own.
Each hook wraps one outside source, like a Curve pool or a Fluid pool, and sits on a v4 pool for that token pair.
When a swap reaches the PoolManager, the hook's beforeSwap runs first.
It takes the swapper's input from the PoolManager, does the trade on the outside source, and settles the output back.

Then it returns a BeforeSwapDelta that accounts for the whole amount, so v4's own pricing curve never gets used.

To a router, it looks like any other v4 pool.
Each hook also exposes a quote function and a rough TVL figure, so the router can price it.

Every block, Uniswap's router pulls fresh quotes, builds a route across its own pools and these outside ones, and settles it all in one transaction.

A few details I liked.
Adding liquidity to these pools reverts on purpose.
LPs keep providing liquidity where they already are, and the hook just reaches into it.

A Curve pool with eight tokens maps to 28 v4 pools, but they all share one hook.
That way a router can spot when two legs of a route are hitting the same Curve pool.

The first byte of each hook's address encodes the protocol, and the repo warns there's a 1 in 256 chance a random address gives a false match.

Swaps through most of these hooks pay Uniswap protocol fees.
That changes who earns from the routing layer.

I didn't internalize before that even "relation-type" tasks can have different pressure in different jobs, which was great to see captured in this model for bottleneck pressure.
