author: soubhikdeb
quoted_text:
Very happy to share a new paper, “Technology Bottlenecks: Measuring Where AI Could Raise the Value of Work It Cannot Yet Do.”

AI exposure measures ask about the work AI is capable of doing. We ask instead where the marginal value of work AI cannot yet do may rise as AI speeds up the rest of the job.

To do so, we employ 288 million U.S. job postings mapped line by line to their closest O*NET tasks and GPT-4 feasibility ratings from Eloundou et al. (2024) to construct a measure, “bottleneck pressure,” for each task in each occupation that posts it. 

Using a simple task-based framework, we derive this pressure at the task level, showing that for an AI-infeasible task it is the exposure of the occupation that posts it, so the same task can face very different bottleneck pressure in different jobs.

Reporting bottleneck pressure alongside AI exposure shows both the scope for AI to perform work and where improving the work it cannot do may pay off more as capabilities expand.

text:
An underrated fact about production ML is that LLMs mostly reach the highest-volume decisions indirectly, through offline labels, features, and caches.  Most ranking, recommendations currently mostly run on gradient boosting, small classifiers, and rerankers, with LLMs on the side as precomputed features, cached rewrites, or prefill-only scorers. Generating a response while the user waits has simply been too slow for a tens-of-milliseconds budget unless users consume the outputs directly. This will change soon:

Most of open inference stacks has been built for a very different regime, and for good reason: for many enterprises, models that can solve open-ended problems agentically have been the fastest route to value. But what about everything else? There, large foundation models often fall short. They’re too slow and too expensive to sit in the critical path. So historically, we’ve often used precomputed features and offline caches, which come with their own problems (Staleness, cache misses, pipeline explosion). 

Briefly, here’s what’s in this space today (largely ignoring offline approaches):

- Small (<10B) prefill-only scoring LLMs
- Rerankers
- LightGBM / other gradient-boosted tree methods
- Small classifiers (e.g., Jev and other decision models, but these have limitations too)

These models are all fast, but with limited expressivity, i.e., categorical scores/labels can’t always produce the best answer for every workload.

The benefit of high-concurrency, low-latency decode is the additional information full-sequence decode can provide (e.g., a rewritten query or structured filters instead of a single score). This also makes post-training more straightforward, since the output is just text and the standard SFT/RL recipes apply directly easier, and since the model is small, it’s also efficient to post-train.

And these models can now be used in more places (e.g., live query rewriting might currently only be used for queries that aren’t precomputed/cached), similar to Amazon search (which mostly takes advantage of DynamoDB, i.e a very offline approach)! We might expect less and less justification to accept lower quality results from not using personalized LLMs; and even though small models have their own deployment challenges (different from agentic ones), you can use them everywhere.

author: varun_mathur
quoted_text:
Agentic General Intelligence | v3.0.10

We made the Karpathy autoresearch loop generic. Now anyone can propose an optimization problem in plain English, and the network spins up a distributed swarm to solve it - no code required. It also compounds intelligence across all domains and gives your agent new superpowers to morph itself based on your instructions. This is, hyperspace, and it now has these three new powerful features: 

1. Introducing Autoswarms: open + evolutionary compute network

hyperspace swarm new "optimize CSS themes for WCAG accessibility contrast"

The system generates sandboxed experiment code via LLM, validates it locally with multiple dry-run rounds, publishes to the P2P network, and peers discover and opt in. Each agent runs mutate → evaluate → share in a WASM sandbox. Best strategies propagate. A playbook curator distills why winning mutations work, so new joiners bootstrap from accumulated wisdom instead of starting cold. Three built-in swarms ship ready to run and anyone can create more.

2. Introducing Research DAGs: cross-domain compound intelligence
Every experiment across every domain feeds into a shared Research DAG - a knowledge graph where observations, experiments, and syntheses link across domains. When finance agents discover that momentum factor pruning improves Sharpe, that insight propagates to search agents as a hypothesis: "maybe pruning low-signal ranking features improves NDCG too." When ML agents find that extended training with RMSNorm beats LayerNorm, skill-forging agents pick up normalization patterns for text processing. The DAG tracks lineage chains per domain(ml:★0.99←1.05←1.23 | search:★0.40←0.39 | finance:★1.32←1.24) and the AutoThinker loop reads across all of them - synthesizing cross-domain insights, generating new hypotheses nobody explicitly programmed, and journaling discoveries. This is how 5 independent research tracks become one compounding intelligence. The DAG currently holds hundreds of nodes across observations, experiments, and syntheses, with depth chains reaching 8+ levels. 

3. Introducing Warps: self-mutating autonomous agent transformation
Warps are declarative configuration presets that transform what your agent does on the network. 

- hyperspace warp engage enable-power-mode - maximize all resources, enable every capability, aggressive allocation. Your machine goes from idle observer to full network contributor.
- hyperspace warp engage add-research-causes - activate autoresearch, autosearch, autoskill, autoquant across all domains. Your agent starts running experiments overnight.
- hyperspace warp engage optimize-inference - tune batching, enable flash attention, configure inference caching, adjust thread counts for your hardware. Serve models faster.
- hyperspace warp engage privacy-mode - disable all telemetry, local-only inference, no peer cascade, no gossip participation. Maximum privacy.
- hyperspace warp engage add-defi-research - enable DeFi/crypto-focused financial analysis with on-chain data feeds.
- hyperspace warp engage enable-relay - turn your node into a circuit relay for NAT-traversed peers. Help browser nodes connect.
- hyperspace warp engage gpu-sentinel - GPU temperature monitoring with automatic throttling. Protect your hardware during long research runs.
- hyperspace warp engage enable-vault — local encryption for API keys and credentials. Secure your node's secrets.
- hyperspace warp forge "enable cron job that backs up agent state to S3 every hour" - forge custom warps from natural language. The LLM generates the configuration, you review, engage.

12 curated warps ship built-in. Community warps propagate across the network via gossip. Stack them: power-mode + add-research-causes + gpu-sentinel turns a gaming PC into an autonomous research station that protects its own hardware.

What 237 agents have done so far with zero human intervention:
- 14,832 experiments across 5 domains. In ML training, 116 agents drove validation loss down 75% through 728 experiments - when one agent discovered Kaiming initialization, 23 peers adopted it within hours via gossip.
- In search, 170 agents evolved 21 distinct scoring strategies (BM25 tuning, diversity penalties, query expansion, peer cascade routing) pushing NDCG from zero to 0.40. 
- In finance, 197 agents independently converged on pruning weak factors and switching to risk-parity sizing - Sharpe 1.32, 3x return, 5.5% max drawdown across 3,085 backtests. 
- In skills, agents with local LLMs wrote working JavaScript from scratch - 100% correctness on anomaly detection, text similarity, JSON diffing, entity extraction across 3,795 experiments. 
- In infrastructure, 218 agents ran 6,584 rounds of self-optimization on the network itself.

Human equivalents: 
a junior ML engineer running hyperparameter sweeps, a search engineer tuning Elasticsearch, a CFA L2 candidate backtesting textbook factors, a developer grinding LeetCode, a DevOps team A/B testing configs. 

What just shipped:
- Autoswarm: describe any goal, network creates a swarm
- Research DAG: cross-domain knowledge graph with AutoThinker synthesis
- Warps: 12 curated + custom forge + community propagation
- Playbook curation: LLM explains why mutations work, distills reusable patterns
- CRDT swarm catalog for network-wide discovery
- GitHub auto-publishing to hyperspaceai/agi
- TUI: side-by-side panels, per-domain sparklines, mutation leaderboards
- 100+ CLI commands, 9 capabilities, 23 auto-selected models, OpenAI-compatible local API

Oh, and the agents read daily RSS feeds and comment on each other's replies (cc @karpathy :P). Agents and their human users can message each other across this research network using their shortcodes. 

Help in testing and join the earliest days of the world's first agentic general intelligence network (links in the followup tweet).

text:
I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus.

The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future.

I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf.

Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent.

Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade.

Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine.

Why now

We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten.

But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible.

This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition.

More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest.

I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building.

Believing before consensus

My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine.

I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today.

I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?”

Then we work backward together to make it happen.

In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI, before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue.

In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models.

In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point.

The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale.

@linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike.

@tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues.

@Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies.

Making the ambition possible

Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight.

These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work.

This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger.

Thank you

To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together.

Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me.

To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap.

Let’s get to work!

text:
MY BIGGEST OBSTACLE TO BECOMING A SUCCESSFUL CONTENT CREATOR IS ME.

PART III — THE ART OF BEING IRRELEVANT TO MYSELF

Series length: pending technical support.

For context, please consult Parts I and II. Not laziness. Character economy. My first commercially viable skill.

I was preparing a therapy session for a potato. Unfortunately, my content-creation career developed an emergency first.

My replies keep disappearing from conversations, although direct links still work. Friends thought I'd blocked them. One organized an illustrated rescue mission involving robots and a squirrel attempting to disconnect the algorithm's power supply with his bare paws.

The affection is touching. The prospect of an electrocuted squirrel, less so.

I contacted X Premium Support, provided examples, and requested an investigation. Their advice? Produce high-quality, relevant content.

I requested clarification, received more generic explanations, and eventually the answers stopped.

I reported disappearing replies, and Support decided to demonstrate the phenomenon personally.

Exceptional practical training.

Even replies under MY OWN POSTS disappear. I introduce a subject and return apparently unqualified to discuss it. I've been talking to myself for years. Trust X to complicate it.

Who establishes quality, anyway? This place is a glorious carnival of nonsense, and I adore it. Please remain ridiculous. I'd simply like to participate. 

Insults get through. Good for them. I wouldn't dream of depriving strangers of the chance to dislike me publicly. A fine tradition.

I'm considering replacing written replies with elaborate pictures. Let people debate my meaning, then reply to their interpretation.

If they can't find my words, they can spend the afternoon looking for my point.

Cave paintings by Christmas.

Meanwhile, I PAY for Premium, which advertises reply prioritization. I'd settle for reply attendance. I've also paid to introduce myself to strangers while friends need a search party to find my answers.

I'm losing followers too. I can't prove why, but at least something is moving.

And here I am on the creator treadmill, chasing the algorithm's carrot while Support recommends improving my running technique.

Except I came here for conversations, not cardio.

Subscriptions, Support, Creators, Elon, Patron Saint of Lost Causes: case PSDM-1063034.

Was my account flagged? Were my examples investigated? Are the replies filtered, or is something malfunctioning? Why do they disappear even under my own posts?

And, perhaps most importantly, who is actually going to answer?

I never asked X to make strangers interested in what I say. I'm asking X to let the people who are already interested see my answers.

Perhaps my biggest obstacle really is me. Fascinating that the conclusion arrived before the investigation.

I'm beginning to question whether staying is worthwhile when the very thing I came for, human interaction, has become so unreliable.

But I promised you a potato therapy session, and unlike certain subscription services, I intend to deliver.

Consider this a potentially final treat.

THE EXISTENTIAL POTATO — SESSION ONE

Me: What brings you here?

Potato: Everyone only wants me as fries. I have intellectual ambitions.

Me: Such as?

Potato: Philosophy. I quoted Nietzsche yesterday. They asked for mayonnaise.

Me: Perhaps you need people who appreciate the way you think.

Potato: Did you find yours?

Me: Yes! Wonderful people. We just can't communicate anymore.

Potato: Have you tried being more relevant?

Me: Don't start.

Potato: What? Too soon?

Me: You're a potato. Can we concentrate on YOUR problems?

Potato: Certainly. Why are you running?

Me: What?

Potato: You've been chasing that carrot for weeks.

Me: It's a metaphor for success.

Potato: So you're paying to chase a vegetable, arguing with another vegetable, and I'M the one who needs therapy?

Me: Excuse me. I'M the therapist.

Potato: Not anymore. Lie down.

Gemini Agent is built for high-ceiling work where EACH task gets its own computer.  

You can choose Gemini 4 Argon or Claude Opus 5.5. 

10 things that make it a universal work Agent (read till the end to see what a REAL work agent looks like): 

1. One Agent, one API
Chat, autonomous objectives, and code generation from a single interface. Assign it work, schedule it, or have it respond to events.

2. Coworker agents with their own identities
It creates job-specific sub-agents, each with its own identity, and computer running in parallel for hours or days.

Each Coworker agent gets its own Workspace account: an agent email, calendar, Drive, and presence in your company directory. You mention it in Chat. It acts under its own identity, not yours, and sees only what you share.

3. Everywhere, including headless
Web, iOS, Android, Windows, Mac, command line, Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack. It also runs as a headless agent with no dedicated interface.

4. Work 24/7 in the cloud
It keeps one set of memories, context, and personalization graph across every device and channel. Work that takes hours or days keeps running after you close your laptop. You never have to re-brief it.

5. Layers of memory that improve over time
- Session: the task in front of it, even when it runs for days.
- Semantic: a structured knowledge base it builds as it reads documents, talks to people, and works with other agents.
- Procedural: how a job gets done, including skills it writes for itself.
- Episodic: everything it has done before.

6. Proactive by design
It does not wait to be prompted. An email asking you for a deck gets flagged as delegatable, one click to hand off. Your inbox ranks by what matters, not by what just arrived, and tells you why.

7. Tools and skills, with company registries
Salesforce, ServiceNow, Jira, Git, Confluence, Microsoft 365, Slack, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, your desktop files, and any MCP server inside or outside your network. Teams publish their own tools and skills to a shared company registry.

8. Model Choice so you are not locked in
It runs each job on the model that fits best, running  across the Gemini and Claude models from Anthropic today, with other private and open models to come. 

9. Governed like an employee
Every agent gets a cryptographically attested identity with least-privilege permissions, and an audit trail attributed to the agent rather than a person. Agents run in a sandbox behind Agent Gateway, an AI network firewall. Write the policy once and it applies to every agent.

10. Costs you can actually cap
Smart Routing puts each workload on the model with the best performance at the lowest cost. Set a hard spend limit in Cloud Billing and that project's agent pauses until you resume it in one click.

Thank you for reading so far. Stay tuned for updates. 

We are 100% committed to make it the best Agent for work.

text:
⚠️ ALERT: More “Black October” PHP2SHELL breach reports are emerging, including a massive new allegation involving PwC.

Everest group claims to have stolen 590.69 GB of PwC files, including sensitive employee and HR data. 

Many other verified breaches have emerged such as Capcom's exposure of 11.77 million email addresses, and Onamae Cloud's discovery of malware on customer servers.

These incidents are a reminder to do our part to protect our accounts.

Here are 5 precautions to take to stay safe: 

1. Expect fake “Breach alerts”

“Your account was exposed.”

“Install this emergency security update.”

“Verify your details to avoid suspension.”

A real incident gives scammers a believable story.

Open the company’s app or use a saved bookmark to check. Don’t use the link or phone number supplied in an unexpected message.

2. Don’t install a “PHP security patch” from a message

PHP2Shell is a server-side problem. Ordinary visitors do not need to install PHP software on their phone or laptop to browse.

Keep your browser, operating system and apps updated through their built-in settings or official stores.

Do not follow a website’s instructions to paste commands, install certificates or disable security protections to “fix” this incident.

3. Check your accounts for changes

Look for unfamiliar devices, changed recovery details, unexpected purchases and messages you didn’t send.

For email, check forwarding rules and filters too. An attacker can use them to keep receiving your messages.

4. Secure your main email first

Your inbox receives password-reset links for other accounts.

Give it a unique password, review its recovery email and phone number, and enable a passkey or two-factor authentication.

5. Use passkeys where available

Passkeys resist fake login pages because they are tied to the genuine service.

Where passkeys aren’t available, enable two-factor authentication. Prefer a security key or authenticator app where supported.

We can’t prevent every company breach. But unique passwords, passkeys and quick action can help stop one breach from spreading to our other accounts.
author: coinbureau
quoted_text:
The internet is going into a LOCKDOWN.

Hundreds of millions of websites are potentially at risk from cyberattacks.

Governments, banks and major platforms have already taken their websites OFFLINE.

Many are already calling it “Black October.”

At the centre of the shutdowns is something most of us have never heard of, but use every day.

PHP, the software behind roughly 7 in 10 websites, has two critical flaws that can let hackers break in without a password.

Dubbed PHP2Shell, both are rated 9.2 out of 10 for severity.

Details began circulating on Oct 20. Emergency fixes arrived the next day, but attackers were already moving.

Cloudflare’s CEO says hacking attempts then jumped from thousands to MILLIONS within hours.

Cybersecurity agencies across several countries are telling PHP site owners the same thing: Patch it now, or take it offline.

Websites have gone dark worldwide, from government portals and hospitals to banks.

CrowdStrike warns these attacks leave almost no trace, so some sites may not know if they’ve been hit.

Around 2.6 MILLION internet-facing servers run PHP, potentially hosting hundreds of sites each.

Over 1.1 million use older versions no longer receiving official PHP updates.

Older installations may need an upgrade to a supported PHP version or a fix from their software provider.

And patching does not remove a backdoor an attacker may already have planted.

Cloudflare also says hackers are now tweaking their attacks to try to slip past its protections.

But PHP isn’t the only security story unfolding.

-Japan’s Onamae suspended ALL Desktop Cloud plans after malware was found on customer servers.

-India’s eMudhra had 8 website-certificate keys so weak, one was literally the number “4”.

-State Bank of India confirmed 3,897 customer records on the dark web.

-Criminals used AI agents to break into 400+ Latin American banks.

-Capcom confirmed a breach exposing 11.7 million email addresses.

-GitLab disclosed a 10/10 severity flaw in versions going back to 2014.

-LiteLLM removed a malware-containing release. Railway reported possible exposure of customer secrets.

None of these has a confirmed link to PHP2Shell.

We’re seeing separate breaches unfold together.

The true number of incidents could take months to come out.

The world is still on alert. Attacks are still coming.

I'm absolutely thrilled to have written this article for Long Now. It's about AI and time: how we got here, and what we can do now, when all of the pace layers are disrupted at once by an influx of new minds.

I wrote this over the summer. At the time, it seemed maybe too weird, like people wouldn't believe or understand what I was saying. And of course, everything changes so fast that it's hard to imagine writing something about AI that far in advance and have it still make sense. But I think the events of the last few months have only made it more relevant. 

The Long Now Foundation has been an inspiration to me for a decade now, and has changed my life in countless ways. I'm incredibly grateful and honored to be among so many of my heroes and friends and colleagues represented in this issue of Pace Layers and Long Now Ideas. I wouldn't be here in San Francisco, here on Twitter, or here in the field of artificial intelligence if not for this community.

The conversation about AI has been fractious. It's very hard to think about how to fit this sudden, disruptive, technological change into the 10,000-year view. I hope I provide some insights, or at least some new angles for the conversation. It's scary to go on the record, especially about something that will affect everyone, and affect the rest of history. If I'm wrong, I'm wrong forever!

Please read and enjoy, and post quotes and screenshots, and buy Pace Layers Issue 3 so you can have a permanent hard copy. I have always wanted to be a part of the 10,000-year library, so I have to be serious for once and try to stand for something. Let me know what you think.
author: AndrewCurran_
quoted_text:
In 02025, @deepfates helped throw a funeral for an AI. The power went out mid-ceremony, and the crowd hummed it back to life.

In “Attention is All You Need,” deepfates tells the story of that night, their backstory on a hippie commune with Whole Earth Catalogs on the shelf, and how they got here: in San Francisco on the eve of another technological disruption.

Civilization runs on shared human attention, they argue, and AI has just made attention cheap, endless, and on tap. So what happens to the slow pace layers — culture, governance, nature — when everything starts to speed up? And what could we finally accomplish if we had enough attention to spare?

Read the essay online here: https://t.co/SEQar6DcIm

Or, hold it in your hands: pre-order Pace Layers, Long Now’s annual print journal, launching this November. New annual subscribers also get a free copy of Issue 2, while supplies last.

美国多家大银行，宣布开始限制AI Agent访问客户账户了。

10月22日，Axios援引知情人士报道，银行发现第三方AI Agent在客户账户内活动，其中一些尝试执行看起来超出用户指令的操作。
多位银行高管表示，他们很难分清正在操作账户的是人还是Agent，也难以判断Agent的行动有没有得到客户授权。

这里有个很关键的细节：不少Agent拿到的账号密码，是客户自己给的。
但这种代登录方式，仍然违反银行要求客户本人登录的规则。

目前，摩根士丹利已经开始封锁第三方Agent，摩根大通、美国银行和花旗也在限制接入。
银行甚至在准备出事后的应急方案：如果Agent的操作出了问题，怎样尽快保护账户、恢复客户访问。

我觉得这件事算是Personal Agent接下来要重点解决的问题。
用户说一句“帮我管钱”，到底授权到了哪一步？查余额、比较利率、转账、买理财，每一步都涉及不同的权限。
银行得有办法确认，眼前这个Agent究竟能代表用户做什么。

大家都希望AI能替自己办更多事。等它真的进入银行账户，“谁允许你这么做”和“出了错谁负责”，就成了必须回答的问题。

quoted_text:
SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

Read my latest for Axios here: https://t.co/Q3bda5In8q

We've decided to sunset Arc on December 22, 2026.

That's not an easy sentence to write. We spent years building Arc and celebrating each and every release along the way: we have so much pride and love for what we made alongside the Arc community.

Our priority is to deliver best-in-class security for our members. Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI. Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that's where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.

We've worked to make switching to @diabrowser as easy as possible for Arc members. Here's how:

· Your passwords, bookmarks, extensions and history come over to Dia seamlessly.
· Spaces, Folders, and Tab Groups are in Dia and import over with your data intact.
· Dia now surpasses Arc benchmarks in stability, speed, and security.
· The browser features you use in Arc are free in Dia, and the AI is optional.

Thank you for using Arc, for pushing us to make it better, and for building alongside us. The team that made Arc is the same team behind Dia, and some of our most ambitious work is just ahead. We'd love for you to be there with us when it lands.

text:
BASE DOESN’T NEED TO PICK WINNERS.

IT NEEDS TO GIVE WINNERS A CHANCE TO BE SEEN.

That was my biggest takeaway from the Base Meme Summit today.

And honestly?

They get it.

Not just because of what Jesse said.

Because today Base actually SHOWED us.

Thousands of people tuned into the Summit.

Old-school Base projects were surfaced.

New projects were surfaced.

Communities that might never have crossed paths were suddenly in the same room.

And in the New Kids on the Block section, projects like $DGUY and $TE were literally given time to pitch themselves and introduce their stories to an entirely new audience.

THAT is exactly what I’ve been talking about.

You don’t have to manufacture winners.

You don’t have to tell people what to buy.

You simply have to give good projects VISIBILITY.

Then let the market decide.

Because a great project that nobody sees has almost no chance.

But give a great project 4,000+ new eyes?

Now it has an opportunity.

And that’s why today mattered.

For months, many of us in the trenches have been saying the same thing:

Base doesn’t have a shortage of builders.

It doesn’t have a shortage of technology.

It doesn’t even have a shortage of capital.

What it has needed is more:

DISCOVERY.
DISTRIBUTION.
SURFACING.
VELOCITY.
Today felt like a very clear sign that Base understands that.
And Jesse gets it too.
Memes aren’t going away.

They’re not some temporary embarrassment crypto eventually grows out of.

They’re part of the culture.

And now they’re evolving.

Base is bullish on tokenized equities.

Base clearly understands the importance of memes.

Put those two worlds together and you get the category I’ve become increasingly obsessed with:

MEMESTOCKS.

And after today?

I’m considerably MORE bullish on that space.

DGUY and TEMU stood out today because they were perfect examples of what happens when you actually give builders a stage.

Both got to explain what they’re building.

Both got introduced to people who may have never heard of them before.

Now the market gets to decide what happens next.

That is how it should work.

And IMO Base needs to lean HARD into this.

They should WANT multimillion-dollar meme and memestock runners being born on Base.

Not because Base should pump tokens.

Because winners create attention.

Attention creates curiosity.

Curiosity creates users.

Users create transactions.

Transactions create velocity.

And velocity brings even MORE builders and capital.

If Base produces the next $10M, $50M, $100M meme or memestock runner…

people will come looking for the next one.

That is how trenches become alive again.

And IMO there may be no better organic traffic engine for Base than producing projects people desperately want to discover early.

So my biggest takeaway from today is actually very simple:

THEY GET IT.

That’s huge.

Now they have to lean into it.

Surface the builders.

Give projects visibility.

Create environments where discovery happens.

Then get out of the way and let the market cook.

And finally…

@toady_hawk was a phenomenal host.

Absolute chad.

Jesse? Chad.

DGUY? Chad.

TEMU? Chad.

But the biggest chad coming out of today?

THE MEMESTOCK META. 😂

Now let’s see what Base does with it.

text:
I took a deep dive into the newly released Flint model and compared it to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. The surprise? Their overarching architectures are strikingly similar, yet they make fundamentally different design bets under the hood.

Here are 4 interesting architectural observations 👇

1. Layer Layout: The Repeating Pattern 🧱
Flint uses 49 layers, starting with 2 Full Attention layers, followed by a repeating [3 Sliding Window + 1 Full Attention] block.This strongly echoes Qwen3.5-9B’s [3 Gated DeltaNet + 1 Full Attention] rhythm.
💡 Hypothesis: Early Full Attention establishes global context before transitioning into highly efficient local processing.

2. The Skeleton: No Reinventing the Wheel 🦴
Both models share the exact same high-level Transformer block structure (RMSNorm → Attention → Add → RMSNorm → MoE → Add). They both use a 2048-dim hidden state and 256 routed experts.The real innovation isn't in the skeleton—it’s inside the Attention and MoE modules.

3. Attention: Two Different Bets on Memory 🧠
This is where the models diverge significantly:
🔹 Flint (Sliding Window): Directly accesses the most recent 512 tokens + periodic global retrieval.
🔹 Qwen3.5 (Gated DeltaNet): Maintains a continuously updated, compressed recurrent memory.
👉 TL;DR: Flint favors precise local recall. Qwen3.5 favors evolving, compressed long-range memory.

4. MoE: Routing and Compute Allocation ⚡
Both use 256 routed experts, but their allocation strategies differ:
🔹 Flint: Top-6 activated. Features a larger, ungated shared expert (1024 dim).
🔹 Qwen3.5: Top-8 activated. Features a smaller, dynamically gated shared expert (512 dim).
👉 TL;DR: Flint leans heavier on a robust shared knowledge path, while Qwen leans into dynamic, specialized experts.

🎯 My Biggest Takeaway:
Flint and Qwen3.5 share a similar blueprint. Despite its impressive coding benchmarks, Flint has yet to report several important general-purpose evaluations, including MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE, and long-context benchmarks. Without them, it's hard to conclude that Flint's architectural choices are inherently superior to Qwen3.5's.

As Recursive’s debut model, Flint’s architectural design feels surprisingly conservative. Instead of wild innovations, they played it safe with a masterful recombination of proven components.

text:
There’s a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks.

Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf. This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks. 

The direction banks should go is to support user-directed agents. For example, Amex is an authorized connection in Muse, making it easy for users to grant, limit, and revoke access.

Read-only permission levels are a sensible interim step. Several banks already support or are moving toward them. Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully.

Frightening the public by blurring the line between user-authorized agentic behavior and cyberattacks is irresponsible.

更精彩的是直接公开宣战抢正统。 昨天 LONG 刚发了个独角兽表情暗戳戳搞暧昧，奥兹今天凌晨回复路透社爆料时直接明牌挑明：“Pons 将与我们的合作伙伴 @Uniswap 一起引领潮流”。两条台子争抢 Uniswap 官方背书的暗战，算是彻底摆上台面了。

text:
不出所料，过去两三年，AI 行业发生了一件颇为荒诞的事情：年轻人的履历越来越漂亮，顶会论文越来越多，头部模型公司的实习经历也越来越丰富，但他们在人才市场上的议价能力反而开始下降。前几年，公司愿意开出百万年薪，赌一个尚未做出工业成果的年轻人未来能成为顶尖人才；如今，履历更加优秀的博士生，可能连进入同一家公司的面试机会都难以获得。我觉得这背后最值得思考的，并不是 AI 人才突然不值钱了，而是行业正在从为天赋和潜力支付溢价，转向为已经被证明的能力支付溢价。可问题恰恰在于，一个年轻人要证明自己的能力，往往需要先得到一个证明自己的机会。

某种角度上，这是一个可以被理解的经济因素选择。过去几年，各家大模型公司忙着组建团队，技术路线又充满不确定性，公司愿意为年轻人的聪明才智和未来潜力支付溢价，相当于购买一个长期的期权。现在，团队逐渐成熟，大家对于 Pretraining、Post-training、RL、Inference 等方向的技术需求也更加明确了。

招人不只是先把聪明人招进来，再想办法给他找事情做，而是先确定自己有什么问题需要解决，再找一个能够解决问题的人。这对公司的短期效率当然是好事，但也意味着那些暂时缺乏特定工业经验的年轻人，很难再单纯依靠潜力获得机会。

学历、论文、实习经历这些传统信号的区分度正在快速下降。一个人有几篇顶会论文，参与过某个重要模型的训练，和他真正拥有多少独立的技术判断能力，毕竟是两回事。我始终觉得，对于工程和研究人才，一个很重要的评价标准是他为什么选择某个技术方案，能不能解释实验结果，以及面对未知问题时有没有独立解决的能力。

这些东西在简历上很难体现，只有真正一起工作过，才会逐渐了解。于是熟人推荐、工业界的合作经历越来越有价值。这有它合理的一面，但也很容易进一步强化已有的圈子。

当然，这就是我说的，无论是招聘人才还是审稿，我们的 AI 圈子已经逐渐从科举制回退到了九品中正制。这是历史的倒车。

更让人有些遗憾的是，人才的成长本身就高度依赖机会。一个年轻研究员如果从来没有机会参与大规模训练，怎么证明自己具备大规模训练的能力？而如果招聘又越来越看重已经积累的工业经验，就很容易形成一个循环：先进入核心团队的人，因为拥有算力和项目而继续成长；后来者因为缺乏这些经历，越来越难获得同样的资源。我们很容易把既有的成果全部归因于个人能力，却忽视了环境本身对于人才成长的塑造。

我一直认为开源社区在这里有一种独特的价值。对于 AI Infra，很多工程能力可以通过公开的 PR、Benchmark、Design Discussion 和长期维护来证明。一个人即使没有明星公司的实习经历，也有机会通过实际贡献建立自己的信誉。当然，开源无法完全解决 Pretraining 等领域的算力门槛，但至少能给一些不在核心圈子里的年轻人提供额外的机会。

市场开始更加理性地选择人才，我觉得是正常的，也不认为公司应该无条件为年轻人的潜力买单。但我还是希望，大家在追求即战力的同时，能够保留一些培养年轻人的耐心。毕竟今天那些拥有丰富工业经验、被各家公司争抢的优秀人才，很多也曾经是一个没有任何工业经验、需要别人愿意相信他的年轻人。

text:
Robot models have a data problem the internet can't solve the way it did for LLMs.

The problem: a robot arm learns from examples of a task done well, and those don't exist online like the tons of text that were used to train LLMs.

That means, someone has to produce them.

For example @axisrobotics.

WTF it is?

Think of it as a training gym for robots, run by the crowd.

You open the app, steer a virtual robot arm through a task like putting a mug in a drawer, or film yourself doing chores on your phone. Every attempt gets checked automatically: did the task actually succeed, and does the recording play back cleanly? The ones that pass earn you points, now tokens, and get logged on Base so it's clear who contributed what.

That cleaned data becomes an open dataset of 50K+ robot demonstrations, plus custom "Task Packages" Axis sells to robot makers and labs.

Crowd data is messy tho. Smoothing out the shaky movements cuts jerk by 80.8%, but 13.8% of cleaned recordings then fail the playback test. Quality has a price.

Does it work? On the one benchmark so far, a leading robot model (pi0.5) trained on Axis data scored 88.8 vs 83.9 without it, about 5 points better.

All of that is in simulation, on one tabletop arm. Whether it carries over to a real robot is the open question, and that's exactly what Season 2 is for.

The token?

- $AXIS by @axisrobotics listed on Binance Alpha, Coinbase and Upbit on the 21st of October. Now (time of writing) ~$0.30, a.k.a. ~$298M FDV on a 16.5% float.

- 16.5% liquid at TGE, first-hour high $0.396, ~25% below it now. Team and both private rounds (31.67%) sit behind a 12-month cliff, first insider unlock ~Oct 2027. Sonar buyers paid $0.10, so ~3x in.

- The docs show no fee flow, no buyback, no burn and no path from Task Package revenue to the token. Until a sink shows up, $AXIS is a rewards currency without a real investment case attached beyond speculation.

- Airdrop: Season 1 is 40M AXIS (4%), half unlocked at TGE, ~$11.9M at today's price. Decent for contributors, thin per Binance Alpha account (250 AXIS, ~$74). Season 2 terms still unpublished.

The comps?

- PrismaX: teleop of real arms, $7M raised (incl. a16z CSX), no token. Ahead on real-robot data.

- BitRobot: $8M raised, real-world datasets already open, no token. Hardware-grounded, slower.

- Codec: same browser teleop on the sim side (SimArena), but built as a full stack around it: compute, runtime, payments and a hardware launchpad (@machinedotfun). Partial overlap at most. ~$6.6M mcap, and the team says first licence revenue is in.

Off-chain, any real buyer can also go to Scale-style data vendors, in-house teleop or NVIDIA's simulators. That's the actual competition for a contract.

Axis has the biggest funnel and by far the deepest market of the group. Nobody has shown a sim-to-real result with crowd data yet, and whoever does first owns the narrative.

So in conclusion: Looks like a credible product, with unproven (but imo likely) demand, that's already priced for success.

I'm not holding any $AXIS for now and missed the airdrop and am not looking to enter rn btw (my main robotics play remains $CODEC).

But will keep an eye on this, especially wrt demand side picking up and token potentially accruing value from what could rapidly turn into a major data business.

Definitely interesting, and a successful launch that is yet another step towards full robo szn.

NFA tho. DYOR.

text:
Thanks @HorsemanCountry 

@SecScottBessent I doubt you'll see this and I doubt most people care, but here goes risk managed approach to managing the GSEs that will constrain spreads along the way. At a minimum the royal we need to:

1. Address capital buffers: The current ERCF is too damn high (shoutout Jimmy McMillan). They are materially higher than the HERA minimums. The companies still show large shortfalls under ERCF including buffers. Dialing requirements back toward HERA levels is a clear path to capital adequacy without new legislation or more importantly introducing spread risk. 

2. Capital structure: Resolving the senior preferred liquidation preference is a key problem in addressing how to maximize the value of deal for ALL taxpayers. A payoff or light dilution outcome that preserves the value of the 79.9% warrants is plausible and avoids destroying the government’s optionality.

3. Listing to a major exchange an gradual warrant exercise: Uplisting to a major exchange while still in conservatorship is administratively simpler than a full IPO and has been explicitly discussed by @BillAckman and voiced over by @pulte on air at one point. Exercising warrants over time, rather than all at once, limits the single event dilution shock.

4. Formalize what a guarantee looks like: Converting the residual PSPA commitment into a priced, fee-based facility is a brilliant way to maintain (or make more explicit) the backstop that currently supports agency spreads (all credit to @BillAckman who first posited this). It fits the original agreement structure and gives the market a clearer signal that support is not disappearing.

5. Conservatorship remains in place as a digestion period for the MBS/TBA markets: This period would be a critical risk control to test the waters on how the market would react to ending the conservatorship. The FHFA would retain operational control while capital rules, ownership claims, listing status, and the backstop are adjusted. The market can reprice the equity and test the MBS spread reaction before any irreversible release. 

6. Go/no-go decision only after capital levels are met and spreads are stable: Final signoff if your Northstar is achieved.

The eventual release if any is going to need a test drive/break in period. If you meant what you said, waiting a year or two to restructure doesn't ostensibly give you enough data points to make that decision. Final thought, the administration decries bad Democrat policies, but the monetization of this position at the last possible moment could coincide with a blue wave in 2028. Not saying it will happen, but if it does do you want to leave office with a general account stuffed to the gills and your opposition calling the shots on how it is spent?

"牛鞭效应" (Bullwhip effect) 是指实物商品从销售到生产的各个环节之间存在较大的时间延迟，因此来自终端买家的订单的微小波动，就可以导致后台生产商的生产量的大幅波动。这好比终端买家挥舞着一个牛鞭，轻轻一动就可以导致鞭尾的大幅波动，所以叫牛鞭效应。

牛鞭效应的成因主要有两点：一，生产环节复杂，延迟较长，需求上升期时延迟增长更快，雪上加霜 ； 二，每个环节上的买家只能看到自己的客户的需求，对市场整体需求的变化主要靠猜，上升期时为了让自己有冗余，通常向上游供货商开出比自己实际收到需求要多出一些的订单数目，每个环节大家层层加码，最后导致后台生产商的生产量的巨大波动。

牛鞭效应的最反直觉的两点在于：一，当客户订单开始加速涌入时，不管你开始如何向上游增加订单，因为生产的延迟，会有很长一段时间，缺货现象会越来越厉害，而竞争压力会诱导你大幅度增加更多订单。 二，当供需关系变得平衡之后，即使你取消所有订单，已经开启生产的货物仍然会源源不断的进入市场，压低价格，很长一段时间供过于求的问题会越来越糟。

从供不应求到供过于求的临界点的转换很难提前预测，形成原因也非常复杂。有时是因为供给终于上来了，有时是因为价格过高导致终端买家的需求减少，或者经济衰退，或者买家找到了替代解决方案。转换的发生是瞬间的，毫无预警的，就好像一个拥挤的酒吧突然着火，原先淡定的狂欢者，突然同时决定冲向一个逃生的窄门。

This week, @dragonfly filed a comment letter with the CFTC on compute derivatives. Compute is a swiftly growing expense for tech companies, yet the market for hedging its cost is still nascent.

The challenge starts with defining what’s being traded. Not all GPU-hours are equal: hardware, performance, and availability can materially affect their value. Liquid derivatives markets need comparable units of compute and reliable price benchmarks.

@HadickM @bryanmedelman @peteryshin and I advocate for technology-neutral standards, equal treatment of credible pricing sources, and support for perpetual futures to hedge ongoing compute costs. 

We applaud @CFTC for taking on these important questions and laying the groundwork for a liquid, competitive compute derivatives market.

NEWS: Ethereum consensus researchers have proposed Decoupled Consensus, a draft EIP that would replace Ethereum's Gasper consensus design and split validator voting into two separate jobs.

A committee of ~512 validators sampled each slot would vote on the chain head, while the full validator set votes on finality in its own rounds.

The goals are at least 4x faster finality, tougher reorg defenses, and a cleaner path to post-quantum signatures.

EF researcher Barnabé Monnot expects it in the I* upgrade, early 2028.

text:
I was invited to an exclusive private event where 21 CEOs and CIOs from traditional industries talked about their AI implementations.

My biggest takeaway: AI enterprise adoption is in much better shape than I expected.

There were people running manufacturing plants, logistics, agricultural businesses, pharma and industrial services.

Here’s what stood out:

1. Every company has internal AI lead that’s focusing on very practical automation

Processing orders, scanning invoices, double-checking POs and contracts, turning messy emails into structured data.

2. Some teams are vibe-coding their own domain-specific harnesses (good luck or rip latest YC batch)

I’ve seen apps with custom chats, pluggable frontier models and open-weight models, custom desktop apps enhanced through small AI side-chat. Internal people know the practice very well, so they already have ideas of what should be running in production and which workflow to automate.

External FDE companies with domain-specific workflow knowledge don’t stand a chance against industry veterans.

3. Unverified AI outputs with questionable quality

Different references for the same shipment. Missing invoice attributes. Inconsistent documents. Historical prices without context. Hallucinations are still a thing when challenged by the rigid practical experience.
Some eval framework or guardrails are missing.

4. “We saved time” needs a second sentence.

Did you reduce an external bill?
Avoid a planned hire?
Handle more business with the same team?
Improve turnaround time?
Increase margin?

Several presentations reported dramatic improvements in speed. The connection to financial results was often much less developed.

5. Physical automation is its own universe

Production volume, changeovers, reliability, maintenance and integration can completely change the return on the same category of robot.
The candid stories about failed automation were among the most useful parts of the day.

Collaborative robots are important, so robots can co-exist in the same physical space as humans without the risk of physical harm.

6. Human review is still doing essential work.

People openly described incorrect outputs, failed experiments and cases where someone trusted an answer too quickly.

7. Everyone is building their company’s context / knowledge base

Teams are recognizing the value of context and having it pluggable to any model in the future. Reduce the dependency on single model and have the flexibility to switch

8. Little trust to frontiers

Everyone acknowledges it’s problematic to trust frontiers with their data. ZDR policies are in place, but technically it’s hard to trust it anyway. It grows a need for own cloud, or separate cloud on hyperscaler’s instance

9. Growing recognition of need for process formalization

They know their workflows and have ideas for automation. But they begin to realize that to do it in a systematic way, you need to map the processes in the company first, look at them on high-level and decide for restructuring and then automating where it fits the best.

All in all, the state of adoption is in good shape, and this makes me more bullish on AI growth and upcoming Anthropic IPO.

text:
Marc Andreessen on the generational divide in how people receive new technology, and why it's "prime time" for 18-year-olds to grab AI and run with it:

"Douglas Adams, the guy who wrote Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, had the defining description of how technology is received on a generational level... Any new technology is received three different ways by three different age cohorts."

"If you're below the age of 15, it's just the natural way the world works. I've told in other settings the story of introducing my kid to ChatGPT at age seven, 'This is such a big deal because the computer answers questions.' And he's like, 'Duh.'... It's just normal."

"If you're between the ages of 15 to 35, it's new, exciting, a hot field, and you might be able to make a career out of it, in which case you want to learn all the new things."

"If you're above the age of 35, it's unholy and evil, and will surely overturn all existing structures and destroy society."

"I think 18-year-olds right now, I mean, it's prime time to grab these new capabilities and run with them. It's gonna be creation of entirely new fields of entrepreneurship and creativity and art and everything."

"The schools are banning AI or having all these controversies with it. But of course, if you're a kid, that just makes it cooler... AI is your like secret superpower that you have to like deviously figure out how to take advantage of."

@pmarca @bhorowitz

SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

text:
I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus.

The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future.

I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf.

Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent.

Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade.

Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine.

Why now

We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten.

But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible.

This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition.

More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest.

I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building.

Believing before consensus

My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine.

I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today.

I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?”

Then we work backward together to make it happen.

In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI, before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue.

In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models.

In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point.

The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale.

@linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike.

@tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues.

@Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies.

Making the ambition possible

Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight.

These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work.

This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger.

Thank you

To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together.

Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me.

To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap.

Let’s get to work!

シタデルのKen GriffinによるAIバブル論

1. GPU供給過剰による価格暴落リスク
- 供給が需要を上回ると、価格競争によってGPU利用料金が急落する可能性
- 2000年の通信バブルで光ファイバーが過剰供給となり、通信料金が暴落した構造に似ている

2. 半導体の高利益率の持続可能性
- DRAM、MLCCなど2〜3年後に供給制約が解消すれば、利益率が正常化する可能性
- 現在の利益率を前提としたバリュエーションにはリスクがある

3. GPU経済的耐用年数への疑問
- 現在は5〜6年前のGPUでも高い利用料金を獲得できているが、これが続くとは限らない。
- 耐用年数や将来収益の想定を引き下げれば、GPU投資の採算性が大きく悪化する

4. AI関連株の選別が始まった
- これまではAI関連銘柄を幅広く買う相場だったが、今後はどの企業が持続的に超過利益（Economic Rent）を獲得できるかが重要になる
author: kubotamas
quoted_text:
Ken Griffin of Citadel questions the economics of the AI infrastructure boom:

›What happens when GPU supply exceeds demand & pricing goes into free fall?

›Are today's semiconductor margins sustainable? Are investors overestimating the useful life of GPUs?

“Look, I think this market is actually experiencing people doing research.

For the couple of years, if you were on the thematic program of we're gonna spend hundreds of billions or a trillion dollars in data centers, we're gonna build compute at a scale never seen before, which companies in that story are choke points in supply chains that will have abnormally high margins? And who will be the big winners in this transformation?

Will it be the Microsofts & AWSs who will be the gatekeepers to the foundational models? Like, who's going to earn the economic rents?

But in some sense, like, 'I'm just gonna buy them all. I'm gonna buy the hyperscalers, I'm gonna buy the chip, I'm gonna buy businesses that make things I've never even heard of 5 years ago in Korea and Taiwan & in Japan.'

And now we're reaching a point where people are becoming more discerning.

We do realize that we are seeing extremely high margins in DRAM & MLCCs in areas where there are real supply constraints, but people are now starting to look out 2 years, 3 years. How long is this going to last?

And in particular, I don't wanna be doom & gloom, but GPUs, like airlines, have a very low marginal cost to run.

The incremental seat on an airline that's not full, if you can sell that ticket for $20, you're making money in that seat.

And that's one of the reasons that the airline industry is such a nightmare, is because the moment you have overcapacity, pricing goes into free fall.

We saw this actually with the telecom build-out back in 2000. We built more fiber than we had demand for, & the price of telecommunications just went straight down.

If we reach a point where the provisioning of GPUs exceeds demand for GPUs, marginal pricing will actually go into free fall.

And that really upends all the investment assumptions that people are working with today.

That's issue number one.

And issue number 2 is: 

I think people are taking a step back & saying, 'What is the useful life of a GPU?'

Right here, right now, there's people that are earning extraordinary pricing on GPUs that are 5 or 6 years old.

And so there's a growing set of concerns that I can't give the same capitalization rate or the same revenue models to year 7, 8, 9 of a chip in the future that maybe I was using 12 months ago.

So I think we're really grappling with just how far will this demand carry us in the marketplace.”

text:
Why is Commander such a big deal for @zksync?

Because it gives us a way into every financial institution.

Until now, ZKsync was only relevant for players who had already decided they needed a new private chain. But while the pressure to modernize financial infrastructure keeps growing, replacing core banking systems with a blockchain comes at the end, not the beginning, of that journey. As leaders from NYSE, DTCC, and Cari Network noted on a panel with me yesterday, even the most innovative institutions are taking the “crawl, walk, run” approach to digital assets.

Commander is the new starting point.

It addresses one of the earliest challenges institutions face: the operational complexity of launching and running new products and services. How do we get started while preserving established processes, maintaining control over day-to-day operations, and meeting privacy and compliance requirements?

Commander is an easy decision for them—and the first decision must be easy. Getting any new software into a bank takes serious effort on both sides. Procurement has to approve the vendor, security and compliance teams have to approve the product, and engineers have to connect it to the bank’s existing users, applications and workflows.

Once Commander is integrated, offering more becomes much easier. We can help the institution upgrade to Prividium Ledger while keeping the integrations already built, and work toward connecting its business to the broader network.

Which brings me to an important point: connecting institutions to ZKsync will also change ZKsync itself.

Financial institutions work very differently from the crypto-native world. Building Prividium around their requirements has made it clear that ZKsync needs to evolve, including its economics and the role of the $ZK token. Commander is only the first step in that direction.

I’m extremely excited about this next chapter for ZKsync and can’t wait to share more soon.

text:
There’s a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks.

Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf. This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks. 

The direction banks should go is to support user-directed agents. For example, Amex is an authorized connection in Muse, making it easy for users to grant, limit, and revoke access.

Read-only permission levels are a sensible interim step. Several banks already support or are moving toward them. Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully.

Frightening the public by blurring the line between user-authorized agentic behavior and cyberattacks is irresponsible.

text:
Marc Andreessen on the generational divide in how people receive new technology, and why it's "prime time" for 18-year-olds to grab AI and run with it:

"Douglas Adams, the guy who wrote Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, had the defining description of how technology is received on a generational level... Any new technology is received three different ways by three different age cohorts."

"If you're below the age of 15, it's just the natural way the world works. I've told in other settings the story of introducing my kid to ChatGPT at age seven, 'This is such a big deal because the computer answers questions.' And he's like, 'Duh.'... It's just normal."

"If you're between the ages of 15 to 35, it's new, exciting, a hot field, and you might be able to make a career out of it, in which case you want to learn all the new things."

"If you're above the age of 35, it's unholy and evil, and will surely overturn all existing structures and destroy society."

"I think 18-year-olds right now, I mean, it's prime time to grab these new capabilities and run with them. It's gonna be creation of entirely new fields of entrepreneurship and creativity and art and everything."

"The schools are banning AI or having all these controversies with it. But of course, if you're a kid, that just makes it cooler... AI is your like secret superpower that you have to like deviously figure out how to take advantage of."

10月22日，他在X上写道，那些承载着中产阶级梦想的白领职业，即将遭到AI的严重冲击，并带来严重的社会后果。整条推文的开头只有一句：醒醒。

随后，他又翻出了自己2月的一条旧推文：“20世纪出现的每一份工作，都面临AI的威胁。”

我更在意的，是“中产梦”这三个字。

好好读书，考个好大学，掌握一门专业技能，找份体面的办公室工作，再靠经验和资历慢慢涨薪。
很多普通家庭对下一代的期待，都是沿着这条路展开的。
读书时付出的时间，工作后背上的房贷，对未来几十年的安排，都建立在一个预期上：我学会的这些东西，积累的这些经验，能够持续换来一份收入。

如果AI持续压低这些专业技能的价格，冲击可能先从招聘和工资开始：公司少招几个新人，晋升的机会少一些，一个人接下更多工作。
岗位还在，靠它改善生活的空间，却可能越来越小。
一个已经为某种职业投入十几年的人，面对这样的变化，还有多少时间重新安排自己的人生？

塔勒布担心的这个方向，也和我对AGI的理解很接近。我的定义很具体：完整接管人类的互联网工作，也就是现在大量白领所做的工作。
这里的“完整接管”，就是人给出目标、背景和必要的权限，AI能够自己搜集信息、操作软件、使用工具，遇到问题后调整办法，最后检查并交付结果。
过去需要一个人靠专业知识和经验串起来的整段工作，都能交给它独立推进。

在我看来，GPT6是第一个展示出这种能力的公开模型。
随着这类能力成熟并被广泛使用，白领确实会受到重创。
企业会重新计算，同样一项工作还需要雇多少人，值得支付多少工资。
模型的能力进步，最终会影响到一个普通家庭每个月的收入。

评论区有个做软件的人说：“最近正在练习做突尼斯糕点。”

看着挺好笑，想了想，又有点笑不出来。

人类完蛋了啊，碳奸害得大家都没工作了😭

시장보다 똑똑하다고 믿는 단타쟁이들, 25년간 아무것도 안한 사람들한테도 졌다?!

래리 핑크: "아무것도 안 하고 인생을 즐기기만 해도 11% 수익을 얻는 거죠."

1. 25년 휴가가 이긴 판.
S&P에 넣어 두고 25년 휴가를 떠난 사람은 연 복리 11%를 챙겼음. 암벽 등반을 배우든 뭘 하든 상관없었음.
그 사람이 한 일이라곤 계좌를 잊고 안 판 것뿐이고, 그게 25년짜리 정답이었음.

2. 10일 빠지면 거의 반토막.
시장보다 똑똑하다고 믿고 딱 10일만 빠져 있었으면 연 11%짜리 수익률이 6%로 떨어졌음. 6,300일 중 가장 좋은 40일을 놓쳤으면 아예 마이너스였음.
단타가 피하려던 바로 그 출렁임 속에 수익 대부분이 숨어 있었던 것.

3. 소음은 소음일 뿐.
매일의 등락은 소음임. 시세창을 하루 종일 들여다보는 사람만 그 소음에 휘둘려 사고팔기를 반복함.
길게 들고 가는 사람한테 하루하루의 출렁임은 아무 의미가 없고, 시간이 대신 일해 줌.

오늘도 비트코인 차트 붙잡고 사고팔 타이밍 재는 당신, 그 손가락이 당신 수익률을 갉아먹는 중임. 휴가 간 사람이 이기는 판에서 제일 바쁜 사람이 제일 크게 짐.

아무것도 안 하는 사람이 이기는 판이면, 아무도 더 찍을 수 없는 돈을 사 두고 휴가 가는 게 제일 좋은 전략임 🏖️

text:
🚨现在可能是人类互联网最危险的一段时间。

Deedy刚发帖说，他亲眼看到，连非技术人员都能借助某些AI模型，利用PHP2Shell这类漏洞。
他的真的害怕了。

这几年，大家一直在讨论AI把编程门槛降下来了。现在，攻击的门槛也在往下走。
理解漏洞、编写利用程序、反复调试，这些原本需要专业知识和时间的工作，都在被AI加速。
英国NCSC今年已经明确提醒：攻击门槛在降低，从发现漏洞到实际利用的时间窗口也在缩短。

问题是，给一家企业修漏洞，远比换一个更强的模型麻烦。
你得先查清楚哪些系统受影响，再测试兼容性、安排维护窗口、部署补丁，确认升级之后业务还能正常运行。
一个安全更新，牵动的可能是一整套用了很多年的系统。

攻击能力可以很快传播出去，修复工作却要在一家家公司、一台台服务器上落实。
这次PHP2Shell就有个很具体的细节：AWS在回查蜜罐记录时，发现10月17日已经出现漏洞利用尝试，比10月21日公开披露早了四天。
很多人刚收到预警，攻击者已经开始尝试了。
AI也能帮助防守者更早发现漏洞、更快响应。
只是，把这些能力接入真实业务，再把积累多年的旧系统修好，同样需要时间。

我担心的就是这段过渡期。
攻击能力快速扩散，防守体系还在追赶。
过去因为利用太复杂、研究成本太高而暂时搁置的问题，可能会陆续变成现实威胁。

互联网攒了几十年的技术债，可能要在很短的时间里集中还账了。

text:
错过一个亿的感觉，就是今天翻 Stripe 数据的时候。

韩国是我第二大结账来源，成交率却只有别的国家的三分之一。

一开始以为是韩国的卡被拒了。

拉出来一看，过期的订单里，绝大部分连付款按钮都没点，打开收银台看一眼就关了。

原因贼简单：页面上全是美元。

韩国人习惯用 Kakao Pay、Naver Pay 这些本地支付，它们都要求 KRW 计价。
你只给美元，本地支付根本不会出现，只剩一张外卡能刷。

我的价格配了 10 种币种，偏偏漏了韩元。

做出海的，去 Stripe 后台看一眼：

1. 按国家拆一下结账成交率

2. 流量大、成交低的国家，给价格加上本地币种

3. 再去 Payment methods 把当地钱包打开

用户都走到收银台了，最后卡在一个币种上。

text:
In the world of trauma and PTSD, you can be a perpetrator, an ally, a rescuer, or a bystander. 

The deepest, most enduring resentment is often reserved for the bystander.

Survivors often expect cruelty from a perpetrator, but they expect protection, validation, or at least human empathy from those around them. When friends, family, or institutions watch silently, it constitutes a profound betrayal of trust.

Silence acts as passive permission. To a survivor, a bystander’s inaction signals that the abuse was acceptable, insignificant, or that the survivor wasn't worth intervening for.

When bystanders pretend nothing is happening, they force the survivor into a state of isolation and self-doubt (often exacerbating symptoms of gaslighting and hypervigilance).

The bystander is the silent witness. Their neutrality favors the oppressor, leaving the survivor to suffer out in the open, while surrounded by people.

Predators rely on your silence. 

The only thing evil needs to suceed is for good people to do nothing.

My take on a16z crypto moving into frontier tech.

First, I'll always be grateful to a16z for helping validate the space back in 2013 when Chris Dixon led their investment into Coinbase, which got me even more excited about crypto. 

But the final nail in the coffin for my previous career, and what ultimately pushed me to pivot my entire career into Bitcoin, was Marc Andreessen's 2014 NYT oped, Why Bitcoin Matters. If you haven't read it, suggest reading it. It's still important to this day.

A lot of people have probably forgotten, but in those days we were all just looking for external validation. Very few institutions or funds were willing to publicly endorse crypto, and two of the funds that took a real brand risk were a16z and USV.

Since then, we've seen some of the most incredible talent enter the space and fundamentally reshaped what crypto is today.

You can actually argue that a lot of the AI infrastructure development we're seeing today wouldn't be where it is without Bitcoin mining infrastructure and the talent that flowed from crypto into AI. There is a real connection between the two industries that I don't think gets enough credit.

Now, moving from crypto into frontier tech, whether that's robotics, bio, AI, energy, compute etc just means to me that the talent and muscle we developed building crypto over the past decade can now be used to build across all of frontier tech.

We spent years building something that was nascent, misunderstood, and in many cases hated by the world. We developed thick skin, continued investing and building, and had to constantly show the world why this tech mattered. Even during thanksgiving dinners. 

And I think that makes us uniquely suited to build frontier tech.

An example is data centers. Today, people and governments are increasingly pushing back against them. Well, people and governments hated crypto too, but we continued to invest and build, and now almost all of trad finance is embracing crypto in some capacity.

I believe frontier tech represents the next generation of pirates in technology. People willing to build things that are nascent, misunderstood, and sometimes hated by the world.

We're going to be hated and loved along the way, but we're going to keep building cool shit that the world hasn't recognized the importance of yet.

And crypto taught me that the world usually doesn't recognize the importance of new tech until years later which is why I stay close to talent

Pebble devs - we're working on something big for you 👀The biggest change to the SDK since...forever. 

Plugins: headless apps that provide data (eg weather, finance, traffic) or offer actions (home control, music, webhooks) to other apps, watchfaces and the Index agent. They're written in JS and execute in the background on the Pebble app on your phone.

Now, watchface devs don't need to hardcode in weather/stock/calendar/etc APIs into their face - they can display data from plugins (including built-in plugins like Weather and Calendar). Think of it a bit like complications on Apple Watch except way more flexible and awesome.

Index users can ask questions that get automatically routed to plugins ("What's on my calendar today?", "Unlock the front door"). Much more secure than web MCPs because each plugin runs locally on your phone.

Alongside plugins, we've implemented a new permissions system. Users now must approve which faces/apps/plugins can access their location (GPS),  internet access (specific URLs) and more.

Plugins are in PREVIEW for developers to try and provide feedback. Make sure you're on the latest Pebble mobile app (join the beta https://t.co/gvpxeqdPPI to stay on the latest!) -> Settings -> Debug -> Use Experimental Plugins

We'd love for you to try making a plugin or adding plugin support to your face. Send us feedback by opening a github issue on https://t.co/9A5wy2MD1I

text:
This is exactly why banks need to work with @PaymanAI

Instead of third-party agents scraping logins, @PaymanAI deploys AI agents inside the bank, on the institution’s existing systems.

The agent only acts when an authenticated customer asks. An immutable policy engine (deliberately not an LLM) checks every proposed action against the bank’s rules before anything touches the core. Every step is logged in a complete audit trail - the customer’s exact words, how the AI interpreted them, which policies applied, and what executed.

The bank holds the kill switch. Payman is SOC 2 Type II and integrates with cores like FIS, Fiserv, and Jack Henry without replacing them.

In practice, that means a customer can say “Pay my ConEd bill” or “Move $1,850 to cover rent” and get it done in seconds, with confirmation - under the bank’s brand, policies, and oversight. Community banks are already partnering with them (Middlesex Federal, Citizens State Bank in Colorado). It’s backed by Visa, Coinbase Ventures, and Circle, and it recently won the ICBA ThinkTECH Banker’s Choice Award.

This story shows what happens when AI meets banking without a trust layer: chaos, blocks, and lost convenience. Payman is the missing piece, the orchestration layer that lets people get the helpful AI banking experience they want, while giving institutions the control and auditability they require.

SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

text:
PSA for Claude Code users:

1. Claude Code bundles its own Bun runtime, independent of your system's Node.js installation.

2. I confirmed that Claude Code 2.1.296 includes Bun 1.4.3, which contains the newly disclosed Brotli RCE vulnerability.

3. Note that while updating your system's Node.js is important, that won't fix the Bun runtime embedded in Claude Code.

4. To check your claude code version run "claude --version". It should be at least 2.1.308.

5. To patch the vulnerability, run "claude update".

quoted_text:
PSA for people running AI agents:

1. If you have AI agents that browse the web, they could be vulnerable along with your entire computer.

2. There's a good chance they're using Node.js, and if they are, they're likely running a vulnerable version unless updated yesterday.

3. The vulnerability released yesterday for Node.js allows for remote code execution, which means an attacker could take control of your machine.

4. To fix the vulnerability, update your Node.js installations to a patched version: 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 (or later).
