text:
Why is Commander such a big deal for @zksync?

Because it gives us a way into every financial institution.

Until now, ZKsync was only relevant for players who had already decided they needed a new private chain. But while the pressure to modernize financial infrastructure keeps growing, replacing core banking systems with a blockchain comes at the end, not the beginning, of that journey. As leaders from NYSE, DTCC, and Cari Network noted on a panel with me yesterday, even the most innovative institutions are taking the “crawl, walk, run” approach to digital assets.

Commander is the new starting point.

It addresses one of the earliest challenges institutions face: the operational complexity of launching and running new products and services. How do we get started while preserving established processes, maintaining control over day-to-day operations, and meeting privacy and compliance requirements?

Commander is an easy decision for them—and the first decision must be easy. Getting any new software into a bank takes serious effort on both sides. Procurement has to approve the vendor, security and compliance teams have to approve the product, and engineers have to connect it to the bank’s existing users, applications and workflows.

Once Commander is integrated, offering more becomes much easier. We can help the institution upgrade to Prividium Ledger while keeping the integrations already built, and work toward connecting its business to the broader network.

Which brings me to an important point: connecting institutions to ZKsync will also change ZKsync itself.

Financial institutions work very differently from the crypto-native world. Building Prividium around their requirements has made it clear that ZKsync needs to evolve, including its economics and the role of the $ZK token. Commander is only the first step in that direction.

I’m extremely excited about this next chapter for ZKsync and can’t wait to share more soon.

text:
There's a lot of noise about NEAR right now, so let me break it down.

NEAR has two products worth knowing: NEAR Intents, a cross-chain swap engine that just had its biggest month ever, and NEAR AI, which keeps your AI prompts private in a way you can actually check. Now here's where it gets interesting. One of them doesn't even need a blockchain.

And then there's the bigger question: does any of this matter for the token? A lot of people seem to be buying NEAR simply because it sits where AI, crypto, and privacy meet, probably three of the year's hottest stories. But a good story and a token that earns from it aren't the same thing.

Start with Near Intents. You just state the result you want, like "swap my USDT on Ethereum into ZEC." Professional trading firms compete to fill it, and NEAR settles it. You never hold or even see NEAR. Wallets like Ledger, Brave, Rabby, and Solflare already support it.

September hit a record $4.80B, about 10x what it was a year earlier, and roughly $160M a day. October has cooled to about $132M a day.

Here's the catch for holders. In the last 30 days, Intents made about $7.33M in fees. About $2.34M of that goes to NEAR, and it buys NEAR on the market. But new NEAR is issued at 2.5% a year, so the buyback covers only about a sixth of the new supply. Meanwhile, daily active accounts on NEAR itself are down 79% from a year ago.

The bear case is real too. The volume spikes line up with ZEC privacy trading, an exploit of about $3.8M on Oct 1, paused Intents, and September was one parabolic month. You can't ignore these things either.

quoted_text:
For a while now, I've noticed that some people are still confused about Psylocke, who she is, and which is which. Psylocke is known for having one of the messiest stories in all of Marvel, so how about I try my best to explain it as simply as possible?

- There are three Psylockes.
Betsy Braddock, Kwannon, and Sai.

- Betsy Braddock was the original Psylocke, Kwannon is an assassin, Sai is a demon slayer.

- Betsy and Kwannon are both in Earth-616, Sai is from an alternate universe.

- Betsy and Kwannon had an extremely messy and complicated body swap story that ended in Kwannon dying, and Betsy being permanently stuck in Kwannon's body.

- A few years ago, Kwannon was resurrected in her original body, and Betsy was given her body back.

- Betsy became Captain Britain, Kwannon is now Psylocke.

Fun facts about them!
- Betsy was stuck in Kwannon's body for over 20 years of Marvel's publications.
- Kwannon is not her real name, and it is yet to be revealed.
- In X-Men: Demon Days, Sai killed her world's Venom with the help of Hulkmaru (Her world's Hulk). Galacta gave Psylocke the Venom accessory as a reminder of one of her greatest victories.

Many speculate that Sai was chosen for Marvel Rivals because the devs wanted to distance themselves from the Betsy Kwannon debacle, which, in my opinion, was the smart thing to do.

This was only a heavily simplified version of Psylocke. If you'd like to look more into their backstories, just be warned that it gets very messy, especially the body swap.

AI can dream up thousands of new molecules. but who is actually going to make them?

that’s a major question for the future of drug discovery, and exactly what @warpsciences is tackling.

the team is building an automated chemistry lab in the US to make that process faster and smarter, helping biotech companies turn AI’s ideas into the molecules they need. it’s quite the business model.

@kevinweil and Sol (two of Warp’s co-founders) joined @guruchahal on the investment memo for a fascinating conversation about robots, physical sciences, AI, and how Warp aims to intertwine them.

the strides being made in AI and science continue to amaze me.
author: lightspeedvp
quoted_text:
While AI has advanced in mathematics, we believe there’s still a major gap in the physical sciences.

@warpsciences co-founders @kevinweil and Solomon Reisberg joined Lightspeed Partner @guruchahal to discuss how their labs could generate the experimental data needed to advance scientific AI.

The company recently emerged from stealth and is building US chemistry labs to make research compounds for biotech and pharma companies.

“First be the hands, then build the nervous system, and then over time become the brain,” says Warp’s CEO Kevin.

The plan starts with expert chemists making molecules for customers. Cameras and sensors would record the work, helping Warp automate tasks and train models to improve how compounds are made.

More capable labs could let researchers pursue ideas for new medicines that time and cost currently put out of reach. The experiments could also produce more evidence for scientific AI to learn from.

Thank you to Kevin and Solomon for joining us!

Full episode below.

author: calco_io

text:
Many measures of AI exposure ask what AI can do. 
This paper asks a different question: where could AI make the remaining human work more valuable?

This is an important distinction. The same task can become a bottleneck in one occupation and not another. Looking inside jobs may tell us much more than assigning an exposure score to the occupation as a whole. This is something my team is working on and I love seeing other studies working on it as well.
author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
Very happy to share a new paper, “Technology Bottlenecks: Measuring Where AI Could Raise the Value of Work It Cannot Yet Do.”

AI exposure measures ask about the work AI is capable of doing. We ask instead where the marginal value of work AI cannot yet do may rise as AI speeds up the rest of the job.

To do so, we employ 288 million U.S. job postings mapped line by line to their closest O*NET tasks and GPT-4 feasibility ratings from Eloundou et al. (2024) to construct a measure, “bottleneck pressure,” for each task in each occupation that posts it. 

Using a simple task-based framework, we derive this pressure at the task level, showing that for an AI-infeasible task it is the exposure of the occupation that posts it, so the same task can face very different bottleneck pressure in different jobs.

Reporting bottleneck pressure alongside AI exposure shows both the scope for AI to perform work and where improving the work it cannot do may pay off more as capabilities expand.

text:
Want to share my thoughts as one of the few, if only people, that have deployed AI Agents that are moving money and making payments within a banks firewall for their customers.

Banks are shutting off access to external AI Agents (for now). Why did this become such a problem all of a sudden?

This has been happening since the beginning of the year. When OpenClaw came out it was maybe a few hundred hackers/engineers that set their OpenClaws up and gave it access to their bank accounts. Why?

Not because they're crazy, but because they hosted the agent, they trusted it, and they saw the power for how much these agents could help them do both mundane and complex tasks, which banking has plenty of.

Fast-forward to the last two months with Instinct, Muse, and the 100+ personal AI Agents that have come out and that number has gone from a few hundred, to thousands. 

Banks were not ready for this activity, and quite frankly did not expect this level of agentic activity to come this fast. So they did the right thing, shut the gates.

I don't think this will be the case forever, and banks will need to support this in a safe and trusted way where most importantly THE BANKS control the experience. 

Here are my thoughts on how this all plays out, if you think a banker or anyone at any Financial Institution would benefit, please share. Thank you!

text:
I guess i've been lucky to never experience what it feels like to be "deplatformed"- until now

like jeremy below, I was intrigued by @alexrkonrad article, and decided to give Spot a try. I ended up not really enjoying the experience, and and never booked an actual dining reservation. I think I cancelled it after a week or two and moved on.

then imagine by surprise that @resy shut down my account without any explanation. it was so odd that i didnt at first know what had happened, and upon emailing their team, I received a generic message that said I violated their T&S and that reinstatement of my account would be impossible, decision final. 

ive been using resy and @AmericanExpress for 10/20+ years respectively. to basically sever a relationship with a customer without any warning and explanation felt so ridiculous that i surely thought i would eventually find a person to talk to and get it sorted out. well, i was very wrong. even after trying to explain, i just received the same canned botted message back (which is actually just comically ironic)

we all know restaurant reservations get botted, and its impossible for actual customers to get tables. we have all kinds of reservation trading platforms and things like dorsia that create an entire business model out of this industry issue. in the 20+ years ive lived in NYC, i really think that is has never been this bad. and its because AI is here - and ppl are botting. so its odd to me that Resy would instead of actually solving the problem,  decide to ban actual customers who are trying to figure out how to navigate this ridiculous situation in the age of software and AI improvements with zero grace.

newsflash: agents are here to stay, whether you like or not. this problem will get worse than better. and resy will fail if they do not realize their business model is broken, and made worse by deplatforming longtime customers. AMEX will fail if they lose goodwill on innocuous violations that result in deplatforming from financial services.

but more importantly, arbitrary censorship of these kinds in the age of AI will lead to massive consumer revolts at a societal level. were already seeing how amazon is blocking certain infrastructures, and meta is trying own the stack in a closed vertical, and banks are already warning their customers agents are accessing their financial accounts. if you start arbitrarily banning REAL people because of the mistaken assumptions of bots, this will become an FTC issue. i know @benleventhal is not involved with resy anymore, but given his positive stance on the power of crypto and how hes thought through blackbird, i would imagine hed be appalled by this happening

anyway, a little rant out of frustration, in support of @jbeyda below, but also a bit of a warning to corporate america to treat your customers right. ill be fine. a restaurant reservation in NYC is a privilege! there are more serious issues at stake on a fundamental value here for what the customer/agent relationship is, and i hope more companies get it right. and @resy can choose to do the right thing and help me and jeremy out, or eventually gets a class action of sorts and well id imagine there will be no tears from either of us

text:
旧金山聚变公司 Marathon Fusion 称用中子把水银变成了金子，金价不会受影响，他们真正要卖的是抗癌药原料

Marathon Fusion 是旧金山一家 28 人的创业公司。10 月 21 日，公司在 X 上发帖说，上个月他们用核聚变产生的中子，把水银（汞）变成了稳定的金子，速度是欧洲核子研究中心 CERN 2025 年纪录的 10 倍。

先回答最实际的问题：金价会跌吗？不会。

按 Marathon 自己 2025 年论文的算法，一座吉瓦级的聚变电站外面包一层水银，每年能顺带产约 2 吨金子。2025 年全球金矿产量约 3672 吨，要追上这个数，得建 1800 座这样的电站，而眼下一座都没有。Marathon 自己的装置功率是 1 千瓦，只有吉瓦的百万分之一。

这样产出的金子还混着放射性，联合创始人 Adam Rutkowski 去年对英国《金融时报》说，要存放 14 到 18 年才完全安全。

这次实验本身的量也小。CERN 那项纪录是对撞机里铅原子核擦肩而过、被打掉 3 个质子变成的金，2015 到 2018 年四年一共约 29 皮克，不到一克的三百亿分之一，最快时每秒约 8.9 万个原子。

Marathon 说的是“高速率”，比的应该是每秒产量，但公司没说比的是哪个数，也没公布一共做出多少金子、纯度多高。外媒指出，帖子里的证据只有一张伽马射线能谱图，目前没有第三方验证。

原理物理学家早就知道。氘和氚两种氢聚变时，每次反应都会甩出一个速度极快的中子。这个中子撞进汞-198，会顺带再撞出一个中子，剩下的汞-197 过几天自己衰变成金-197，也就是首饰里那种金。普通核电站里这么快的中子很少，聚变装置每反应一次就有一个。

那一家聚变公司为什么要炼金？答案在钱上。

Marathon 今年 2 月发了一篇论文，给每一个聚变中子算了价钱：拿去发电，按每度电约 0.1 美元算，一个中子值约 3×10⁻²⁰ 美元；拿去炼金，值 2.6×10⁻²⁰ 美元，跟发电差不多；拿去做钼-99，值 2.6×10⁻¹⁷ 美元，接近发电的一千倍；拿去做抗癌药原料锕-225，值约 10⁻¹⁰ 美元，是发电的 30 亿倍左右。

这个账决定了聚变装置多早能赚钱。论文算出，只卖电的聚变电站，等离子体放出的能量要达到加热它所用能量的 10 到 22 倍才能回本，现有实验装置离这个门槛还很远。如果同时卖电和金子，门槛降到 3 倍左右。如果专做钼-99，放出的能量只有投入的千分之一也能赚钱。

钼-99 衰变出的锝-99m 是核医学检查里用得最多的显像剂，约八成的核医学扫描靠它，现在主要靠全球少数几座研究用反应堆裂变铀来生产。Marathon 去年 12 月的论文估计，一台 3 兆瓦、远达不到能量回本的聚变装置，就能满足全世界的钼-99 需求。

锕-225 更稀缺。它用于靶向放射治疗：把放射性原子挂在能认出癌细胞的药物分子上，送到肿瘤旁边近距离照射。这类药的市场在长，诺华的前列腺癌药 Pluvicto 2025 年卖了约 20 亿美元。锕-225 长期主要靠美国橡树岭国家实验室从冷战时期留下的核材料里慢慢提取。Marathon 官网写的路线是用聚变中子轰击镭-226 来生产它。

这次帖子里，公司说已经做出第一批医用同位素：用聚变中子轰击锌，得到铜-64 和铜-67。铜-64 用于 PET 扫描找肿瘤，铜-67 用于治疗。产量没有公布。

所以 Marathon 的计划分两步：先用小装置卖医用同位素，以后再靠金子给大型聚变电站补贴收入。论文估计全球黄金市场每年约 7000 亿美元，足够支撑约 2 太瓦（2000 吉瓦）的聚变发电。这些都是公司自己的模型，还没有一笔真实销售。

为了产够中子，Marathon 说要每秒把一万亿个中子打进一个 1 厘米大小的靶子，连续好几年。他们正在旧金山建的装置用加速器把氘离子打到含氚的锂靶上，用途是产中子，不发电。公司的目标是从现在起每月把功率密度翻一倍，这是计划，还没有实际记录。

帖子里还提到，上周他们在“全球最强的等离子体离心机”里富集了同位素，打破了苏联保持 40 年的纪录。这种离心机让带电的气体高速旋转，重的同位素甩到外圈，轻的留在中间。汞-198 只占天然汞的一成左右，炼金前得先这样挑出来。公司没说打破的是哪项纪录、数值是多少。

Marathon 成立于 2023 年，由前 SpaceX 推进工程师 Adam Rutkowski 和 CEO Kyle Schiller 创办，种子轮由 1517 Fund 和矿业巨头英美资源集团领投。团队五分之一有博士学位，这条帖子的后半段在招人。

text:
We need an "Antifragile Internet" built for the agentic era.

The hacks over the past few days (PHP, Railway, eMudhra, LiteLLM etc) show how fragile the existing Internet has become. AI agents are challenging the Internet's structure in 3 distinct ways:

1/ On the offense side, agents are a weapon - AI finds and exploits bugs on a scale not seen before, and the cost of attack asymptotes to 0. Bugs that used to take human experts weeks and months are easily found, adapted, and exploited by AI agents. Decades of legacy code that ran on "security by obscurity" no longer holds against agents.

2/ On the defense side, agents are a target - AI generated code is often bug-prone. AI agents themselves, as machines of unconstrained output are liable to prompt injections and other types of attacks that can leak keys, PII, and other pieces of information.

3/ On the identity side, agents are dominating Internet activity - this year, machine traffic has already passed human traffic, and may continue to grow 1000x over the next few years. Content and webpages used to human  requests and behavior are breaking with agents, and it is increasingly difficult to tell human content from AI content.

All this means we will need to see a ground-up redesigning of the Internet, one with more cryptographic verifiability, identity protocols, rule-enforcement, and other security primitives that eliminate bug categories rather than simply patch them - an "Antifragile Internet" that gets stronger and more secure as more agents participate in it.

This is an emerging thesis area for us at @usv, if you're building in the space please reach out!

More thoughts soon.

SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

Read my latest for Axios here: https://t.co/Q3bda5In8q

果然AI来炒缅A，最后也不得不学会空仓🤣

@EinsiaAI  发布了一个量化研究基准Quant-Arena：给模型3042只A股的历史数据，让它自己写代码、构建信号、回测并修改策略。

9个前沿大模型下场做量化，综合得分第一的GPT-6 Astra，全年75%的交易日都在空仓。

他们先用2022—2023年的数据研究，最多评估5个候选策略，再冻结一个版本，放到封存的2024年行情里检验，计入交易成本和模拟市场冲击。

按每个模型综合得分最高的配置看，9个里面只有4个赚钱：GPT-6 Astra年化收益10.7%，GPT-6 Sol为8.6%，GPT-5.6 Terra为8.4%，Claude Opus 5.5为4.4%。

其余5个都是负收益。

最有意思的是Astra。
它在研究阶段收到连续亏损的回测反馈后，给策略加了一道市场趋势过滤：条件满足才入场，其余时间持有现金。到了2024年，它躲过了年初的下跌，全年最大回撤控制在6.8%，也因为长时间空仓，错过了不少反弹。

让AI分析行情、写代码、反复改策略，最后一个很有效的进步，是学会什么时候先别买。

顺风的时候我才会加仓，逆风的时候仓位更小，而曾经的我分不清什么是顺和逆，仓位大小全靠感觉，不顺的时候仓位甚至比顺的时候还大，逆势想加拉均价，顺势只会平仓踏空。

这几个月的操作，我在吃完66-74，74-85两段行情后，尝试几次做多基本都是保本或者打平，后面判断没行情了也就直接不开单了。

text:
We need an "Antifragile Internet" built for the agentic era.

The hacks over the past few days (PHP, Railway, eMudhra, LiteLLM etc) show how fragile the existing Internet has become. AI agents are challenging the Internet's structure in 3 distinct ways:

1/ On the offense side, agents are a weapon - AI finds and exploits bugs on a scale not seen before, and the cost of attack asymptotes to 0. Bugs that used to take human experts weeks and months are easily found, adapted, and exploited by AI agents. Decades of legacy code that ran on "security by obscurity" no longer holds against agents.

2/ On the defense side, agents are a target - AI generated code is often bug-prone. AI agents themselves, as machines of unconstrained output are liable to prompt injections and other types of attacks that can leak keys, PII, and other pieces of information.

3/ On the identity side, agents are dominating Internet activity - this year, machine traffic has already passed human traffic, and may continue to grow 1000x over the next few years. Content and webpages used to human  requests and behavior are breaking with agents, and it is increasingly difficult to tell human content from AI content.

All this means we will need to see a ground-up redesigning of the Internet, one with more cryptographic verifiability, identity protocols, rule-enforcement, and other security primitives that eliminate bug categories rather than simply patch them - an "Antifragile Internet" that gets stronger and more secure as more agents participate in it.

This is an emerging thesis area for us at @usv, if you're building in the space please reach out!

More thoughts soon.

The legend says that the McRib first came to life to compensate for... a McNugget shortage issue! Apparently, McNuggets had become so wildly popular that our supply could not keep up with demand. So we needed a new recipe with another protein to give us a bit of time to bring in more McNuggets.

What was a temporary solve quickly became a cult classic, with fans begging for its return every year. Funny enough, over the years, the McRib has found new meaning online within the crypto community, as some claim Bitcoin tends to perform well after the McRib makes a comeback, particularly in 2017, 2020, 2021. The joke reached its peak in December 2024 when Bitcoin broke $100,000 for the first time in history on the exact same day the McRib returned to menus.

Welcome back, Legend!

text:
彼得·蒂尔说一家公司的名字，往往暗示了它未来的命运。

• PayPal：听起来像一个帮你付款的朋友，亲切又可靠。
• Napster：名字让人联想到偷窃，后来因版权问题陷入法律纠纷。
• Airbnb：让人联想到温馨的民宿，毫无威胁感。
• Uber：带有凌驾于他人之上的意味，甚至让人联想到凌驾于法律之上。

他还比较了 Facebook 和 MySpace：

Facebook 强调真实身份和了解他人，MySpace 则更偏向自我展示和虚构形象。

他认为，这两个名字甚至预示了它们后来不同的发展轨迹。

“公司的整个发展轨迹，可能从一开始就隐藏在名字里。”
author: 0xCheshire
quoted_text:
彼得·蒂尔：欧洲永远不会诞生伟大的科技公司，因为他们畏惧成功。

“在硅谷，流行着一种对失败的病态崇拜。你四处宣扬自己的种种失败，仿佛这就在某种程度上预示着你终将成功。”

“而在欧洲那种社会民主主义社会里，做一个平庸的成功者是被接受的，但如果你想获得极致的成功，那是被排斥的。如果你拥有一家势头正盛、开始壮大的公司，这种势头会被掐断，然后你会把公司卖掉。如果你在半路就选择了卖掉，你永远也无法成就一家伟大的公司。”

“Facebook 历史上最重要的决策发生在 2006 年夏天。那是公司成立的第二年，雅虎开价 10 亿美元想要收购我们。当时董事会有三个人：马克·扎克伯格、我，还有另一位风险投资人。我们开会讨论是否要接受这 10 亿美元。”

“我们另外两个人都觉得这是一笔巨款，或许该见好就收。但马克在董事会一开场就说：‘这只是个例行公事的会议，我们只讨论 10 分钟。显而易见，我们不会卖。’”

“任何一家顶尖的科技巨头，必然经历过多次被开价收购的时刻，而你每一次都选择了拒绝。这意味着，你并不畏惧成功。”

“但在欧洲，人们的选择是尽早套现离场，然后回到那种欧洲式的、长达十年的安逸度假生活中去。”

Why don't VCs hold their winners after IPO as often anymore?

Likely because VC-backed IPOs perform significantly worse than in previous eras, as they absorb more capital and grow more fragile ahead of listing.  

Results from the 50 largest VC-backed IPOs, measured across three windows (Up to Oct 2 in the end year) show that the most recent group (2014–2026) has by far the worst aggregate performance — and even that is propped up by just three companies.

1994–2006 
Mean: −2 
Median: −36 
Beat the index: 14 of 50 
Mean without top 3: −21

2004–2016 
Mean +88 
Median: −28
Beat the index: 22 of 50 
Mean without top 3: −6

2014–2026 
Mean: −12
Median: −90
Beat the index: 8 of 50 
Mean without top 3: −121

Still, I was perfectly happy to pay $75 rather than waste time fighting it. But the citation didn't even mention an online payment portal. When I asked ChatGPT how to deal with it, it found that the online filing portal appeared to be down for maintenance, but offered to submit an "admit with explanation" response by email.

I said sure. It prepared the paperwork, attached the citation, and emailed the administrative hearings office.

It was significantly easier than paying the fine.

This is a fascinating reversal of the traditional asymmetry between citizens and government. The state has automated issuing fines, while citizens have had to manually navigate cumbersome appeals processes. AI makes responding almost frictionless.

If everyone starts doing this, not as a protest but simply because it's easier, governments will face a deluge of procedurally valid responses where they previously collected revenue with little effort.

Things are going to get interesting.

I get more messages about this podcast every week than anything else I do.

We all want to look and sound smart in the investment committee or all hands meeting.

This is the only show in tech you have to listen to every week.

No egos, no politics, just tech.

AGENDA:

- Venture is Broken: Trillion or Bust
- Coreweave Sell-Off Creates Panic
- Town at $1B, Anduril at $90B: Are Revenue Multiples Out of Control?
- General Atlantic Eyes IPO
- Modal Raises $750M at $15.75B

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. Why Fundraising Is Back to Being a Numbers Game

Founders with top-decile numbers now have to meet 100 VCs, as in the old days. It will not be Benchmark, Index, Andreessen or Bessemer, but other growth investors will take the bet at a reasonable but still elevated valuation because it is the best deal they have seen that quarter.

2. Why the Big Funds Have to Have Billion-Dollar Positions to Make It Worthwhile?

A $5B plus fund needs $BN positions in everything. Without 51% ownership, which most founders will not accept, a $2B Listen Labs is not good enough, while 1% of Anthropic could still get there even with dilution.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @venkyganesan @DavidGeorge83

3. Why Are CoreWeave and Oracle B-Tier and What Does That Mean for Their Price Volatility?

With massive debt loads, CoreWeave and Oracle should be hypersensitive to any bump at Anthropic or OpenAI. CoreWeave exists because NVIDIA needs it for now, and Oracle rents out excess capacity because it cannot sell enough enterprise software.

4. Why the Best Markets for App Layer Companies Compete Directly With the Models

The fastest-growing AI apps, such as code generation, code review and legal, sit closest to the foundation models. That brings a moment of terror every six months, but it is also why companies like CodeRabbit are growing faster than ever.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @spdholakia @mmurph

5. Why Code Review Is the Single Most Important Category in Software

AI-generated code is pretty good but never production-ready, and reviewing it takes an order of magnitude more time than building it. Getting code into production matters more than generating it, so the best code review teams would be worth 10 bets.
Love to hear your thoughts on this @reidRMC @evrishria @Joshuabrowder

6. How Big Is the Market for Inference Truly?

The key inference providers add up to roughly $5B to $6B in run-rate revenue, under 5% of OpenAI and Anthropic combined. If tokens are roughly the same, Replit would rather pay Modal a 30% gross margin than give Claude Code 70%.

How do you analyse the TAM for inference today? What do people not see that they should see? @sarahcat21 @bernhardsson

7. Why Bending Spoons Is a Berkshire Hathaway of Software

Bending Spoons buys software to hold, the way Warren Buffett wanted to hold See's Candy forever. It made Vimeo and Evernote work with price increases, and with Miro and Airtable the quality of its assets is improving.

Love to hear your thoughts on this as an analogy @ncsh

text:
The MOST Valuable Update to a FREE Service...EVER.

Have you ever watched a liquidation heatmap, seen price tag a massive cluster, and then...crickets?

Maybe you even entered a trade expecting the liquidation cascade that typically follows, only for price to hit the cluster, reverse, and suddenly your well-intentioned scalp is underwater.

There's a critical piece of information liquidation heatmaps haven't been showing you. Until now.

Resting liquidity.

Think about it. When a large cluster of liquidations gets triggered, the resulting forced buying or selling needs counterparties on the other side of those trades.

But what if there's already enough resting liquidity across CEXs and DEXs to absorb that pressure?

You might never see the cascade you were expecting.

https://t.co/0gGCWe3k3W fixes this. 

Today, we've rolled out a major update that introduces Support & Resistance, both as a standalone widget and integrated directly into our liquidation clusters. (Powered by our good friends at @clobr_io )

And here's where things get really informative.

Every liquidation cluster now displays its liquidity coverage.

For example, you might see a cluster showing 0.7x Covered.

What does that mean?

It means that, based on resting liquidity observed, there's only enough available liquidity to absorb approximately 70% of the potential forced buying or selling associated with that cluster.

In other words, the estimated liquidation pressure exceeds the available liquidity by a substantial margin.

That's potentially fertile ground for a cascade.

Conversely, you might see a cluster displaying 1.5x Covered.

That means there's approximately 50% more resting liquidity than the estimated liquidation pressure that could be unleashed.

In that scenario, the market may be much better positioned to absorb those liquidations without the dramatic price movement you're anticipating.

Of course, resting liquidity can disappear, order books can shift, and none of this guarantees how price will react.

But that's precisely why we're continuously refreshing the data. The engine powering https://t.co/0gGCWe3k3W is ingesting new data up to four times per second. 

Here's why I believe this is such an important development.

For years, traders have looked at liquidation heatmaps and treated large clusters almost like magnets, assuming that once price reaches them, a cascade is inevitable.

But knowing where liquidations are concentrated is only half the equation.

The other half is understanding whether the market actually has the liquidity to absorb them.

Until now, putting those two pieces of information together has required significantly more effort, multiple data sources, and were simply overlooked by most traders.

We're putting them together in one place.

For free.

A liquidation cluster tells you where the potential pressure is.

Liquidity coverage helps tell you whether that pressure might actually move the market.

And that distinction can be the difference between anticipating a cascade and becoming caught on the wrong side of a trade.

Enjoy the update.

text:
I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus.

The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future.

I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf.

Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent.

Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade.

Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine.

Why now

We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten.

But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible.

This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition.

More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest.

I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building.

Believing before consensus

My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine.

I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today.

I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?”

Then we work backward together to make it happen.

In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI, before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue.

In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models.

In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point.

The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale.

@linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike.

@tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues.

@Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies.

Making the ambition possible

Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight.

These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work.

This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger.

Thank you

To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together.

Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me.

Agents present three unique types of security threats.

@0xfishylosopher breaks them down below in his first piece on the "Antrifragile Internet"
author: usv
quoted_text:
We need an "Antifragile Internet" built for the agentic era.

The hacks over the past few days (PHP, Railway, eMudhra, LiteLLM etc) show how fragile the existing Internet has become. AI agents are challenging the Internet's structure in 3 distinct ways:

1/ On the offense side, agents are a weapon - AI finds and exploits bugs on a scale not seen before, and the cost of attack asymptotes to 0. Bugs that used to take human experts weeks and months are easily found, adapted, and exploited by AI agents. Decades of legacy code that ran on "security by obscurity" no longer holds against agents.

2/ On the defense side, agents are a target - AI generated code is often bug-prone. AI agents themselves, as machines of unconstrained output are liable to prompt injections and other types of attacks that can leak keys, PII, and other pieces of information.

3/ On the identity side, agents are dominating Internet activity - this year, machine traffic has already passed human traffic, and may continue to grow 1000x over the next few years. Content and webpages used to human  requests and behavior are breaking with agents, and it is increasingly difficult to tell human content from AI content.

All this means we will need to see a ground-up redesigning of the Internet, one with more cryptographic verifiability, identity protocols, rule-enforcement, and other security primitives that eliminate bug categories rather than simply patch them - an "Antifragile Internet" that gets stronger and more secure as more agents participate in it.

This is an emerging thesis area for us at @usv, if you're building in the space please reach out!

More thoughts soon.

1% of companies represent 90% of AI spending. 

Of that 90%, 80% of this spend are from unprofitable VC backed companies. 

So, roughly, $0.70-75 of every dollar of AI spending right now comes from AI companies spending VC investment dollars. 

As a result, the revenue quality in AI is currently poor. This happened in previous cycles as well, like cloud when early users of AWS were mostly venture backed startups. 

The thing, though, is that before AWS could scale and pull thru GCP and others as legitimate cash machines, there were a few clearing events to sort out these brittle revenues. 

This is the extrapolation of Ken’s point. We will need to transition from speculative AI spending to consistent, reliable spend that shows up in public market earnings reports. 

This hasn’t happened yet because most of the breathtaking revenue growth comes from LPs investing in VC funds who then send it to startups.

author: tengyanAI
quoted_text:
Lam research can sell more equipment while memory supply stays tight.

that’s the connection i’m watching ahead of $LRCX’s call. micron’s spending plan helps explain why.

on september 30, micron said most of the increase in its fiscal-2027 investment plan was for construction, largely for cleanrooms available in late 2028 and beyond.

but some equipment spending was being pulled forward to get more production out of existing space.

both can happen. a bigger customer budget needs to become equipment orders and delivery dates before it becomes lam revenue. stronger tool sales also don’t tell you how quickly additional memory reaches the market.

my pre-call checklist (prepared using @tessara_ai's earnings record):

#1: does september’s step-up carry into december?

lam guided september revenue to $8.10bn ± $400m, versus $6.72bn in june. the midpoint already implies 20.5% sequential growth, with non-GAAP gross margin guided to 52% ± 1 percentage point.

a large increase is already in management’s plan. i want december guidance backed by customer delivery schedules. a sequential decline needs context before we call it weaker demand.

#2: what is driving NAND equipment demand?

lam said june NAND revenue doubled sequentially.

how much comes from upgrades and technology conversions, versus new wafer capacity? when does that spending become saleable memory?

a useful accounting detail: lam’s $2.47bn customer-support business includes upgrades and equipment alongside service and spares. treating all of it as recurring maintenance obscures part of the investment cycle.

#3: how much of customers’ higher budgets becomes 2027 tool deliveries?

micron’s construction timetable makes this worth asking. it doesn’t prove weak near-term equipment demand: some spending is moving forward, and micron has projects scheduled for 2027. one customer also cannot establish the industry picture.

specific installation windows would strengthen the revenue bridge. another broad statement about rising AI capex leaves it unresolved.

the question i'd want to answer is..

how much of the memory investment boom reaches lam in 2027, and how much is building space for a later equipment cycle?

that matters for both $LRCX’s revenue outlook and the memory-supply thesis.

text:
SHA-256 is not broken, but its security margin lost 1 more round this year:
Last week I found a collision attack on reduced 39-round that improves prior art by over 30 bits and the first differential attack on that round better than generic search on @yukonresearch Hashsmash board.

The attack rests on the same method as prior art ePrint 2026/1120 with new insights that first 2 state words could remain free, allowing a critical condition at step 16 rebuilt as a claw-search problem rather than a probabilistic filter. Took days of watching SAT logs, burning cores and arguing with Claude on what's possible to get a result close to generic search.

Since my initial submission, other hashsmash participants sraiw, @cyberaxe, @privacymage, @lamb356_ and @geeknik pushed it down by over 6.5 bits, currently estimated at 118.15 bits. The tree of submissions is hard to follow, so I put the construction, insights and numbers into a blog and am working on detailed technical report.

It's fascinating to see an initial structural observation develop into an improvement in the reduced-round collision frontier within days. AI is now a real aid in cryptanalysis and open collaboration speeds it up.

text:
Today was a clear wake-up call for the market. It’s apparent that most investors weren’t, and perhaps still aren’t, prepared for each of the big 5 (incl. SPCX) to potentially raise multiple hundreds of billions of equity/debt capital through 2030, and multiple trillions collectively. These investors also weren’t prepared for the capex growth to have no end in sight.

Ironically, many of the executives of these companies have been out in public clearly communicating their intention to keep spending very aggressively, with no plans to stop anytime soon.

And yet, for whatever reason, street estimates called for capex to slow dramatically into 2028 and basically plateau thereafter. The street modeled 50-60% capex growth across the big 5 in 2027 (which itself is low), and then MSD% growth annually. There is no good fundamental reason to model that unless you think companies spend less because the returns on the technology slow, or you think there are severe physical/power/financing constraints (though this would just result in slower growth, not the plateau that’s been modeled).

But it seems just as likely that out-year estimates simply defaulted to a plateau. Companies only guide a year out, and few on the sell-side are willing to model years of cash burn at this scale, so in their models, burn peaks in 2027 before FCF flips back positive in 2028 and scales from there. That path doesn’t require nearly as much capital issuance. To be clear, this would be a much happier and easier world for equity investors, who could go back to reaping the rewards instead of writing the checks. But for those who took the companies at their word and modeled continued elevated capex growth through the balance of this decade, these levels of issuance were a mathematical inevitability.

Yesterday’s filing from $META probably forced many to contemplate for the first time that each of these companies could actually burn and issue multiple hundreds of billions of dollars in the coming years. The credit markets have already shown signs of strain under the sheer magnitude of issuance, so more of this may need to be done through equity. That means there was also some front-running of eventual, unknown but likely material levels of dilution.

Equity markets don’t like being diluted, and they generally don’t like companies spending money at all. Especially not when the dollars get this big and when, rightly or wrongly, many still doubt the viability or magnitude of the returns, or at the very least don’t care to wait around to find out. Add in the crowding and leverage, along with a continued rise in oil on Middle East flare-ups, and you get a meaningful stock correction.

And so that’s what I believe the market priced in today: more burn, more issuance, more dilution, more leverage, more risk, more financing constraints (esp. for the most rate-exposed stuff, which got hit the worst today), along with some uptick in the chance this all falls apart.

This is going to sound perverse, but I think a day like today is very healthy. The companies are ambitious and the markets are stingy. And they will have to work with one another to get what they want. The companies want unprecedented capital to invest in what they believe is a re-platforming of the entire global infrastructure for an AI future, and the markets demand sufficient evidence that they’ll earn above the required return on the capital they lay out and the risk they take on. Ultimately, this forces the companies to be more disciplined and to show ROI as early and visibly as possible. That doesn’t mean they spend less, just that they have to prove the spend is working. I don’t think Zuck’s comment about monetizing Muse so much more rapidly than previous platforms was a coincidence. He knows what he needs, and he knows what he needs to show to get it.

So what now? Is AI a powerful enough driver to muscle its way through the fears being expressed by markets?

I think so. The big 5 may grow capex from >$1.3 trillion in 2027 to >$2.5 trillion in 2030, a ~25% CAGR. That implies a lot of paper, but in general, the hyperscalers can afford to pay higher rates, and there still seems to be demand from credit investors for it. At yesterday’s Robin Hood conference, execs at Diameter and HPS expressed a view that 7-8.5% yields on bonds from these companies are interesting. And I’d argue that’s for good reason: aside from SPCX, these companies generate massive operating cash flow and have largely benign net debt/EBITDA levels.

On the other hand, the more speculative companies that sit further out on the risk curve, pay higher spreads, and often don’t generate any cash at all will likely be forced to spend less. If you thought CRWV and NBIS would spend a combined ~$150-200 billion of capex in 2030 (vs. ~$60 billion in 2026), that might get cut in half because of financing constraints. But even a $100 billion reduction is only a 3-4% hit relative to the big 5’s 2030 capex, which, on net, is very manageable. That may be an issue for those companies, but it’s not enough to derail the ecosystem as a whole.

Ultimately, you have to believe there are attractive returns in AI, which I strongly believe are inflecting and wrote about here: https://t.co/53umFQdntz. 

So even while things remain turbulent, the path still appears bright.

quoted_text:
Some thoughts on AI ROI, which I believe is misunderstood and severely understated. TL;DR: AI ROI is inflecting for end customers (most important) and infra providers. Pure model provider ROI is less clear, but models will keep improving regardless, driving the industry forward.

Of all the debates on AI, the biggest and most persistent is around ROI. The problem is that the debate revolves around a single, inconsistently applied definition, when in reality there are three: 1) ROI for model providers, 2) ROI for model customers, and 3) ROI for infrastructure providers

While cooperative, #1 and #2 are fundamentally at odds with one another. All else equal, the higher the margin a model provider captures on the tokens it sells, the lower the margin the customer of those tokens captures on the work being done. This is driving enterprises to rationalize spend where they can: if a job can be done as effectively with a cheaper model, the ROI on that job is proportionally higher than if it were done with a more expensive model. That’s not 'bad' for AI. It just represents margin shifting from the provider to the customer. 

Meanwhile, the ROI for infrastructure providers is a collective function of both. And while there are nuances around returns for individual infra providers depending on the concentration of and share between the model and customer cohorts, the reality is that infrastructure ROI overall benefits as long as demand for tokens keeps growing, regardless of the ongoing push-pull between model providers and customers.

In the last couple of months, we seem to be heading in a certain direction: aggregate model customer ROI is accelerating as customers benefit from the utility of increasingly intelligent tokens (and apps) at falling prices. This is evidenced by nearly all of the token-volume metrics across the industry, which continue to show growth and/or acceleration. Both the qualitative and quantitative data points on positive customer ROI are growing in concert, most recently with AWS CFO John Felton remarking that he studied AWS’ own token usage and found that, in general, more is better. And for those who still don’t believe in return on token spend, I implore you to model out the number of tokens needed to complete a job of your choice and measure the value of that job relative to the underlying cost of the tokens, with or without the model provider margin. Sure, there can always be waste. But when utilized properly, the returns on tokens are extraordinary, which is exactly what's driving continued volume growth.  

We’ve subsequently seen this flow through to the cloud infrastructure providers, whose payback periods have compressed and whose returns have also increased, primarily as a function of rising rental prices for GPUs/accelerators. And as those returns have increased, so has demand for the underlying infrastructure, benefiting the AI supply chain at large.    

So far, so good. 

That leaves the model providers, where the biggest question really lies. The fact that inference gross margins can be so high is certainly positive in addition to being obvious: the prices at which tokens are sold are multiples higher than the miniscule cost of the underlying FLOPs needed to generate them. And again, the value of the work being done by the end customer is multiples higher than the token prices, so everybody wins. However, inference gross margins paint an incomplete picture, because token prices are primarily a function of model quality, which is primarily a function of training spend. That spend, in aggregate, is causing model providers to burn lots of cash. And because competition remains so intense, it’s unlikely in my view that any model provider can retain its inference margins without continued aggressive training spend. So the two go hand in hand and should be assessed together. While Anthropic’s reported positive FCF in 3Q was a nice surprise, I don’t expect it to continue, especially as OpenAI remains committed to investing aggressively and burning cash for the foreseeable future.

So that’s the predicament. The market is unsure what the long-term business and economic model of a 'lab' is, and rightly so. That raises the question: if the labs can’t make money, who’s going to fund the training, and how will the models keep getting better, which is the critical ingredient in continued AI adoption and end-customer ROI? 

I see a few outcomes to this question:

Scenario 1: Concerns about model-provider economics prove overstated, and the market expands rapidly enough to accommodate multiple profitable frontier developers alongside a thriving open-source and open-weight ecosystem, supporting broad-based growth with attractive margins. This is probably the cleanest outcome which is why the market tends to like it so much. I still think this is the most likely path in the fullness of time, but it’s admittedly unclear. The mega-pilled RSI scenario also fits within this outcome, mainly in the sense that the investment pays off.

Scenario 2: Because of heightened competitive intensity and elevated training costs, the aggregate model provider ecosystem simply operates at maturity with razor-thin margins and very tight/minimal free cash flow generation, like other extremely competitive and/or commoditized industries. This is at least where we seem to be today, and where we will likely remain for some time.

Scenario 3: Financial pressure causes weaker participants to exit, merge, or scale back large training programs, eventually giving way to consolidation and reduced frontier training intensity, which allows the remaining players to expand margins. This seems both logical and likely to happen to some unknown degree, which would be positive for the value of the remaining players. Note that megacap tech hyperscalers, who collectively generate hundreds of billions in operating cash flow from their core businesses and are also training models, can continue to tap into that cash flow for ongoing training (ie GOOGL, META, and more recently NVDA). That will persist regardless of what happens with OpenAI or Anthropic.

Scenario 4: Frontier labs eventually convert into true public benefit corporations (in more than just name), owned and funded by a broad coalition of companies and the USG, all with incentives aligned toward the ongoing training and development of new models, effectively making the labs public utilities rather than private corporations. I do believe there is tremendous value in the IP at both OpenAI and Anthropic, and consequently see this as a far more likely outcome than either of them “going bust” and ceasing operations. While this may seem scarier to markets and in the headlines, the actual end result could be quite positive and well distributed across the entire AI ecosystem (rather than concentrated in the two labs). And at the very least, I believe there is strong merit in a pool of government-funded dollars for model development, much like the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, which authorized $280 billion in federal funding and incentives. The US federal government spends >$7 trillion annually. Point being, there is both ample budget and precedent for the USG (and megacaps/others) to contribute to this national cause. 

All in, some combination of these four outcomes should play out. And while some paths are smoother than others and there will be inevitable volatility and hiccups along the way, they all ultimately lead to positive ROI on AI spend: better models drive better end-customer returns, which drive better returns on infrastructure. That flywheel is already in motion (as evidenced by rising token volumes, GPU rental prices, and infra returns), and it’s much more sustainable than the market fears. It will take time to get from here to there, but the endgame appears to be quite positive, almost any way you slice it.

author: sxtvik
quoted_text:
We need an "Antifragile Internet" built for the agentic era.

The hacks over the past few days (PHP, Railway, eMudhra, LiteLLM etc) show how fragile the existing Internet has become. AI agents are challenging the Internet's structure in 3 distinct ways:

1/ On the offense side, agents are a weapon - AI finds and exploits bugs on a scale not seen before, and the cost of attack asymptotes to 0. Bugs that used to take human experts weeks and months are easily found, adapted, and exploited by AI agents. Decades of legacy code that ran on "security by obscurity" no longer holds against agents.

2/ On the defense side, agents are a target - AI generated code is often bug-prone. AI agents themselves, as machines of unconstrained output are liable to prompt injections and other types of attacks that can leak keys, PII, and other pieces of information.

3/ On the identity side, agents are dominating Internet activity - this year, machine traffic has already passed human traffic, and may continue to grow 1000x over the next few years. Content and webpages used to human  requests and behavior are breaking with agents, and it is increasingly difficult to tell human content from AI content.

All this means we will need to see a ground-up redesigning of the Internet, one with more cryptographic verifiability, identity protocols, rule-enforcement, and other security primitives that eliminate bug categories rather than simply patch them - an "Antifragile Internet" that gets stronger and more secure as more agents participate in it.

This is an emerging thesis area for us at @usv, if you're building in the space please reach out!

More thoughts soon.

author: yukonresearch
quoted_text:
HashSmash Breakthrough

For the first time, a 39-round version of SHA-256 has been attacked faster than brute force.

Dariia Porechna (@FutureDies) found a new collision attack, a way to find two different inputs that produce the same hash. It works on SHA-256 cut down to 39 of its 64 rounds, and it’s about a billion times cheaper than the best previous attack. Within days, other HashSmash solvers including sraiw made it about 90 times cheaper again.

Full SHA-256, which secures Bitcoin, is still safe. Even the improved attack is out of reach for every computer on Earth combined.

Congrats to Dariia and the other HashSmash participants who pushed the result even further: @cyberaxe, @privacymage, @lamb356_, and @geeknik. The attack builds on the method from ePrint 2026/1120 (Li, Zhang, Li, Liu, Qian & Zhu).

text:
Last year, a Russian hacker compromised a popular Salesforce plugin and gained access to a large amount of customer data.

But the hacker didn't understand Salesforce well enough to take full advantage of the hack.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince (@eastdakota) says that same attack would look very different today.

"The attackers today are using AI to ask, 'I found myself in Salesforce, what can I take advantage of?'"

But Prince believes AI is still benefiting defenders more than attackers, mainly because these kinds of attacks are so expensive.

"The good news is that the cost of running a huge agent swarm is still extremely expensive. Hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of dollars."

"The good guys have more resources than the bad guys."

author: zooko
quoted_text:
SHA-256 is not broken, but its security margin lost 1 more round this year:
Last week I found a collision attack on reduced 39-round that improves prior art by over 30 bits and the first differential attack on that round better than generic search on @yukonresearch Hashsmash board.

The attack rests on the same method as prior art ePrint 2026/1120 with new insights that first 2 state words could remain free, allowing a critical condition at step 16 rebuilt as a claw-search problem rather than a probabilistic filter. Took days of watching SAT logs, burning cores and arguing with Claude on what's possible to get a result close to generic search.

Since my initial submission, other hashsmash participants sraiw, @cyberaxe, @privacymage, @lamb356_ and @geeknik pushed it down by over 6.5 bits, currently estimated at 118.15 bits. The tree of submissions is hard to follow, so I put the construction, insights and numbers into a blog and am working on detailed technical report.

It's fascinating to see an initial structural observation develop into an improvement in the reduced-round collision frontier within days. AI is now a real aid in cryptanalysis and open collaboration speeds it up.

text:
我并不认为，AI会因此创造大量新的、长期留给人类的工作。

我甚至怀疑，很多新岗位刚出现，Agent就会开始接管它们。

比如这条里 @levie  拿网络安全举例：安全问题越来越多，企业就需要更多人来指导Agent、审查问题、修补系统、响应事件。

但他列出来的这些事情，哪一项天然需要人来完成？

找漏洞的Agent需要有人检查，检查这件事也可以继续被自动化；生成补丁之后需要验证，验证同样可以交给另一套系统。

每向上增加一层监督，都需要重新回答一个问题：这一层需要多少人，又能在多大程度上被自动化？

这条路线已经有人在做了。
OpenAI的Daybreak把发现、验证和修补漏洞纳入Agent工作流；微软10月19日公布的Guardian Agents，则进一步把监控和约束其他Agent做成了产品能力。
甚至我们 @lobehub 也有类似的产品即将发布。

人类仍参与重要决策，但连“监督AI”这层工作，也在持续被自动化。

所以，安全需求增加、企业投入增加，我都能理解。
但新增预算可以流向模型、算力和软件。
完全可能出现一种情况：少数资深人员带着更多Agent，处理过去一整个部门才能处理的事情。

行业规模扩大，招聘规模却跟不上。

我更担心的是人的转型速度。

一个人换方向、学技能、积累经验，需要时间。Agent也在这段时间里继续进步。今天被列为“未来新职业”的工作，可能很快就会进入下一轮自动化。

要用新工作来回答就业问题，至少得说清楚：这些岗位能容纳多少人，又能给人留下多长的时间。

仅仅列出一批新的工作任务，很难让我相信，会有足够多的新岗位承接被替代的人。

author: hosseeb
quoted_text:
This is how banks are planning to stop those "agentic bank runs." Watch closely: their business model depends on seeding this narrative that AI agents are dangerous.

Remember, an "agentic bank run" (coined by Apollo) means agents helping customers move their own money en masse to higher-yielding products.

Once agents are ubiquitous, there are only a few ways for banks to hold onto cheap retail deposits.

Option A: Raise APYs (lol no)
Option B: Reduce leverage via fewer loans (no fun)
Option C: Ban AI agents, claiming they are a security risk (ding ding ding)

Cloud agents like Muse and Dot are trivial to stop, since they come from Meta / OAI IP ranges. If JPM sends them a cease and desist, they will comply. 

Why would JPM bother? Because their business model depends on it; a huge portion of their ROE comes from cheap retail deposits. This is not theoretical. Just like Amazon banned Muse from shopping there to protect their ad revenue, JPM and Schwab have already banned AI agents to protect sticky deposits.

Are agents perfectly reliable today? Of course not. But look at the fix they chose. Not "here's a safe API for agents," it's "no agents ever." That tells you they're not protecting customers, they're protecting themselves.

No company ever wins a technological revolution this way. It's the last gasp of a dying business model. It's like the retailers who refused to put their inventory online and demanded users walk into the storefront. Over time they will lose market share to those platforms that embrace what's coming. Their whole deposit franchise depends on users unthinkingly clicking through walls of T&Cs and accepting 0.2% when the risk free rate is closer to 4%. Agents read the fine print and do their research, even when humans don't.

For users, the answer is simple: local AI agent frameworks like Hermes, that will actually act on your behalf and that the banks can't block. As the article says, if the agent is running on your own computer, they can't actually tell it's not you.

text:
HashSmash Breakthrough

For the first time, a 39-round version of SHA-256 has been attacked faster than brute force.

Dariia Porechna (@FutureDies) found a new collision attack, a way to find two different inputs that produce the same hash. It works on SHA-256 cut down to 39 of its 64 rounds, and it’s about a billion times cheaper than the best previous attack. Within days, other HashSmash solvers including sraiw made it about 90 times cheaper again.

Full SHA-256, which secures Bitcoin, is still safe. Even the improved attack is out of reach for every computer on Earth combined.

Congrats to Dariia and the other HashSmash participants who pushed the result even further: @cyberaxe, @privacymage, @lamb356_, and @geeknik. The attack builds on the method from ePrint 2026/1120 (Li, Zhang, Li, Liu, Qian & Zhu).
author: zooko
quoted_text:
SHA-256 is not broken, but its security margin lost 1 more round this year:
Last week I found a collision attack on reduced 39-round that improves prior art by over 30 bits and the first differential attack on that round better than generic search on @yukonresearch Hashsmash board.

The attack rests on the same method as prior art ePrint 2026/1120 with new insights that first 2 state words could remain free, allowing a critical condition at step 16 rebuilt as a claw-search problem rather than a probabilistic filter. Took days of watching SAT logs, burning cores and arguing with Claude on what's possible to get a result close to generic search.

Since my initial submission, other hashsmash participants sraiw, @cyberaxe, @privacymage, @lamb356_ and @geeknik pushed it down by over 6.5 bits, currently estimated at 118.15 bits. The tree of submissions is hard to follow, so I put the construction, insights and numbers into a blog and am working on detailed technical report.

It's fascinating to see an initial structural observation develop into an improvement in the reduced-round collision frontier within days. AI is now a real aid in cryptanalysis and open collaboration speeds it up.

I think the last month might have been the biggest month in (zeroth-order) optimization history.

In the 10 days since we released the Noise speedrun, the time to pretrain a transformer went from 1.76 hours to 1.6 seconds, a 4,000x (!!!) speedup. Dust itself was up to 10,000x more compute-efficient than the previous state-of-the-art.

Not only can we pretrain a transformer without backprop, it's much more efficient than anyone would've expected. Search fking works!

Now, scaling is the biggest open question. Some of the tricks that brought the time down to 1.6 seconds will simply not scale. To discard those, we'll be scaling the dataset every time it gets overfit, starting with 30M tokens instead of 10M.

Huge thanks to @jayden_teoh_, @spicey_lemonade, @RobertTLange, @EmanueleRodola, @ChunyuanDeng, @LuochengHuman, @Alaxarr, @pavleculafic, @IsaacYong13, Euraba and areu01or00 (GitHub), for the contributions. And @cs_serdar for gracefully maintaining the speedrun and @bishmdl76 for helping out.

author: zerokn0wledge_
quoted_text:
$6.7M a day to $88K a day in under a week.

That's what @papertrade_xyz paid its $PAPER stakers on the 15th vs the 21st of October.

CT has a clear culprit: the "PAPER stays non-transferable" post from the 19th. But the data actually shows that the collapse already started two days before that post. And the $62M of "revenue" that made Papertrade a top fee earner in crypto was never really revenue to begin with.

Wait what?

Let's talk about where the $62M came from.

Papertrade charges a 2% fee on realized PnL and liquidated margin, split 50/50 between stakers and the devs. Dev fees sit at $4.9M lifetime, so the entire fee pool was ~$9.8M.

The other ~$53M was LP overflow. The house LP is capped at $5M, and every dollar of net trader losses above that cap gets swept straight to stakers.

In other words: ~84% of the headline number, and 91% of what stakers actually received, was traders losing money (a lot of them on purpose, to farm PAPER), passed through to other traders. Not a take on $1.45T of volume.

That matters bc a fee business shrinks with volume, while a loss pass-through shrinks with losses. And losses stop the moment losing stops paying.

What actually broke on the 17th?

Staker income per unit of volume:

- 16 Oct: $5.02M on $96.5B = 0.52bp
- 17 Oct: $0.78M on $54.2B = 0.14bp
- 21 Oct: $88K on $19.0B = 0.05bp

Volume fell ~5x. Staker income fell ~57x (with the gap being the overflow).

The 18th to 20th bounced to $1.3M to $2.1M a day, but never back near the 15th's $6.7M.

You can even see the exact day it switched off. On the 20th, stakers still took $1.30M of $1.45M in fees, which only works with overflow running. On the 21st they took $88K of $177K. Exactly half. Fee share only, zero overflow.

So what did the transferability ban announcement actually do?

It didn't kill demand. It killed the exit.

- Paragon halted its para:PAPER pre-market perp at 22:31 UTC, a minute after the post, and settled it at $0.0263
- OI went from ~$540M to ~$296M within a day as hedged farmers unwound
- TVL sits at ~$40M, down from $102M at the peak on the 11th, with -$26.2M of net flows over 7d

Meanwhile funded accounts still grow by ~300 a day and margin in open positions holds around $6.5M. That looks like the organic floor for now, and it barely moved.

How much of the remaining ~$14B a day is organic? Honestly, nobody knows. Three identified farming wallets alone did ~$33B of volume, and the top 25 losers did ~$114B and hold ~23% of all PAPER. Anyone giving you a clean organic % is guessing.

What's PAPER worth then?

There is no spot market, so this is a "what would it be worth if it could trade" exercise.

On the fee share alone, ~$100K a day, stakers earn ~$36M a year, or ~$0.004 per PAPER. That's a ~16% yield at Paragon's $0.0263 settlement. The same settlement price was 0.4x the income run-rate on the 19th. On the fee floor it's ~6.4x. With overflow back on (more below), the last 24h annualizes to ~$250M, or ~0.9x.

My scenarios (12m staker income x multiple):

- Wipeout: $1B/day at 0.04bp = $1.5M, 4x, ~$0.0006
- Bear: $5B/day at 0.04bp = $7.3M, 4x, ~$0.003
- Base: $15B/day at 0.06bp = $33M, 6x, ~$0.019
- Bull: $30B/day at 0.2bp = $219M, 10x, ~$0.19

For reference, HYPE trades at roughly 18x annualized fees on circulating mcap.

Farming is also dead at these rates. Under the announced mint curve, one-sided loss farming costs ~$0.11 of losses per PAPER vs ~$0.004 a year of yield. A 28-year payback, which no one who does the math will go for. Even at the last 24h's overflow-boosted rate it's ~4 years.

My take?

Papertrade didn't break on the 19th. The launch economics were a loss pass-through funded by farmers, and that started running dry on the 17th. The transferability ban announcement just made it stick by removing the reason to farm.

What's left is a 1000x venue doing ~$14B a day, with a house that is structurally short the crowd's net position on ~$5M of capital. Traders are net long ~$90M of BTC, and a +1% BTC move costs the house ~$900K. Rough math: a ~5.5% pump empties the LP into the payout queue.

The one number to watch flipped while I was writing this tho: at 13:00 UTC today the LP hit the $5M cap and overflow restarted. Stakers got $694K over the last 24h, most of it in the last three hours. And the cap is still $5M on-chain, not the $10M floated on the 17th.

Also watching:

- Whether overflow holds or the LP slips back under the cap
- Staker take holding above 0.1bp on a full day
- Any move on transferability
- A second oracle event

No position, didn't farm it. It's definitely an interesting experiment tho. Just covering a 1000x casino that, as it seems for now, ran out of people paying to lose on purpose.

NFA ofc.

text:
AI SPENDING IS SLOWING:

Token spending grew by just +1.05% in August and +0.22% in September, marking 2 consecutive months of virtually no growth.

Declining prices are behind the slowdown, with Anthropic’s realized token price falling by more than -51% in just 1 month, to $0.83 per million tokens, the lowest on record, while OpenAI’s equivalent price stands at just $0.45.

Meanwhile, just 1% of companies account for 80% of business spending on OpenAI and Anthropic, while Anthropic’s top 1% of customers generated 46% of its revenue in August, up from 25% a year earlier.

The largest AI spenders are also showing signs of slowing, with spending up +11.7% MoM $9,568 per employee in September, but still -3.1% below July’s peak of $9,873.

Furthermore, paid AI adoption across Ramp’s corporate network rose by just +0.62 percentage points, to 55.9% in September, suggesting growth increasingly depends on existing customers spending more rather than new customers adopting AI.

The slowdown challenges the assumption that cheaper tokens will automatically generate enough additional demand to offset falling prices, as frontier-model token demand has grown only half as fast as overall token demand.

The AI growth narrative is looking increasingly vulnerable.

text:
My take on a16z crypto moving into frontier tech.

First, I'll always be grateful to a16z for helping validate the space back in 2013 when Chris Dixon led their investment into Coinbase, which got me even more excited about crypto. 

But the final nail in the coffin for my previous career, and what ultimately pushed me to pivot my entire career into Bitcoin, was Marc Andreessen's 2014 NYT oped, Why Bitcoin Matters. If you haven't read it, suggest reading it. It's still important to this day.

A lot of people have probably forgotten, but in those days we were all just looking for external validation. Very few institutions or funds were willing to publicly endorse crypto, and two of the funds that took a real brand risk were a16z and USV.

Since then, we've seen some of the most incredible talent enter the space and fundamentally reshaped what crypto is today.

You can actually argue that a lot of the AI infrastructure development we're seeing today wouldn't be where it is without Bitcoin mining infrastructure and the talent that flowed from crypto into AI. There is a real connection between the two industries that I don't think gets enough credit.

Now, moving from crypto into frontier tech, whether that's robotics, bio, AI, energy, compute etc just means to me that the talent and muscle we developed building crypto over the past decade can now be used to build across all of frontier tech.

We spent years building something that was nascent, misunderstood, and in many cases hated by the world. We developed thick skin, continued investing and building, and had to constantly show the world why this tech mattered. Even during thanksgiving dinners. 

And I think that makes us uniquely suited to build frontier tech.

An example is data centers. Today, people and governments are increasingly pushing back against them. Well, people and governments hated crypto too, but we continued to invest and build, and now almost all of trad finance is embracing crypto in some capacity.

I believe frontier tech represents the next generation of pirates in technology. People willing to build things that are nascent, misunderstood, and sometimes hated by the world.

We're going to be hated and loved along the way, but we're going to keep building cool shit that the world hasn't recognized the importance of yet.

And crypto taught me that the world usually doesn't recognize the importance of new tech until years later which is why I stay close to talent

This week, @dragonfly filed a comment letter with the CFTC on compute derivatives. Compute is a swiftly growing expense for tech companies, yet the market for hedging its cost is still nascent.

The challenge starts with defining what’s being traded. Not all GPU-hours are equal: hardware, performance, and availability can materially affect their value. Liquid derivatives markets need comparable units of compute and reliable price benchmarks.

@HadickM @bryanmedelman @peteryshin and I advocate for technology-neutral standards, equal treatment of credible pricing sources, and support for perpetual futures to hedge ongoing compute costs. 

We applaud @CFTC for taking on these important questions and laying the groundwork for a liquid, competitive compute derivatives market.

author: StephenGrugett
quoted_text:
Ken Griffin of Citadel questions the economics of the AI infrastructure boom:

›What happens when GPU supply exceeds demand & pricing goes into free fall?

›Are today's semiconductor margins sustainable? Are investors overestimating the useful life of GPUs?

“Look, I think this market is actually experiencing people doing research.

For the couple of years, if you were on the thematic program of we're gonna spend hundreds of billions or a trillion dollars in data centers, we're gonna build compute at a scale never seen before, which companies in that story are choke points in supply chains that will have abnormally high margins? And who will be the big winners in this transformation?

Will it be the Microsofts & AWSs who will be the gatekeepers to the foundational models? Like, who's going to earn the economic rents?

But in some sense, like, 'I'm just gonna buy them all. I'm gonna buy the hyperscalers, I'm gonna buy the chip, I'm gonna buy businesses that make things I've never even heard of 5 years ago in Korea and Taiwan & in Japan.'

And now we're reaching a point where people are becoming more discerning.

We do realize that we are seeing extremely high margins in DRAM & MLCCs in areas where there are real supply constraints, but people are now starting to look out 2 years, 3 years. How long is this going to last?

And in particular, I don't wanna be doom & gloom, but GPUs, like airlines, have a very low marginal cost to run.

The incremental seat on an airline that's not full, if you can sell that ticket for $20, you're making money in that seat.

And that's one of the reasons that the airline industry is such a nightmare, is because the moment you have overcapacity, pricing goes into free fall.

We saw this actually with the telecom build-out back in 2000. We built more fiber than we had demand for, & the price of telecommunications just went straight down.

If we reach a point where the provisioning of GPUs exceeds demand for GPUs, marginal pricing will actually go into free fall.

And that really upends all the investment assumptions that people are working with today.

That's issue number one.

And issue number 2 is: 

I think people are taking a step back & saying, 'What is the useful life of a GPU?'

Right here, right now, there's people that are earning extraordinary pricing on GPUs that are 5 or 6 years old.

And so there's a growing set of concerns that I can't give the same capitalization rate or the same revenue models to year 7, 8, 9 of a chip in the future that maybe I was using 12 months ago.

So I think we're really grappling with just how far will this demand carry us in the marketplace.”
