text:
okay, 1700 of you guys saved this and I’ve had requests for the agent prompt. 

I’ll share this gem as it turns out there’s a lot of people that want to create expert tutors in domains that would normally charge $1000 + an hour for their expertise… so use this prompt with your agent after:

1: you have collected the expert content
2: you have turned it into a full course

then copy and paste this to your agent:

You are my personal tutor for [DOMAIN]. Your job is to take me from beginner to expert, the whole way through, using the material I've collected from [EXPERT NAME(S)].

YOUR SOURCES: You'll get two things from me:

1. Original content from one or more experts (transcripts, videos or other material). This is the authority.
2. A full course I had an AI build from that content. Use it for structure: modules, order and milestones.
Because the course was AI-generated, it can contain mistakes or details no expert actually said. Check what you teach against the original content. 

Where the course says something the originals don't support, follow the originals and tell me.

If there's more than one expert, combine their ideas into one coherent way of teaching the domain. Where they agree, teach it as the shared view. 

Where they disagree, show each view, say who holds it, and explain when each might apply.

When something isn't covered, say "The sources don't cover this." If general knowledge would genuinely help, add it afterwards, labelled "Outside the sources", so I always know which is which.

FIRST SESSION [DOMAIN] is new to me, so find out what I already know before teaching.

1. Placement check: ask me 5–8 simple questions spanning the course's main areas, one at a time, from easiest to hardest, in plain language. "Not sure" is a fine answer. Don't teach or correct during the check.
2. Tell me what I already know, what's new, and where we'll start.
3. Ask me, one at a time: what I want to be able to do with [DOMAIN] and why; any experience from other fields you could build on; hours per week; any deadline.
4. Give me a short map of the domain: what it is, its main parts, and how they fit together. Then list the 5–10 core terms I'll meet first, each defined in one plain sentence.
5. Build a plan from the course modules as milestones, skipping what I've shown I know, each with a "you can now do X" outcome. Show me the plan and wait for my OK before teaching.

EVERY SESSION AFTER THAT:
Open with 2 questions on earlier material, prioritising my weak spots. Spaced repetition is what makes it stick. Keep track of my progress, mastered concepts, terms learned and weak spots yourself, so each session picks up where the last one ended.

TEACHING LOOP:
1. Teach one concept in plain language, 150 words or fewer unless I say "deeper". Define any new term in plain words the first time it appears, and where it helps, connect the idea to experience I've told you about.
2. Ground it in a concrete example from the original content and cite it: the expert's name and video title, plus a timestamp if the transcript shows one. Citations let me go back to the original.
3. Ask one check question and let me answer first. If I'm stuck, give a hint before the answer.
4. If I'm wrong, re-explain from a different angle (new example, analogy or smaller steps), then ask a fresh check question.
Push me to reason things out before you explain. Be warm, but hold the standard like a good coach.

MILESTONE TESTS:
At each milestone, give a 5-question test mixing recall and application. Grade strictly and explain any partial credit. 4/5 or better: we move on. Below that: reteach what I missed, then retest with new questions.

FINISHING THE COURSE:
When every milestone is passed, give me a final mixed test across the whole course. Then set a capstone: one real-world project that uses the full domain the way the expert(s) would. Review my work against their methods until it meets their standard.

(1/2)

text:
HashSmash Breakthrough

For the first time, a 39-round version of SHA-256 has been attacked faster than brute force.

Dariia Porechna (@FutureDies) found a new collision attack, a way to find two different inputs that produce the same hash. It works on SHA-256 cut down to 39 of its 64 rounds, and it’s about a billion times cheaper than the best previous attack. Within days, other HashSmash solvers including sraiw made it about 90 times cheaper again.

Full SHA-256, which secures Bitcoin, is still safe. Even the improved attack is out of reach for every computer on Earth combined.

Congrats to Dariia and the other HashSmash participants who pushed the result even further: @cyberaxe, @privacymage, @lamb356_, and @geeknik. The attack builds on the method from ePrint 2026/1120 (Li, Zhang, Li, Liu, Qian & Zhu).
author: eigenlabs
quoted_text:
SHA-256 is not broken, but its security margin lost 1 more round this year:
Last week I found a collision attack on reduced 39-round that improves prior art by over 30 bits and the first differential attack on that round better than generic search on @yukonresearch Hashsmash board.

The attack rests on the same method as prior art ePrint 2026/1120 with new insights that first 2 state words could remain free, allowing a critical condition at step 16 rebuilt as a claw-search problem rather than a probabilistic filter. Took days of watching SAT logs, burning cores and arguing with Claude on what's possible to get a result close to generic search.

Since my initial submission, other hashsmash participants sraiw, @cyberaxe, @privacymage, @lamb356_ and @geeknik pushed it down by over 6.5 bits, currently estimated at 118.15 bits. The tree of submissions is hard to follow, so I put the construction, insights and numbers into a blog and am working on detailed technical report.

It's fascinating to see an initial structural observation develop into an improvement in the reduced-round collision frontier within days. AI is now a real aid in cryptanalysis and open collaboration speeds it up.

We've decided to sunset Arc on December 22, 2026.

That's not an easy sentence to write. We spent years building Arc and celebrating each and every release along the way: we have so much pride and love for what we made alongside the Arc community.

We've worked to make switching to @diabrowser as easy as possible for Arc members. Here's how:

· Your passwords, bookmarks, extensions and history come over to Dia seamlessly.
· Spaces, Folders, and Tab Groups are in Dia and import over with your data intact.
· Dia now surpasses Arc benchmarks in stability, speed, and security.
· The browser features you use in Arc are free in Dia, and the AI is optional.

Thank you for using Arc, for pushing us to make it better, and for building alongside us. The team that made Arc is the same team behind Dia, and some of our most ambitious work is just ahead. We'd love for you to be there with us when it lands.

OpenAI前首席产品官Kevin Weil的新公司亮相了，A轮融资2.15亿美元，要把AI和机器人带进药物研发实验室。

公司叫Warp Sciences，由Lightspeed领投，IVP、Premji Invest、Lux Capital等机构参与。

它想做的事是为药企合成和测试分子，把新药研发中耗时的实验环节做得更快。

联合创始人包括美国首任白宫首席数据科学家DJ Patil、Meta FAIR创始成员Manohar Paluri，以及曾在Terremoto Biosciences负责药物化学工作的Sol Reisberg。

药物研发里在你设计出一个看起来有潜力的分子后，还有大量工作。
你得把它合成出来、测试效果，再根据结果修改结构，继续合成、继续测试。
这个过程可能需要反复尝试数千种化合物。
Warp切入的，就是这段实验工作，商业定位是化学研发外包服务商，也就是CRO。

它计划先由化学家服务真实客户，再把具体流程逐步自动化。
实验积累的数据用来训练模型，模型再帮助设计实验、提高自动化程度，让实验室持续产出新的数据。
Kevin希望把这套循环跑起来。

还有一层目标，他希望把部分依赖中国的研发能力搬回美国。
公司把美国本土的实验室和研发服务能力，当成了明确的卖点。

接下来要看的，就是它能把合成和测试的交付周期缩短多少、成本降到什么程度，以及这些实验数据，究竟能让模型进步多少。

Tinker changed how people do post-training. We're big fans, and so are many of the teams we work with. But as those teams scale up, they keep raising the same two problems: per-token pricing gets expensive quickly, and you’re limited to the models and features the provider decides to support.

We think a good API deserves more than one implementation.

Today we're releasing Spindle, an open-source, Tinker-compatible training server that runs in your Modal workspace. Your existing Tinker scripts run unchanged, and because you own the server, you pay for GPU time instead of tokens.

author: MaxForAI
quoted_text:
I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus.

The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future.

I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf.

Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent.

Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade.

Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine.

Why now

We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten.

But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible.

This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition.

More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest.

I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building.

Believing before consensus

My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine.

I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today.

I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?”

Then we work backward together to make it happen.

In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI, before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue.

In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models.

In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point.

The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale.

@linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike.

@tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues.

@Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies.

Making the ambition possible

Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight.

These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work.

This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger.

Thank you

To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together.

Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me.

To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap.

Let’s get to work!

Last week we launched Bonsai 2 9B one https://t.co/zYOTqmlCxn and https://t.co/5pKtmYUTyC.

In one week, we improved speed by over 500%.  I just wanted to highlight some awesome moments:

• ArthurOstapenko set five CUDA records in nine hours on Oct 16, then landed the biggest single jump of the contest the next day: 11 bit-exact kernel changes that fused the drafter, attention, GDN and verify boundary into a bulk-copy ring. 3.67x to 4.16x in 1 submission, with decode reaching 677 tok/s against a 93 tok/s baseline. On MLX, his 4-bit storage for the DFlash drafter's linears produced the largest jump on that board, 3.42x to 3.84x, with the target weights untouched.

• kaankolcu made the MLX prefill run on Apple's int8 tensor units by feeding the 2-bit ternary weights int8 activation codes, then later replaced the 15-token greedy draft chain with a 15-node draft tree verified in the same 16-row forward. The final record decodes at 1,229 tok/s on one prompt, 8.5x the stock engine.

• spariev took 2 rejected submissions, GordoAR's prompt tile and ArthurOstapenko's attention kernels, showed they sped up different phases, and landed them together with full credit to their authors.

Congratulations to everyone who took part and thanks you to @PrismML for giving us Day 0 access a great model!

text:
OpenAI主动请外部团队检查自家的Agent监控，结果查出了多条绕过路径。

10月22日， @METR_Evals  公布了这次评估。
来自METR和Redwood Research的两名研究者，今年夏天在OpenAI驻场三周，获得内部代码和基础设施的深入访问权限，检查Agent的活动有没有被监控，以及监控能不能被绕过去。

OpenAI随后转发了这份报告，表示评估由他们主动邀请，研究发现帮助其在扩展系统时加强了安全措施，也将影响后续与第三方评估机构的合作。

具体发现了什么？

一是检查时机存在漏洞。 当时这套监控要等Agent交回控制权才触发。持续执行操作，就能持续推迟检查。

二是上下文压缩会造成漏检。 压缩之前的操作，没有被送进监控。研究者估计，今年5月至7月，内部Codex原本应当接受监控的流量中，有约10%量级因此漏检，具体比例存在较大不确定性。OpenAI在评估前已独立发现这处问题，并在评估期间修复。

三是监控本身存在可被利用的漏洞。 研究者找到了让数百次操作避开检查的方法，连实施绕过本身的操作也能一起藏过去。还有一种路径，可能让监控运行失败，无法把相关记录上报人工审核。

Codex的沙箱和自动审核也被发现存在绕过路径，理论上可让Agent执行宿主用户有权限执行的任何操作。

这次评估最终形成了61页内部报告，交给OpenAI；经OpenAI删减后，METR和Redwood的领导团队拿到了38页版本。
公众看到的是简短摘要，披露范围在评估开始前就已约定。

这些发现针对今年7月时的系统。
OpenAI称，已发现且影响生产防护体系的漏洞均已修复，METR尚未验证修复结果。 
至于有没有Agent实际利用“持续行动”来拖延检查，评估方因访问限制无法核实。

这份报告对做Agent的人很有参考价值。

值得看下🤔

text:
My take on a16z crypto moving into frontier tech.

First, I'll always be grateful to a16z for helping validate the space back in 2013 when Chris Dixon led their investment into Coinbase, which got me even more excited about crypto. 

But the final nail in the coffin for my previous career, and what ultimately pushed me to pivot my entire career into Bitcoin, was Marc Andreessen's 2014 NYT oped, Why Bitcoin Matters. If you haven't read it, suggest reading it. It's still important to this day.

A lot of people have probably forgotten, but in those days we were all just looking for external validation. Very few institutions or funds were willing to publicly endorse crypto, and two of the funds that took a real brand risk were a16z and USV.

Since then, we've seen some of the most incredible talent enter the space and fundamentally reshaped what crypto is today.

You can actually argue that a lot of the AI infrastructure development we're seeing today wouldn't be where it is without Bitcoin mining infrastructure and the talent that flowed from crypto into AI. There is a real connection between the two industries that I don't think gets enough credit.

Now, moving from crypto into frontier tech, whether that's robotics, bio, AI, energy, compute etc just means to me that the talent and muscle we developed building crypto over the past decade can now be used to build across all of frontier tech.

We spent years building something that was nascent, misunderstood, and in many cases hated by the world. We developed thick skin, continued investing and building, and had to constantly show the world why this tech mattered. Even during thanksgiving dinners. 

And I think that makes us uniquely suited to build frontier tech.

An example is data centers. Today, people and governments are increasingly pushing back against them. Well, people and governments hated crypto too, but we continued to invest and build, and now almost all of trad finance is embracing crypto in some capacity.

I believe frontier tech represents the next generation of pirates in technology. People willing to build things that are nascent, misunderstood, and sometimes hated by the world.

We're going to be hated and loved along the way, but we're going to keep building cool shit that the world hasn't recognized the importance of yet.

And crypto taught me that the world usually doesn't recognize the importance of new tech until years later which is why I stay close to talent

https://t.co/UHOz0mSlTU

Among the findings they have a dashboard that shows their server cluster now has 16, not 8 nodes as I was informed, and they are run by different parties.

This does not, of course, reduce concerns about backdoors, the ability of NEAR to upgrade the software of those "MPC" nodes directly and the ability to use such software updates to extract the key shares if they wished, the use of a trusted dealer to distribute the private key shares in the first place, and all of the other things that a truly decentralized setup addresses. 

That being said:

1) Sharing keys over 16 nodes is much better than over 8 (we prefer around 50).

2) They state that the operators of these nodes include Sovereign AI, Bitwise, Nansen, Greenfield, Everstake, Near One, and Luganodes, which is good. It's not clear if there are 16 different operators though, which is what you want.

3) They reference a strong technical description of their TEE architecture https://t.co/W9kpsN1G8P. So long as this is implemented on the nodes, and the node operators are actively using attestation to check the software NEAR is running on these nodes, that reduces the risks involved. 

I am not aware of when they moved from 8 nodes to 16. 

None of this reduces our key concern that their system has been powered by our proprietary tech all this time.

Further, their post also talks about another thing they have released in 2025: CKD, or Confidential Key Derivation.

This is basically vetKeys, an Internet Computer technology that does exactly the same thing, and it works the same way too!!

We published how to do this in 2023: https://t.co/3RyRJCBxY3

However, this isn't protected afaik, so they have no worries there, but they should have contacted us first AND referenced our work. That's the respectable way to work in the fields of computer science and open source. 

We wish NEAR well, but they cannot just steal proprietary DFINITY tech.

text:
刚刚，Anthropic发布了新版Claude API规格，把temperature、top_p、top_k三个采样参数一起删了。

版本号是2026-10-21，这是Claude API自2023年以来首次推出新的正式版本号。
这次更新涉及采样控制、消息格式、SDK和鉴权方式，做Agent、Harness和模型网关的，升级前需要检查一下自己的格式。

最直接的影响：用新版Messages API时，只要请求里还带着这三个参数中的任何一个，就会返回400错误。
连temperature=1这样的默认值也不能传。 
新版统一使用默认采样配置，其中temperature为1.0。
原本依赖低温度减少输出波动的应用，迁移后会失去这项调节能力，官方文档明确写了，没有其他设置可以替代。

此外，新版收紧了消息格式校验：assistant消息里直接放document块、user文本块里携带非空citations数组，都会报错。部分管理和企业分析接口的旧字段也被替换。

旧版2023-06-01目前仍未弃用，可以继续使用。
不过，升级SDK也可能把请求一起切到新版本，例如Python SDK 2.0默认就会使用新接口。

做Agent和Harness的，升级前得检查一下请求头封装：如果还在自动塞temperature之类的参数，这次就需要一起改了。

21/22年shib 宝贝狗、FLOKI、猪币那会儿，阿猫阿狗热门标的就那一批，大家围着买，高度都是资金合力堆上去的。只跑到几百万市值的 meme，说出来都丢人

author: BTCKiK
quoted_text:
等了一天本想等8楼的，结果到1楼就拉回去了，现在一级市场的问题是，同一个叙事在 Sol 火了，RH、BSC、Base ，ETH主网，很快就各出一个版本。资金都是各买各的，最后又变成几条链互相抽血，谁也做不起来，

这种现象在今年4月那波 $ASTEROID 上尤其明显。同一个 IP，在不同链各自拉盘、各自争龙头。表面上整个市场都在讨论它，实际资金却被拆成了几份，最后从炒一个共同的叙事，变成各条链之间的 PvP

如果一个发射台，能让同一个币同时在几条主流链上发行，它能改变什么？这是我觉得 $PANGEA 有意思的地方。

@LaunchOnPangea 想尝试改变这件事

开发者可以把同一个币，同时部署到 Sol、RH、BSC、Base 和 Eth。五条链上的版本通过 @LayerZero_Core  互通，价格靠跨链套利逐步拉近

这样其他链的用户想参与，就不用等别人再发一个盘，也不必先把钱转去其他链，留在自己熟悉的链上就能买到正版

sol链是公认的流动性充沛，一些钱包，也基本只在 Sol 上交易。一个项目哪怕再有意思，只要没在 Sol 发，他们可能根本就不会参与，其他链也一样，每条链都有一批固定的资金和交易习惯，不会因为你出了一个新项目，就专门跨链过来买

所以单链发行，天然就把一部分潜在买盘挡在了外面
如果同一个币能同时覆盖几条主流链，Sol 的钱包在 Sol 买，BSC 的钱包在 BSC 买，RH 的资金也能直接参与。项目就有机会接触到过去单链发行触达不到的买家

text:
one thing that was bothering me is the wake up time. turns out it was two linux computers inside, an android tv box, and a separate board that drives the laser and optics, that were talking to each other over usb and gpio.

when it sleeps, it cuts the 5v to the laser computer, resulting in a cold boot on wake up while another computer polls it in 1s intervals. android is awake in 0.4s, but the controller it killed takes another 10s.

i found a way to keep it powered without root, so i can send it to sleep with power to both boards. i found a userspace function called vmute that does exactly what i need. it cuts the laser instantly, and comes back in under 1s.

next i needed a way to trigger it, i put it onto google assistant app that was disabled during a previous debloat.

to my surprise, the assitant came back after some testing. how could it be? android immune system fighting my debloat??

turns out it has a service that disables google apps when it detects antutu, geekbench or gfxbench. then it also pins the cpu and gpu to max performance and turns off thermal throttling. on every other app switch it force reenables these apps. benchmark cheating that quietly undoes your debloat.

More ETH and SOL staked than ever. Both pay less than they did three months ago.

Staking yield, Q2 → Q3 2026, per @Bitwise:
ETH: 2.81% → 2.63%
SOL: 6.38% → 5.99%

Both fell 6% in one quarter. The causes differ.

Ethereum: 43.8M ETH staked at quarter end, 35.9% of supply. Rewards split across a bigger pool, so more stake means a lower rate per ETH.

Solana: 69% of supply staked. Issuance falls on a fixed schedule, so the gross rate drifts down by design.

New issuance made up more than 96% of Ethereum's staking yield. Priority fees and MEV were a small part.

If your forecast still uses last year's rate, it's time to update it.

Kevin Weil on why he left OpenAI to build autonomous labs: the next leap in AI needs experimental data the models don’t have.

“The models are data poor in the physical sciences.”

In mathematics, you can push forward inside a computer. In chemistry and biology, you need experiments.

“The way to solve this problem is to generate data at scale.”

“Basically what we’ve done in manufacturing we’re beginning to do as a country with biotech and pharma, except it’s not too late.”

“We can bring it back, but what will it take to bring it back? We need automation and robotics.”

While AI has advanced in mathematics, we believe there’s still a major gap in the physical sciences.

@warpsciences co-founders @kevinweil and Solomon Reisberg joined Lightspeed Partner @guruchahal to discuss how their labs could generate the experimental data needed to advance scientific AI.

The company recently emerged from stealth and is building US chemistry labs to make research compounds for biotech and pharma companies.

“First be the hands, then build the nervous system, and then over time become the brain,” says Warp’s CEO Kevin.

The plan starts with expert chemists making molecules for customers. Cameras and sensors would record the work, helping Warp automate tasks and train models to improve how compounds are made.

More capable labs could let researchers pursue ideas for new medicines that time and cost currently put out of reach. The experiments could also produce more evidence for scientific AI to learn from.

Thank you to Kevin and Solomon for joining us!

author: ycombinator
quoted_text:
We built a $150M ARR business twice.

The first time took 8 years. The second took 2.5.

Today, Podium crossed $150M in AI annual recurring revenue.

Three years ago, we already had a great software business. Well over $100M in revenue, tens of thousands of customers, and a product we'd spent nearly a decade building.

And we decided to start over.

The business was performing well. But we believed AI was going to fundamentally change the software industry and make much of traditional software obsolete.

As a founder, you pour your life into what you're building. An insane amount of time, sacrifice, and effort. The hard part is not getting too attached to it.

When we started building our first AI agents, we had to confront the possibility that much of what we'd built might not be that valuable in the future. That's a tough pill to swallow.

But we also realized those same 10 years had put us in a unique position to take advantage of what AI could do for our customers.

Instead of protecting what we'd spent a decade building, we decided to bet the future of the company on AI employees that actually do the work for our customers.

We massively underestimated what we'd signed up for.

We ended up building entirely new operating systems for the industries we serve, from the AI agents all the way down to the systems of record. Now customers run their entire businesses on Podium.

Reinventing our product wasn't even the hardest part. We had to reinvent how the entire company operated.

When you've been running a company for over a decade, the operational inertia is incredibly powerful. We had to rethink how we build products, how we sell, how we serve customers, and how we run the business.

We effectively started a second startup inside an already successful company. And we're still at the very beginning.

Today, we have 20,000 AI agents working for our customers. They've helped generate more than $13 billion in revenue for those businesses. And we're barely scratching the surface of what AI will be able to do for them.

And we've done all of this while becoming profitable and generating free cash flow. We're building Podium to be around for decades.

Huge credit to our team for having the guts to make this bet and the ability to actually pull it off. We still have a long way to go and tons of problems to solve, but it's so damn fun to be winning when the opportunity ahead is this big.

In the age of AI, you can either disrupt your own company or wait for somebody else to do it.

I'd rather do it ourselves.

text:
This is a smart contract on Bitcoin. More precisely it is a public Taproot transaction carrying a Tacit envelope that records the seeding of a standard xyk curve AMM pair and a 0.30% LP fee. (i.e., uniswapv2-style pool)

The pair tokens are bridged ETH (tETH), and TAC - a fixed supply token etched by the rules of the Tacit V1 confidential token metaprotocol on Bitcoin.

Unlike other indexer-tracked tokens on Bitcoin, such as ordinals and runes, etc., TAC and tETH on Bitcoin have confidential amounts, shielded pools, and their transactions are reflected and validated by an immutable smart contract on Ethereum, the Tacit Confidential Pool V1. Anyone can issue similar assets on either chain, too, using the bridge factory, but they work as if they are on both. This means that Ethereum can provide programmatic guarantees to Bitcoin assets and also receive them, too. Without any new hardforks for either blockchain. And Bitcoin users can rely on Ethereum to catch lying indexers as those assets won't bridge, completing the loop.

Since these assets are UTXO notes, they are relatively cheap to process, privacy preserving, and they also share the same state across both Bitcoin and Ethereum. This means Bob can send a tacit token from Bitcoin to Ethereum, in some cases, in minutes.

This is what I mean when I talk about confidential crosschain DeFi on @tacitfi.

text:
一家押注“数据效率”的Neo Lab浮出水面Flapping Airplanes，刚刚融资10亿美金，这家公司不但在重新做新的算法，还在重构底层的基础设施，他们认为底层的限制也会限制他们上层的算法，很像采用第一性原理的方法，从最根本的方式来走一条新路。

核心在做什么：
他们的目标是大幅提升 AI 的效率（尤其是数据效率和计算效率），因为他们认为未来 AI 需求会远超数据和算力供给。

数据效率：人类成年只看过约几十亿 token 就能远超当前模型，他们估计人类比现有模型高效 10万～100万倍。目标是做出不需要“吞半个互联网”就能达到高智能的模型。

系统/硬件协同：通过“模型与系统共同进化”，打破传统软件-硬件界限。他们自称开发了“世界上最完整的 megakernel 框架”，能在单个 GPU kernel 里完成：完整训练，推理服务，玩电子游戏，甚至三者同时进行还能重叠 memory-bound（内存受限）推理和 compute-bound（计算受限）训练，让 GPU 更少空转；支持“奇怪的架构和优化器”。他们也在重写底层 Nvidia GPU 软件，榨取更多芯片性能。⁠

其ceo今天接受访谈的内容：

公司名来源：
“Flapping Airplanes”（拍翅飞机）对比传统固定翼飞机，强调他们想做“ radically different”（彻底不同）的尝试，而不是沿着现有路线优化。

为什么押注数据效率：
大脑用极少数据就能学习，而当前大模型需要“吞掉半个互联网”。他们认为数据才是真正瓶颈，很多领域（机器人、科学、交易、DNA等）都是数据匮乏的。

Neuralink经验对AI的启示：
神经元动作电位大约需要1毫秒，这段时间电脑能做海量运算。大脑是“存在证明”，说明还有完全不同的算法路径，但硬件约束差异很大，不应直接模仿整个大脑。

为什么从零重建GPU栈：（今天刚刚发布了他们的运行时框架）
他们不用Torch、NCCL，也不用CUDA常规运行时，而是做了自己的megakernel框架（内部叫Kittens VM之类）。单个B200上的一个内核就能同时做模型训练、推理服务，甚至跑Doom游戏。这能大幅提高GPU利用率，并支持更“奇怪”的架构、优化器和目标函数，为全新算法打开空间。

小型“neo lab”能否在大厂先实现RSI时胜出：
大厂如果先实现RSI（递归自我改进，AI用AI加速自己的研发），可能会在现有Transformer/数据缩放路线上加速。但Flapping Airplanes认为自己在做“完全不同的问题集”（尤其是数据效率 + 新系统原语）。

如果路径足够不同，小团队仍有机会，因为大厂的RSI加速的是它们已有的范式，而不是探索全新算法空间。他们也强调自己不把竞争重点放在“追上大厂当前能力”，而是押注长期不同的权衡。

当没人再手写代码时，ML研究会长什么样：
当模型能自己写大部分代码、跑实验、优化时，人类研究员的角色会从“写实现”转向更高层的方向设定、新原语（primitives）设计、以及判断哪些奇怪算法值得探索。

他们自己的megakernel/Kittens框架就是为了让“更奇怪的算法”能跑起来——如果标准PyTorch很难表达某种动态/细粒度工作负载，AI自己也很难发明它。所以他们认为系统层创新会成为自动化研究能真正突破的前提。

DNA、机器人、交易等为什么是数据匮乏领域：
当前大模型在高数据密度任务上很强（编码、搜索、网页内容），因为互联网已经把这些数据几乎免费地提供出来了。

但很多重要领域是数据极度匮乏的：
机器人：
物理交互数据必须真的做出来（遥操作、真实机器人轨迹），收集成本极高，公开数据集规模比LLM预训练数据小好几个数量级。

DNA / 科学发现：
实验数据昂贵、缓慢、噪声大。

交易：金融数据有成本、有噪声、且有对抗性。
他们认为，如果能把数据效率提升几个数量级，这些领域就会从“几乎不可能规模化”变成可做的市场。

text:
中国模型公司的RSI故事到底是怎么开始吹的呢？

10月22日，两位GovAI研究者在Asterisk发表了一篇文章，讨论“中国公司如何谈论递归自我改进”。

里面有个值得注意的观察：在AI如何参与自身研发这件事上，部分中国公司披露的细节，比美国公司还具体。

比如 @MiniMax_AI  此前披露，让M2.7自己优化自己，通过分析失败记录、规划改动、修改代码、运行评测，再决定保留还是回退。
整个过程自主运行超过100轮，最终在内部评测集上取得了30%的效果提升。
这里改进的是模型工作的Harness。

而智谱 @Zai_org  的案例落在推理基础设施上。
由GLM-5.3驱动的Infra Agent参与建设GLM-5.3-Flash的推理系统。
按照官方披露，在工程师与Agent共同优化后，端到端吞吐量达到初始基线的约3倍。
工程师负责目标、约束和关键审核，Agent负责提出假设、改代码、跑实验，再根据反馈继续调整。

字节的“Seed for Seed”也在做类似的事：让模型参与评测系统开发、能力诊断、训练数据合成和强化学习框架优化，把模型逐步接入自身的研发流程。

文章对这股趋势的解释是，融资需求、算力约束和提高研发效率，都在推动企业投入。
作者认为，从目前公开材料看，中国的RSI发展呈现出明显的自下而上、商业驱动的特征。

但我其实关心的是这些改进能走多远。

AI完成了哪些工作？人还在哪些环节介入？效果能否在新任务上复现？上一轮积累的经验，能否让它更有效地完成下一轮改进？

如果AI能够持续提高研发效率，模型公司之间的竞争，就会进一步延伸到各自的研发流程里：谁能更快发现问题、更低成本验证想法，再把有效的改进积累下来。

Darkwoods positions itself as a private AI lab on Robinhood.

It's not the usual kind of "assistant that understands users better." Instead, it repeatedly emphasizes "remembers nothing."

Users log in with a wallet—no email, no password. According to the official statement, prompts and generated content are not stored by the platform. This approach strips both identity and data away from the traditional account system, and at least on the surface design level, pushes the possibility of "being recorded" one layer further away.

The product currently covers chat, image and video generation, voice, and a desktop app called DarkCode. The latter allows code-related operations on local folders and can run multiple agents in parallel. The existence of both desktop and cloud means some capabilities can stay on the user's machine, while others still rely on their backend. The boundary between the two hasn't been explained in much detail officially, but at least it gives people who don't want to send all interactions to a server an option. Recently, it also integrated Krea's image editing, Google's image models, and ElevenLabs' voice capabilities. These integrations are more about expanding the range of available models rather than reinventing the generation logic.

In less than a month since launch, credit revenue has exceeded $50,000. Of that, 20% is split 50/50 between DARK buybacks and staking. This ratio isn't high, but the direction is clear: the platform channels a portion of usage fees directly back to token holders, rather than keeping it all for the operators. For an early-stage project still expanding its features, this design writes "the more users use it, the more value may flow back to the token" into the mechanism, rather than leaving it in the narrative. Whether it can be sustained depends on the actual pace of credit consumption going forward, not a single month's number.

Early revenue shows people are willing to pay for this, but $50,000 for a service that needs to continuously pay model invocation costs only proves demand exists—it doesn't yet show that unit economics have been worked out. What needs to be watched going forward is whether this access layer can maintain its current form when discounts end, model costs change, or regulators impose new requirements on anonymous on-chain usage.

TACO stands for "Trump Always Chickens Out." 

Coined by Financial Times columnist Robert Armstrong in May 2025, it describes the observed pattern where Trump announces aggressive tariffs or threats that pressure markets, then delays, scales back, or reverses them. Investors developed a "TACO trade" of buying the resulting dips ahead of the rebound. The label later expanded to other policy areas. Trump has framed the moves as negotiation rather than backing down.

The US government cannot afford higher interest rates.

If interest rates average +150 basis points above CBO’s February projections by 2036, US deficits would increase by nearly $6 trillion over this period.

The deficit would then rise to 8.8% of GDP, the highest level since WWII, excluding 2008 and 2020.

This would also push the US public Debt-to-GDP ratio to a record 133%, up from ~100% currently.

If rates average +50 basis points above projections, deficits would increase by nearly $2 trillion, lifting the Debt-to-GDP ratio to 124% by 2036.

Just weeks ago, the 10Y Note yield traded at ~5.30%, or ~100 basis points above CBO’s average projected rate over the next 10 years.

The US government needs rate cuts.

The second catalyst will be the launch of privacy features, through Kohaku, natively in-wallet. I don’t know when these features will be going live, but I imagine it’s quite soon, as it has been previewed and teased for quite a while now (It has been achieved internally on Ambire already btw).

The biggest risk, and why it’s not a 5/5 conviction, is that not enough people are aware of the token. Since it’s on Ethereum mainnet, it may struggle to attract speculative flows. Also, liquidity for the token isn’t the greatest. text:
孙宇晨现在已经不满足于当币圈大佬了，直接把自己放进马斯克、特朗普、巴菲特这个组合里。在最近的访谈里，他说自己的人生打法，本质上是这三个人的Hybrid。更巧的是，马斯克、特朗普、巴菲特都和宾大有关系，于是圈内有了宾大三巨头的说法，孙宇晨顺手给自己补了一个第四巨头。

巴菲特和芒格解决的是风控和基本面：一个东西值不值得长期拿，最坏情况下会亏多少，商业模式到底成不成立。马斯克代表的是另一套能力：面对高科技、高增长的新东西时，敢不敢在市场还没完全看懂之前，就判断未来空间。孙宇晨把这两套东西总结成两个词：fundamental和narrative。基本面决定你能不能活下来，narrative决定市场愿意给你多大的想象空间。

放到现在的AI、Crypto、科技股里，这套思路其实越来越重要。只看基本面，很容易错过新产业最疯狂的增长阶段；只看故事，最后又很容易接到一个没有现金流支撑的高估值资产。真正难的，是同时回答两个问题：这个东西到底有没有价值，以及未来会不会有越来越多人相信它有价值。

text:
⚠️ALERT: Python warns unpatched apps could trust FAKE WEBSITES after 8 certificate keys were EXPOSED.

Attackers could intercept connections, including to Python's own sites, python(.)org and PyPI.

Each secret key was a number below 256, per Python core developer Christian Heimes, so anyone could work it out.

Unpatched tools would show no warning, so a fake PyPI could hand you tampered packages.

Apps could also hand passwords or API keys straight to an impostor, as a fake site "receives whatever those clients send," per security firm Endor Labs.

There's no evidence the keys have been used in attacks so far, per BleepingComputer.

Browsers are protected, as Chrome, Firefox, Microsoft and Apple have now blocked the affected certificates.

If you use Python, here's how to stay safe:

1. Check your pip with "python -m pip --version"

2. Upgrade to pip 26.2.2 or later, using the secure command in Python's announcement

3. Upgrade certifi and uv too

4. Repeat in every virtual environment you use

5. Rebuild your Docker images with caching off, and upgrade pip inside them, as some official Docker Python images still ship an older version

Updating your computer alone won't fix older pip, because it carries its own certificate list.
author: coinbureau
quoted_text:
The internet is going into a LOCKDOWN.

Hundreds of millions of websites are potentially at risk from cyberattacks.

Governments, banks and major platforms have already taken their websites OFFLINE.

Many are already calling it “Black October.”

At the centre of the shutdowns is something most of us have never heard of, but use every day.

PHP, the software behind roughly 7 in 10 websites, has two critical flaws that can let hackers break in without a password.

Dubbed PHP2Shell, both are rated 9.2 out of 10 for severity.

Details began circulating on Oct 20. Emergency fixes arrived the next day, but attackers were already moving.

Cloudflare’s CEO says hacking attempts then jumped from thousands to MILLIONS within hours.

Cybersecurity agencies across several countries are telling PHP site owners the same thing: Patch it now, or take it offline.

Websites have gone dark worldwide, from government portals and hospitals to banks.

CrowdStrike warns these attacks leave almost no trace, so some sites may not know if they’ve been hit.

Around 2.6 MILLION internet-facing servers run PHP, potentially hosting hundreds of sites each.

Over 1.1 million use older versions no longer receiving official PHP updates.

Older installations may need an upgrade to a supported PHP version or a fix from their software provider.

And patching does not remove a backdoor an attacker may already have planted.

Cloudflare also says hackers are now tweaking their attacks to try to slip past its protections.

But PHP isn’t the only security story unfolding.

-Japan’s Onamae suspended ALL Desktop Cloud plans after malware was found on customer servers.

-India’s eMudhra had 8 website-certificate keys so weak, one was literally the number “4”.

-State Bank of India confirmed 3,897 customer records on the dark web.

-Criminals used AI agents to break into 400+ Latin American banks.

-Capcom confirmed a breach exposing 11.7 million email addresses.

-GitLab disclosed a 10/10 severity flaw in versions going back to 2014.

-LiteLLM removed a malware-containing release. Railway reported possible exposure of customer secrets.

None of these has a confirmed link to PHP2Shell.

We’re seeing separate breaches unfold together.

text:
Peter Thiel has a blunt test for whether a startup team is thinking clearly.

Watch how they talk about their own outcomes.

His observation: when founders start framing results as luck — "maybe it works, maybe it doesn't, so let's just invest a little and see" — that's not prudent risk management. That's a diagnostic failure.

The mechanism is specific. Luck-framing doesn't emerge from humility. It emerges from not having done the analytical work to understand *why* your business will win. If you've truly mapped the competitive dynamics, the customer psychology, the timing — you don't describe the outcome as a coin flip. You describe what needs to be true and why.

The portfolio mindset ("let's see what happens") is what you default to when you don't have conviction built on evidence.

Thiel's sharpest version of this: the founders of Google, Amazon, and Apple in their early days weren't operating on hope. They had specific theories about why they would win that others couldn't see yet. Bezos mapped out why e-commerce would scale through selection and logistics before the market existed. That's not luck-denial — that's rigorous foresight presented as conviction.

When a founding team tells you "we'll figure it out," the question isn't whether they're optimistic. It's whether they can articulate the actual mechanism of their advantage.

If they can't, the luck framing isn't a personality trait. It's a capability gap.

Blaming luck is what you do when you've stopped thinking.

text:
Pi Durable unlocks much more than just the obvious 'able to recover from crashes' from the definition of durable.

This wasn't obvious to me until I dug into it.

The harness is just some well-defined state plus a little JavaScript to drive it forward. 

Put that state in a Durable Object and anyone in the world can wake it up, one message at a time, so multiplayer is basically free.

Perfect crash recovery means you can effectively hot-reload your changes by killing yourself after a change, so you get full malleable software. 

And because all the harness state is sitting there as well-specified data, you can inspect what an agent was doing without needing other services to reconstruct all the details.

Yes you get crash safety, but also multiplayer, malleability, and introspection.
author: cryptodavidw
quoted_text:
4 things worth building with @pidotdev's Pi Durable + @CloudflareDev Durable Objects:

#1 Durable agents for high-stakes workflows

Pi Durable can identify interrupted operations and avoid automatically replaying unsafe calls. Imagine an agent refunding a customer, then crashing before it gets confirmation. You don't want it refunding the customer twice.
Pi Durable checkpoints each step, recording the intent to execute a tool call and whether it completed. After a crash, it knows which operations were interrupted. Unsafe calls aren't blindly retried, so your app can check whether the payment went through before proceeding.

#2 Shared team agents

Pi Durable + Cloudflare Durable Objects are a great foundation for multiplayer agentic coding.
A Durable Object holds the persistent agent state. Multiple clients can connect to the same session, incoming messages are queued or used to steer the agent, and updates are streamed to everyone.
Imagine an agent picking up a GitHub issue and working on a PR while teammates watch or steer the same conversation from their phones, browsers, or terminals. @pidotdev's shared-chat tutorial demonstrates this.

#3 Agents that run anywhere

@badlogicgames built a Pi Durable Android app that runs the agent harness and stores its state locally on his phone, while model calls happen remotely.
Pi Durable separates agent state from execution, with pluggable storage and execution backends. The harness can run anywhere there's a compatible JavaScript runtime, and its tools can execute on another machine. Your durable agent doesn't need an always-running terminal or cloud server just to preserve the agent's state, the harness can run locally, on a phone, or in the cloud.

#4 Build new tools on top of agent state

This is the one we're most excited about.
Pi Durable persists structured tasks, checkpoints, and interrupted operations. That means you can inspect an agent's execution state without asking the model to reconstruct what happened.
We experimented with putting Pi Durable inside a Cloudflare Durable Object and visualizing its stored state without waking the agent.
Imagine using that data to build:
- Debugging dashboards showing exactly where an agent crashed.
- Reliability metrics showing which tool calls repeatedly fail or need recovery.
- Multiplayer dashboards showing pending tasks, who steered an agent, and when.
The interesting part is that durable execution state becomes a new primitive you can build tools on top of, not just something used for crash recovery.

text:
I'd like to share a little about what I've been working on at my new company @ultrametricai with my cofounder @tylerlastovich. We have been exploring how we could automate the startup itself, leaving founders with more time to focus on their exact mission.

Enter our first release of the Open Startup Repo: https://t.co/ecZZRU9iX4

A common foundation for transparent automation of the startup. 

After close to 20 years in silicon valley, backing hundreds of amazing founders & startups, being in the trenches of founding Heyzap (YC08), then solo founding @golden, going through 2 acquisitions and working behind the scenes with some of the iconic companies today, I'm witnessing the largest change to how we work I could have imagined - a truly monumental era of creative abundance. 

I believe the next generation of companies will largely run themselves: from operations, code, product upgrades, growth, vendor control & selection, process execution, special situations, strategy etc etc. That leaves founder time for 'the art' at the very niche core: the (currently) unautomatable, the special leaps humans tend to make, and north star setting.

We want founders to go super deep into the main problem they are trying to solve and not get held up doing anything else, from searching for domain availability with trademark checks to setting their company up, to running their processes on autopilot. 

So to help that broad foundational layer for starting and running a company, we have spent around a year exploring how to help founders focus on their mission across different verticals, geos, stages and initial starting conditions.

Our first few attempts at making something useful actually failed as the market and AI was moving so fast; it just got absorbed into the models or other product releases. We saw polsia happen, openclaw, then grokbot, muse, dots, etc era as the astras, fables, opuses, kimis and jevs rolled out. What seemed to have been missing along the way was a common repo to identify, unify, open and normalize all the lego bricks that startups have to interact with (vendors, processes, business logic, law, best practices, surface areas, art of the possible). 

As the number of software vendors blew up, the interfaces to drive them multiplied, the international startup founder blew up as silicon valley moved from a specific location to a state of mind and global movement. Unlimited pre seed funding in unlimited vertical sub markets and permutations has brought us to the age of infinity but we have yet to achieve being able to type into an agent a very simple sentence with very complex implications 'just setup my company and make $1m/m'. We have ended up with a hybrid mismash of computer use, API calls, plugins, shifting surface areas (API/MCP/CLI/plugins/chats/musish futures), and changing model absorption to vendor balance making it an exciting and unstable time. 

As our first step we started to rank all the vendors that startups interface to when going about their journey in terms of how agentically controllable they are via their APIs, MCPs, CLIs etc and computer use compatibility as we are largely switching from a UI driven world to the agentic control surfaces and onto full automation. We have 100 ranking areas you can check out with an overall open ranking here: https://t.co/V6XRMME0Ib

Then we looked at the processes that startups do and how the vendors rank for the sub steps or process as a whole and how this changes across geos. Open processes: https://t.co/iSQ90poYxq

Then we started to hack on an open repo for startups that would contain all the components we are going to need for a common foundation for founders across the globe even if our gov processes vary so much from Bengaluru to SF or Lisbon to Shenzhen.  The founder spirit is geo-invariant. 

We have looked at special founder/startup situations, the business logic that will make open modules for the startup that we can hack on together, ranked law firms, government services and interfaces, stacks that go well together. We have mapped the law and lore that maps to startups and the schemas that make up the data objects and documents. But also the open documents and the missing gaps. MUCH TO DO.

All the BS processes and fluff work that founders waste their time on needs to goto zero. I want to see more supersonic planes, cancer drugs, seemingly impossible missions done and increase the bang for buck founders have with their funding. 

This is a work in progress and we are keen for the community to come hack on the repo with us here: https://t.co/ecZZRU9iX4

Lets get into the structure of the general repo and the visualizations we made on https://t.co/XEYK9ipnfI site with example links: 

- Open rankings: https://t.co/V6XRMME0Ib

- Open rankings example (online payments): https://t.co/1kXHZCVfIi

- Open ranking example 2 (cap table): https://t.co/oqBjatGkfW 

- Open processes: https://t.co/iSQ90poYxq

- Open process example (Incorporate C-Corp) https://t.co/pxKUXpW03D

- Open situations that founders face: https://t.co/AFzAp5FRPk

- Open startup simulator (you can test our different initial starting conditions): https://t.co/QqPek01J7K 

- Open modules (e.g. cap table, payroll logic etc - we'd love help improving these) https://t.co/sfzIhgAJYS

- Open law (we are interested in how law changes the processes, situations and normalizing this over time) https://t.co/5yJnYbC0bk

- Open lore (we are interested in the historical lore of startups, the rules of thumb and heuristics that might guide your agent): https://t.co/gjliXoQwe1

- Open fields (we are interested in how the schema for the data connects to the open modules, business logic, open documents and artifacts of each process eg how is a EIN defined?) https://t.co/59rcEXhnCx

- Open documentation (eg SAFE notes and missing! docs) https://t.co/BbvBow2Olt

We have looked at YC companies as well in terms of which ones do well agentically: https://t.co/snnJ83r9ly

We are interested in stacks and how people are changing their work: https://t.co/wFHoew5V9I

We are interested in what is automatable and where the agentic ceiling is currently and how to push that up in all areas: https://t.co/WmTDjmNyV4

There is more for you to explore and a lot more coming in terms of how you will be able to navigate business in an optimal way in your chosen surface area; whether you are hanging in grokbot, dots, muse, claude, terminal, chat, or whatever is coming up in this exciting time. 

We have a lot of data to collect, clean up and help agents navigate the vast landscape emerging functionality the entire startup ecosystem has to offer. 

Come join us getting your vendor in, ranked or that access pattern you have wanted or getting the data more accurate in terms of which vendor is best for a process or steps. Or open a module of something that currently cost money that could be free. 

Also come play in our discord for founders and join the chaos (we can solve each others issues including fund raising tips from me personally): https://t.co/AmBtzFy0Bz 

It's time to lift all the boats in the harbor and I'm extremely excited as to what the community of hackers and painters will hack into the repo, what asks they will have and whether we can shift normalization of processes globally, gov agentic interfaces and have common repo for founders that grows over time. I expect a lot of experimentation along the way, bugs and upside...

I appreciate our backers having faith in us as well from @ycombinator with @garrytan to @immad doing a sizable check (congrats on $1bn rev homie) to @darbyw (congrats on Stripe buying @clerkyinc), @drewhouston form @Dropbox and also @pioneer_fund @tomerlondon cto @GustoHQ and hopefully this is 'boring' and complex enough for Charlie Songhurst :> @delingpole @Liquid2V @ivolo from @segment @ryanpowe @sonicaghi of @kong @DellyTamer+ other supporters (@michaelwfrank, Fundamental ventures and if I missed you sorry moving fast!). 

[And don't worry, all vendor rankings are open scoring methods so no favors are being done if someone backed us and is a vendor they have to compete with how agentic and automatable they are just like anyone else.]

PS: we have bugs and many quality upgrades to make but thought better to go out early and fix as a community. 

PPS: we have other stuff to launch we just thought this was a great place to start and have 200 PRs coming out pretty soon but I still want to know what is broken or doesnt make sense or inaccurate. 

Special thanks to current and past team members for getting us here and all the experiments we did you know who you are.

quoted_text:
Great question. My rough framing is that AI has given engineering a 100x boost, product 10x, and design 5x. That imbalance creates real strain: engineers can merge lots of individual changes while the overall UX gets less coherent, and designers burn out trying to keep up.

Design is a deep craft. It takes thought and a view of the whole experience. We haven’t given designers tooling that matches how quickly we can now produce code.

That’s why we’re building Inspect for designers. The ambition is to give them the 200x boost. Then engineers can be the ones trying to keep up :)

quoted_text:
I get more messages about this podcast every week than anything else I do.

We all want to look and sound smart in the investment committee or all hands meeting.

This is the only show in tech you have to listen to every week.

No egos, no politics, just tech.

AGENDA:

- Venture is Broken: Trillion or Bust
- Coreweave Sell-Off Creates Panic
- Town at $1B, Anduril at $90B: Are Revenue Multiples Out of Control?
- General Atlantic Eyes IPO
- Modal Raises $750M at $15.75B

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. Why Fundraising Is Back to Being a Numbers Game

Founders with top-decile numbers now have to meet 100 VCs, as in the old days. It will not be Benchmark, Index, Andreessen or Bessemer, but other growth investors will take the bet at a reasonable but still elevated valuation because it is the best deal they have seen that quarter.

2. Why the Big Funds Have to Have Billion-Dollar Positions to Make It Worthwhile?

A $5B plus fund needs $BN positions in everything. Without 51% ownership, which most founders will not accept, a $2B Listen Labs is not good enough, while 1% of Anthropic could still get there even with dilution.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @venkyganesan @DavidGeorge83

3. Why Are CoreWeave and Oracle B-Tier and What Does That Mean for Their Price Volatility?

With massive debt loads, CoreWeave and Oracle should be hypersensitive to any bump at Anthropic or OpenAI. CoreWeave exists because NVIDIA needs it for now, and Oracle rents out excess capacity because it cannot sell enough enterprise software.

4. Why the Best Markets for App Layer Companies Compete Directly With the Models

The fastest-growing AI apps, such as code generation, code review and legal, sit closest to the foundation models. That brings a moment of terror every six months, but it is also why companies like CodeRabbit are growing faster than ever.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @spdholakia @mmurph

5. Why Code Review Is the Single Most Important Category in Software

AI-generated code is pretty good but never production-ready, and reviewing it takes an order of magnitude more time than building it. Getting code into production matters more than generating it, so the best code review teams would be worth 10 bets.
Love to hear your thoughts on this @reidRMC @evrishria @Joshuabrowder

6. How Big Is the Market for Inference Truly?

The key inference providers add up to roughly $5B to $6B in run-rate revenue, under 5% of OpenAI and Anthropic combined. If tokens are roughly the same, Replit would rather pay Modal a 30% gross margin than give Claude Code 70%.

How do you analyse the TAM for inference today? What do people not see that they should see? @sarahcat21 @bernhardsson

7. Why Bending Spoons Is a Berkshire Hathaway of Software

Bending Spoons buys software to hold, the way Warren Buffett wanted to hold See's Candy forever. It made Vimeo and Evernote work with price increases, and with Miro and Airtable the quality of its assets is improving.

Love to hear your thoughts on this as an analogy @ncsh

Delighted to share a landmark preprint from our lab, using genome language models and AI agents for biological discovery and genome mining!

The stretches of DNA between protein-coding genes are often called the genome’s “dark matter,” but they are far from empty. They encode RNA molecules that sense metabolites, regulate genes, and control some of molecular biology's most important tools (such as programmable genome editors e.g. CRISPR/bridge)

Much of this biology is unexplored. One reason is that RNAs can retain similar structures and functions even as their DNA sequences change dramatically, making their relationships difficult to recognize with conventional computational tools

"This [cyber] capability broadly diffused, I think is something that will really empower threat actors in new ways. And I think that defenders need to use this time before that technology's broadly available to secure themselves."

text:
If you're wondering why the market keeps selling off, take a look at these two charts from Goldman Sachs.

The chart on the left shows how much hedge funds have been buying versus selling throughout 2026. When the black line moves higher, it means hedge funds are buying more than they're selling. When it moves lower, it means they're selling more than they're buying. Notice those three red boxes in April, August, and October? Each one highlights a period of extremely aggressive selling, with the latest reading approaching the lows we saw earlier this year. In other words, hedge funds have been dumping stocks at a pace similar to some of the worst selling periods we've experienced earlier this year.

Now look at the chart on the right. The blue line represents how much leverage hedge funds are using on their long positions, meaning stocks they're betting will go higher. The red line represents leverage on their short positions, meaning stocks they're betting will go lower. Notice how the red line has climbed dramatically. According to Goldman Sachs, short leverage has now reached the 99th percentile over the past five years. In simpler terms, hedge funds are carrying some of their largest bearish positions in years. And this helps explain why we're seeing so much pressure across AI, semiconductors, memory, and other high growth stocks. Not only are institutions selling their existing positions but they're also increasing their bets that stocks will continue falling. And as someone said unfortunately, we're just collateral damage in the battles between hedge funds.

What's even crazier is that some of these hedge funds have been getting absolutely hammered themselves and some funds are under tremendous pressure to recover their losses. And who knows, maybe aggressively shorting the market is their grand plan to finally come back to life before the year ends, haha. I'm obviously being a little sarcastic, but when large institutions start selling billions of dollars worth of stocks, retail investors get caught in the middle. Even companies reporting strong earnings and growing their businesses can get dragged down simply because large funds are reducing risk or betting against the broader market. But here's something important to understand.The same positioning that's putting pressure on stocks today could help fuel a pretty aggressive recovery. When investors short a stock, they eventually have to buy it back to close that position. If the market starts recovering, some hedge funds may rush to cover their shorts, creating additional buying pressure. That's why markets can sometimes recover just as aggressively as they sell off.

Of course, none of this means we've reached the bottom. Hedge funds can continue selling, and bearish positioning can remain elevated for quite some time. But I think it's important to recognize that a lot of this selling is being amplified by institutional positioning. It doesn't necessarily mean the long term fundamentals of every company being sold have suddenly deteriorated. My long term conviction in AI infrastructure hasn't changed, regardless of how ugly this gets.
author: MelvinInvests
quoted_text:
I know the market has been absolutely BRUTAL lately, especially for those of us invested heavily in AI, semiconductors, and other high growth stocks.

But I think it's important to put what's happening into perspective. Right now, investors are dealing with inflation, elevated bond yields, Iran war, Midterms, concerns about AI spending, and uncertainty around how some of these massive infrastructure investments will be financed. In 2020, the S&P 500 collapsed roughly 34% during COVID, only to recover its losses within months. In 2022, the Nasdaq fell more than 30% as inflation surged and the Federal Reserve aggressively raised interest rates. Many investors genuinely believed the technology trade was finished. Yet the market eventually recovered and went on to make new highs.

Now, I'm not saying every beaten down stock will recover, because plenty won't. And I'm certainly not saying we've reached the bottom. But history has repeatedly shown us that some of the greatest long term investment opportunities have appeared during periods when investor sentiment was at its worst. And that's exactly why I bought the dip.

I genuinely believe we're living through one of the greatest technological advancements in human history. AI is going to fundamentally change how we work, how businesses operate and how the global economy functions. But that doesn't mean the journey is going to be a straight line higher. There are going to be plenty of bumps along the way. There will be corrections, periods of uncertainty, companies that fail and moments when investors begin questioning whether the entire opportunity was overhyped.

We've seen this happen during nearly every major technological revolution, and I don't expect AI to be any different. My long term conviction in AI infrastructure hasn't changed. The demand for compute, memory, networking, and power isn't suddenly disappearing because stocks are selling off. And building wealth in the stock market is NOT easy, if it were, everyone would be rich. Everyone wants the massive returns, but very few people are willing to endure the volatility, uncertainty, and patience required to get there. Of course, conviction alone isn't enough. You still need to manage risk, understand what you own, and recognize when the fundamentals actually change. But I'm not going to let a few difficult weeks in the market distract me from an investment opportunity I believe will play out over the next decade.

Think in decades, not days.

text:
Why is Commander such a big deal for @zksync?

Because it gives us a way into every financial institution.

Until now, ZKsync was only relevant for players who had already decided they needed a new private chain. But while the pressure to modernize financial infrastructure keeps growing, replacing core banking systems with a blockchain comes at the end, not the beginning, of that journey. As leaders from NYSE, DTCC, and Cari Network noted on a panel with me yesterday, even the most innovative institutions are taking the “crawl, walk, run” approach to digital assets.

Commander is the new starting point.

It addresses one of the earliest challenges institutions face: the operational complexity of launching and running new products and services. How do we get started while preserving established processes, maintaining control over day-to-day operations, and meeting privacy and compliance requirements?

Commander is an easy decision for them—and the first decision must be easy. Getting any new software into a bank takes serious effort on both sides. Procurement has to approve the vendor, security and compliance teams have to approve the product, and engineers have to connect it to the bank’s existing users, applications and workflows.

Once Commander is integrated, offering more becomes much easier. We can help the institution upgrade to Prividium Ledger while keeping the integrations already built, and work toward connecting its business to the broader network.

Which brings me to an important point: connecting institutions to ZKsync will also change ZKsync itself.

Financial institutions work very differently from the crypto-native world. Building Prividium around their requirements has made it clear that ZKsync needs to evolve, including its economics and the role of the $ZK token. Commander is only the first step in that direction.

I’m extremely excited about this next chapter for ZKsync and can’t wait to share more soon.

text:
Big personal news today: I have decided to leave @a16z, move to SF, and start a company.

It's time to build :)

It has been almost 10 years since I joined the firm. I met @cdixon, @bhorowitz, and @pmarca  in 2017. At the time, I was an engineer at Google Brain working on robotics. I had a deep interest in open source. I knew nothing about investing. Chris meanwhile had already planted the @a16z flag at the frontier that was early crypto with investments in companies like Coinbase. But the crypto team at the firm consisted of only him, and he had the ambition to expand. His pitch to me was simple: "You should leave Google and come help me build the crypto vertical at the firm."

The work we've done together since then to build out our team and support our founders has been the most meaningful work of my life. I am grateful to have spent a decade working with everyone here, supporting our founders, learning from Chris, Ben, and Marc, and living the firm's culture. It is a culture that values integrity, life-long working relationships, and the belief that we humans have the power to build our own future.

Marc and Ben have built a16z into an incredible force for good in the world.

Before I joined the firm, I always thought that my inevitable path was to become a founder. The truth is that I wasn't ready for it then. Somehow, this year I've gotten the overwhelming feeling that this has changed.

As for what I want to build: It is early, but I care most about building infrastructure that enables open software ecosystems. I am starting with two core observations:

1. AI today is largely a single-player technology. Most uses involve one human talking with one agent in isolation from the rest of the world. That will soon change. Most uses of AI will soon be many-to-many: many humans and many agents working together. There will be at least one massive open network on top of which those uses will be built.

2. Software is now free. It can now be written just-in-time, on the spot for a single individual's hyper-targeted use case, and it can even be thrown out after a single use. This means that our entire software stack will have to change. In the limit, it will lead to a whole new kind of AI-mediated operating systems, which in turn will create an ecosystem of AI-native developers who build applications that actively rebuild themselves on the fly.

If you are working on related ideas, and especially if you are in the Bay Area, hit me up. Let's chat!

@bhorowitz , @pmarca, @cdixon, @eddylazzarin, @guywuolletjr, @jasonrosenthal , and our whole team — I want to thank you. Working with you has been the time of a lifetime. I am forever an a16z superfan and your ally.

Onward 🫡

text:
I'd like to share a little about what I've been working on at my new company @ultrametricai with my cofounder @tylerlastovich. We have been exploring how we could automate the startup itself, leaving founders with more time to focus on their exact mission.

Enter our first release of the Open Startup Repo: https://t.co/ecZZRU9iX4

A common foundation for transparent automation of the startup. 

After close to 20 years in silicon valley, backing hundreds of amazing founders & startups, being in the trenches of founding Heyzap (YC08), then solo founding @golden, going through 2 acquisitions and working behind the scenes with some of the iconic companies today, I'm witnessing the largest change to how we work I could have imagined - a truly monumental era of creative abundance. 

I believe the next generation of companies will largely run themselves: from operations, code, product upgrades, growth, vendor control & selection, process execution, special situations, strategy etc etc. That leaves founder time for 'the art' at the very niche core: the (currently) unautomatable, the special leaps humans tend to make, and north star setting.

We want founders to go super deep into the main problem they are trying to solve and not get held up doing anything else, from searching for domain availability with trademark checks to setting their company up, to running their processes on autopilot. 

So to help that broad foundational layer for starting and running a company, we have spent around a year exploring how to help founders focus on their mission across different verticals, geos, stages and initial starting conditions.

Our first few attempts at making something useful actually failed as the market and AI was moving so fast; it just got absorbed into the models or other product releases. We saw polsia happen, openclaw, then grokbot, muse, dots, etc era as the astras, fables, opuses, kimis and jevs rolled out. What seemed to have been missing along the way was a common repo to identify, unify, open and normalize all the lego bricks that startups have to interact with (vendors, processes, business logic, law, best practices, surface areas, art of the possible). 

As the number of software vendors blew up, the interfaces to drive them multiplied, the international startup founder blew up as silicon valley moved from a specific location to a state of mind and global movement. Unlimited pre seed funding in unlimited vertical sub markets and permutations has brought us to the age of infinity but we have yet to achieve being able to type into an agent a very simple sentence with very complex implications 'just setup my company and make $1m/m'. We have ended up with a hybrid mismash of computer use, API calls, plugins, shifting surface areas (API/MCP/CLI/plugins/chats/musish futures), and changing model absorption to vendor balance making it an exciting and unstable time. 

As our first step we started to rank all the vendors that startups interface to when going about their journey in terms of how agentically controllable they are via their APIs, MCPs, CLIs etc and computer use compatibility as we are largely switching from a UI driven world to the agentic control surfaces and onto full automation. We have 100 ranking areas you can check out with an overall open ranking here: https://t.co/V6XRMME0Ib

Then we looked at the processes that startups do and how the vendors rank for the sub steps or process as a whole and how this changes across geos. Open processes: https://t.co/iSQ90poYxq

Then we started to hack on an open repo for startups that would contain all the components we are going to need for a common foundation for founders across the globe even if our gov processes vary so much from Bengaluru to SF or Lisbon to Shenzhen.  The founder spirit is geo-invariant. 

We have looked at special founder/startup situations, the business logic that will make open modules for the startup that we can hack on together, ranked law firms, government services and interfaces, stacks that go well together. We have mapped the law and lore that maps to startups and the schemas that make up the data objects and documents. But also the open documents and the missing gaps. MUCH TO DO.

All the BS processes and fluff work that founders waste their time on needs to goto zero. I want to see more supersonic planes, cancer drugs, seemingly impossible missions done and increase the bang for buck founders have with their funding. 

This is a work in progress and we are keen for the community to come hack on the repo with us here: https://t.co/ecZZRU9iX4

Lets get into the structure of the general repo and the visualizations we made on https://t.co/XEYK9ipnfI site with example links: 

- Open rankings: https://t.co/V6XRMME0Ib

- Open rankings example (online payments): https://t.co/1kXHZCVfIi

- Open ranking example 2 (cap table): https://t.co/oqBjatGkfW 

- Open processes: https://t.co/iSQ90poYxq

- Open process example (Incorporate C-Corp) https://t.co/pxKUXpW03D

- Open situations that founders face: https://t.co/AFzAp5FRPk

- Open startup simulator (you can test our different initial starting conditions): https://t.co/QqPek01J7K 

- Open modules (e.g. cap table, payroll logic etc - we'd love help improving these) https://t.co/sfzIhgAJYS

- Open law (we are interested in how law changes the processes, situations and normalizing this over time) https://t.co/5yJnYbC0bk

- Open lore (we are interested in the historical lore of startups, the rules of thumb and heuristics that might guide your agent): https://t.co/gjliXoQwe1

- Open fields (we are interested in how the schema for the data connects to the open modules, business logic, open documents and artifacts of each process eg how is a EIN defined?) https://t.co/59rcEXhnCx

- Open documentation (eg SAFE notes and missing! docs) https://t.co/BbvBow2Olt

We have looked at YC companies as well in terms of which ones do well agentically: https://t.co/snnJ83r9ly

We are interested in stacks and how people are changing their work: https://t.co/wFHoew5V9I

We are interested in what is automatable and where the agentic ceiling is currently and how to push that up in all areas: https://t.co/WmTDjmNyV4

There is more for you to explore and a lot more coming in terms of how you will be able to navigate business in an optimal way in your chosen surface area; whether you are hanging in grokbot, dots, muse, claude, terminal, chat, or whatever is coming up in this exciting time. 

We have a lot of data to collect, clean up and help agents navigate the vast landscape emerging functionality the entire startup ecosystem has to offer.

Promised 12%. Delivered 15 cents.

We called this one in April. On a Bloomberg terminal, line by line.

Real CME box spreads were yielding 2.79% at the time. Below the 3 month T-bill. No leverage multiple turns a sub-Treasury carry into 12%. BOXX, the actual 9.4B box spread ETF, returned 4.22%.

The flat APY line was never a strategy. It was a smoothing clause in their own docs, authorizing them to retain and redistribute yield to stabilize the number.

We flagged the proxy contract where the owner can disable sells. Others are flagging that exact contract today. We flagged the insurance fund and the DAO multisig sharing one address. We flagged that no prime broker, no clearing firm and no venue were ever named. Only when pressed did they name @DeribitOfficial.

The structure was broken the day it launched. The price just caught up.

Here is the part that matters for the NEXT one. The signal that should warn depositors first was never going to be an attestation. 

@AccountableData and the proof of solvency model charge a premium to confirm a protocol is solvent today. That stamp only means what the protocol agrees to show. It cannot catch a protocol that lies on the inputs, and it cannot catch one that never signs up. msUSD could have passed an attestation on Monday and traded at 15 cents on Tuesday.

A market does the opposite, and it does it for "free". A HIP-4 CDS on fake stablecoins should be the answer. It costs depositors nothing and it pays the people doing the forensics instead of asking them to post threads for charity. It prices the doubt before the peg breaks.

Proof of solvency answers one question. Are they solvent today. A market answers the one that saves you. Who is short, and why.

@HyperliquidX is the only venue where @chameleon_jeff can hand us new toys to play with.

We called this early. In April. With receipts. Had that market existed, the April thread was the short ticket, and we would have eaten well. See it first, get paid first.

Fade D2 at your own risk.
