author: cdixon
quoted_text:
Big personal news today: I have decided to leave @a16z, move to SF, and start a company.

It's time to build :)

It has been almost 10 years since I joined the firm. I met @cdixon, @bhorowitz, and @pmarca  in 2017. At the time, I was an engineer at Google Brain working on robotics. I had a deep interest in open source. I knew nothing about investing. Chris meanwhile had already planted the @a16z flag at the frontier that was early crypto with investments in companies like Coinbase. But the crypto team at the firm consisted of only him, and he had the ambition to expand. His pitch to me was simple: "You should leave Google and come help me build the crypto vertical at the firm."

The work we've done together since then to build out our team and support our founders has been the most meaningful work of my life. I am grateful to have spent a decade working with everyone here, supporting our founders, learning from Chris, Ben, and Marc, and living the firm's culture. It is a culture that values integrity, life-long working relationships, and the belief that we humans have the power to build our own future.

Marc and Ben have built a16z into an incredible force for good in the world.

Before I joined the firm, I always thought that my inevitable path was to become a founder. The truth is that I wasn't ready for it then. Somehow, this year I've gotten the overwhelming feeling that this has changed.

As for what I want to build: It is early, but I care most about building infrastructure that enables open software ecosystems. I am starting with two core observations:

1. AI today is largely a single-player technology. Most uses involve one human talking with one agent in isolation from the rest of the world. That will soon change. Most uses of AI will soon be many-to-many: many humans and many agents working together. There will be at least one massive open network on top of which those uses will be built.

2. Software is now free. It can now be written just-in-time, on the spot for a single individual's hyper-targeted use case, and it can even be thrown out after a single use. This means that our entire software stack will have to change. In the limit, it will lead to a whole new kind of AI-mediated operating systems, which in turn will create an ecosystem of AI-native developers who build applications that actively rebuild themselves on the fly.

If you are working on related ideas, and especially if you are in the Bay Area, hit me up. Let's chat!

@bhorowitz , @pmarca, @cdixon, @eddylazzarin, @guywuolletjr, @jasonrosenthal , and our whole team — I want to thank you. Working with you has been the time of a lifetime. I am forever an a16z superfan and your ally.

Onward 🫡

text:
Speaking of the ruthlessness of the sage
I think that by Q1 2027 we'll see the second wave of Chinese AI startup die-off (since they're Chinese, they might keep resisting as they get Baichuanized, but…); more decent ones will go this time, ones I root for, even. Capex needs are growing exponentially and nation-scale compute scarcity bites in. PMF for "slightly different… but slightly slower and more expensive" is disappearing as models become more general. Xi is getting tougher on involution and wants international competitiveness. Industrial and financial capital is betting on winners. Major IT companies with independent revenue (Alibaba, JD, Tencent) will keep their internal labs afloat, depressing the state's willingness to support startups for anti-monopoly reasons; even then, something like Meituan LongCat might be deemed too costly as Meituan bleeds money from involutionary warfare on its main turf. Finally, DeepSeek's policy of MIT'ing its flagships and Apache'ing its codebases will discourage demand for an internal full-stack fallback at other companies with AGI ambitions (a big reason they even do this is lack of faith in third party providers). 

Cynically, I expect that by the end of 2027, there may be as little as two major startups still growing, as Wenfeng deems "enough"; and the #1, I believe, will be DeepSeek, scaling towards gigawatts of capacity and serious, no-caveats competition with Western frontier on AGI and ASI. The most probable #2 is Zhipu, due to good product velocity, financials and, tbh, state ties. I'd rather it be MoonshotAI, which is the second most probable; I believe GLM 5.5 and K3.1 will strongly indicate who is who. It would be nice if the losers of the race gracefully "transform", as Wenfeng puts it, by joining the winners. I know that some of their staff are very much in awe of DeepSeek, which is understaffed, and perhaps a dignified consortium deal may be had. 
But I am already bittersweet for the era of Chinese Cambrian explosion of AI that I see coming to an end.
author: teortaxesTex
quoted_text:
> Am I being a schizo to think that this could be a Chinese government ploy
Yes. Meds, now.
But there does exist a cynical read of DeepSeek's moves. Because V4.1 line is very strong, cheap and has zero strings attached, they destroy the case for hosting anything like K3 ($3/$15) by Western partners, so starve their domestic rivals of revenue. Moreover DeepInfer is useless for anything not shaped just like V4.1 (so, it'll be DeepSeek's models and finetunes). They also make compute ownership more valuable by having created mutual knowledge about its profitability even at "shockingly low" prices. Frontier labs and hyperscalers already understood how valuable compute is, so they can't go harder on securing allocation, but neoclouds will now ask premium.
Flash, in effect, requires a full NVL72 GB200 rack to hit these margins. V4.1 Pro and Ultra (hypothetical for now) will make the issue even more pronounced. When you need a whole cluster to run an 8T DeepSeek model efficiently, *but* it prints you like $40/GPU/hour, this removes a lot of colocated GPUs from easy access. And DeepSeek had little hope to tap into this pool, so they lose nothing, gain mindshare and keep building their new power base around Ascend, which will also become increasingly Whale-shaped due to co-design. In the end, DeepSeek will have defined the entire upstream and downstream AI ecosystem in China, harvesting a tiny slice of the profit in the process.

Heavenly Demon Sage 梁圣, ruthless in his benevolence…

等了一天本想等8楼的，结果到1楼就拉回去了，现在一级市场的问题是，同一个叙事在 Sol 火了，RH、BSC、Base ，ETH主网，很快就各出一个版本。资金都是各买各的，最后又变成几条链互相抽血，谁也做不起来，

这种现象在今年4月那波 $ASTEROID 上尤其明显。同一个 IP，在不同链各自拉盘、各自争龙头。表面上整个市场都在讨论它，实际资金却被拆成了几份，最后从炒一个共同的叙事，变成各条链之间的 PvP

如果一个发射台，能让同一个币同时在几条主流链上发行，它能改变什么？这是我觉得 $PANGEA 有意思的地方。

@LaunchOnPangea 想尝试改变这件事

开发者可以把同一个币，同时部署到 Sol、RH、BSC、Base 和 Eth。五条链上的版本通过 @LayerZero_Core  互通，价格靠跨链套利逐步拉近

这样其他链的用户想参与，就不用等别人再发一个盘，也不必先把钱转去其他链，留在自己熟悉的链上就能买到正版

sol链是公认的流动性充沛，一些钱包，也基本只在 Sol 上交易。一个项目哪怕再有意思，只要没在 Sol 发，他们可能根本就不会参与，其他链也一样，每条链都有一批固定的资金和交易习惯，不会因为你出了一个新项目，就专门跨链过来买

所以单链发行，天然就把一部分潜在买盘挡在了外面
如果同一个币能同时覆盖几条主流链，Sol 的钱包在 Sol 买，BSC 的钱包在 BSC 买，RH 的资金也能直接参与。项目就有机会接触到过去单链发行触达不到的买家

you're underestimating the state space of all possible ways to compromise a company. no amount of astra or mythos tokens is going to fundamentally change the asymmetry anytime soon. it is also very clear that every model is opening up new vulnerability space with no saturation anytime soon. with all the insane vibe coding and expanding agentic attack surfaces, it's only going to get worse.

even if we somehow saturate vulnerability discovery and patching, attackers will move to social engineering, with insanely capable models persuading people to click things, grant access, or make mistakes.

i don't see a future where cybersecurity becomes defense-dominant without just cutting down software, and continuous agents monitoring and stopping attacks across individuals and organizations, and even then, it might require something like 30% of all inference compute devoted to defense

text:
解读下今早 Hyperliquid 的新公告，开头又是「Based on user feedback」。最近的更新，基本都在精修细节。

先说背景：Hyperliquid 对每个地址的「下单/撤单次数」是有限速的，历史累计成交量越大，能发的订单和撤单次数就越多。

之前 HIP-3 永续的成交量贡献，只按「协议那份」手续费折算成交量。其实还是不够人性化，毕竟不代表实际真实的成交量。

因此下次升级后，就改成按「全部」手续费 (部署者那份 + 协议那份) 来计算。

大多数 HIP-3 市场是 50/50 分成，所以升级后同一笔成交对限速额度的贡献会变成 2 倍。

交易所应该靠技术、产品和服务赚钱，而不是靠客户的资金赚钱。

这是我一直坚持的原则，也是 OKX 十几年发展过程中始终坚守的底线。

金融行业最重要的资产是信任。无论市场如何变化、公司规模如何增长，保护客户资产安全，都不应该成为可以妥协的商业选择。

客户的资产属于客户，不属于交易所。

我们应该把精力放在打造更好的产品、更深的流动性、更高效的技术基础设施和更优质的服务上。

靠创造价值赚钱，而不是靠承担客户无法知情的风险赚钱。

text:
中国制造业越来越强，为什么不少中产却越过越紧？李录这场对谈，把这笔账摊开了。

这位1997年创立喜马拉雅资本、早年投资比亚迪的投资人，在哥伦比亚商学院举办的对谈里，聊了家庭财富、芯片和中国股票。最值得听的，是他把几件看似矛盾的事放到了一起：工厂在升级，有人却不敢花钱；市场没什么起色，有些公司却越来越能打。

有几段值得单独拎出来。

1. 房子跌了，房贷可不会陪着一起跌。

李录估计，2021年，一个典型中国中产家庭约70%的净资产都压在住房上，房产还背着大约50%的按揭杠杆。房价往下走，损失落到家庭自己的那部分钱上，会更疼。

举个简单的假设：400万元的房子，欠银行200万元，你自己的那份是200万元。如果房子跌到300万元，贷款还是200万元，自己那份就只剩100万元。房价跌了四分之一，自己的净值少了一半。

明白这笔账，再看李录说的“少消费、多储蓄、尽量还债”，就不难理解了。家里最大的资产缩水，欠的钱还在，换谁也得先捂紧钱包。光催人花钱，实在有点站着说话不腰疼。

2. 芯片企业最需要的，有时候就是有人下单。

李录谈到一个反直觉的变化：在他看来，美国的技术限制，反而给中国半导体企业带来了订单。

他的解释很朴素：有收入，才有利润；有了钱，才能继续研发、改进产品，再去争取更多订单。

这个说法比空喊“突破”有意思。技术当然重要，可对一家企业来说，客户肯不肯买、能不能靠订单继续做下去，同样是硬问题。没收入的时候谈研发，和手里有订单再谈研发，底气完全不一样。

3. 以前被推着往前走的行业，也可能变成承担代价的那一个。

李录拿房地产举例：城市化的时候，要盖房、建城，开发建设是被推动的方向；到了新的转型阶段，房地产调整却成了代价的一部分。

所以他提醒投资人和企业家，得弄清楚自己究竟是被推动的目标，还是需要付出代价的一方。

这话挺重的。一个行业以前风光，并不代表以后还会一直被托着走。只拿过去的成功经验往后套，可能连周围的方向变了都没察觉。

4. 市场冷清，不等于里面的公司都没长进。

李录认为，中国金融市场约十年没什么明显进展，但其中一些企业已经有了全球竞争力，交易价格却很低。这是他看到的投资机会。

我喜欢他把这两件事分开讲：市场给多少钱，和企业到底做成了什么，不能混成一回事。聊中国资产，聊到最后如果只剩一句“看好”或“不看好”，那些真正值得研究的公司，反而全被一句话盖过去了。

text:
看到一姐在聊币安广场获奖kol的投票问题，我也想借机聊聊公平的事情。

首先请大家认可一个事实，那就是面对有限的位置和“无限”的竞争者，就没有办法做到百分百的公平。无论是币安广场的kol投票，亦或者Axis的空投，让所有人都满意，做到0差评，是不可能的。

其次，币安广场经过数年发展，已经从聚焦数字货币交易的垂直平台，逐步转型为泛流量平台。往泛流量方向演进，也是绝大多数内容平台发展的共同趋势。比如知乎、小红书：知乎从小众互联网社区发展成综合长文信息社区；小红书则从主打女性向的垂直社区，成长为全民信息社区。所以正如一姐所说，有实盘类kol，但广场也会包容跳舞的kol。

我一直觉得kaito的最大竞争者并不是同类数据和工具公司，而是币安广场，因为广场依托币安，自带海量的加密用户以及这些人的精准交易标签。对项目方来说，在广场做投放，应该比在推特做投放要精准太多了。

可惜目前广场的商业化潜力没有被完全开发出来，当然也许币安也并不需要/想要去特别商业化这块业务。

当然了，作为一个每天在思考增长和营销的cmo，我从去年就开始思考怎么在广场投流的事情。其实，对所有项目来说如果能最大化的利用广场做好营销，应该是事倍功半的。而且广场真的还很早期。机会太多了。

text: Compute is to the future what Oil has been to the industrial age. We commend the @CFTC for their innovative thinking on this topic and are excited to be able to help contribute through these comment letters.
author: HadickM
quoted_text:
This week, @dragonfly filed a comment letter with the CFTC on compute derivatives. Compute is a swiftly growing expense for tech companies, yet the market for hedging its cost is still nascent.

The challenge starts with defining what’s being traded. Not all GPU-hours are equal: hardware, performance, and availability can materially affect their value. Liquid derivatives markets need comparable units of compute and reliable price benchmarks.

@HadickM @bryanmedelman @peteryshin and I advocate for technology-neutral standards, equal treatment of credible pricing sources, and support for perpetual futures to hedge ongoing compute costs. 

We applaud @CFTC for taking on these important questions and laying the groundwork for a liquid, competitive compute derivatives market.

author: 0xcyp
quoted_text:
Once again the Canadian government FAILS to understand the problem

I would know, I founded and ran a tech company for a decade and raised MILLIONS from investors

And it was HORRIBLE doing business here

Let me explain

This isn't a "money issue"

This is a regulatory, economic and taxation issue combined with a deep cultural problem

Back in 2015 I founded a tech company, using my own money from working in the Alberta oil field

We developed our MVP in Montreal and launched our proof of concept right here in the West Island

Our first ever investors were our own first clients. We raised $150,000 from them

But things got harder when it came time to raise our seed round

I met with EVERY SINGLE VC in Montreal.

All told us NO

Why? 

Too risky

lol... its the very definition of Venture Capital

They wanted a pitch deck, projections on 5 years, cashflow, business plan, go-to-market strategy, communication strategy, marketing strategy, Tech reviews, C.V. of founding team, financial disclosure etc

We spent more time preparing documents for them than we did scaling our business

Worse of all, they all wanted something different and would give contradicting requirements

I remember this interaction at the Espace CDPQ, the headquarter for all Venture firms in Montreal 

ie: 

Investor: How much do you need
Me: $1 Million
Investor: So if you only raise $750k what happens?
Me: Well we'll adapt XYZ
Investor: So then never EVER tell me a fix number. Give me a range. $750K-$1.5M or else you look foolish

I went home, reworked the pitch deck

The very next day:

New investor: How much you need
Me: $750K-$1.5M
New investor: What... you don't even know your number???
Me: well... yes but what if we raise less or more
New Investor: No, you look foolish

We said screw it. Approached American Investor

Our first was a VC firm out of Houston, Texas

Took less than 1 month from initial pitch, to closing.

In USD. For more money than what Canadians wanted to offer. 

Best of all, they understood the fluid nature of a startup. No onerous and rigid plan. No overburdened documentation. Every second wasted on non-operating activities was sucking productive time away from scaling. 

But Elliot... what about BDC and other AMAZING institutions in Canada

We did business with the BDC. a $250,000 loan. Which I had to personally guarantee. 

Which 25 year old has assets and the balls to guarantee that amount? Very few. It's prohibitive. And reduces capital available to our homegrown companies

And this was AFTER MONTHS of explaining to them what we were doing. It was clear the BDC was setup to support traditional brick-and-mortar companies only.

Think Manufacturers or Commerces. But a tech startup? They could NOT wrap their heads around it.

Canadian banks? Forget it. Outright. Too risky

Then I watch fellow startups do the same. And move to the US.

Why wouldn't they?

In Quebec, I had to pay an extra 15% on top of my payroll as taxes. QPIP, QPP, FSS, CNESST... all to satisfy the government non-stop appetite. 

Consequences: Well for a startup where every dollar counts, this means lower salaries thus harder to attract top talent (vs American competitors)

or

I simply hired less staff... thus slowly growth for both my company and the country's economy.

But wait it gets worse.

Revenue Quebec and CRA both required a plethora of compliance documents filled monthly or quarterly. GST and QST tax fillings, CNESST Salary equity (yes lol) documents, Source deduction documents, RL-1 fillings, Income tax (both QC and CAN), Workplace sexual harassment policy, OQLF policy, CNESST training and certification... the list goes on

At least 1 day a month was spent by me and some of my executives preparing and fulfilling these documents. This means we were't scaling our business and instead working for FREE for the government. 

Then there is the tax burden.

Why would top talent want to come here and get taxed at up to 52% marginal rate? 

While a Miami startup offers higher salary and the State taxes you 0%

Finally investor behaviour

In Canada... safe. steady return. Great for a Series C. Great for an established companies. No desire for risk. No understanding of the ecosystem.

HORRIBLE FOR VENTURE

Meanwhile the U.S. , they understand the ecosystem. 90% of their investment will go down to 0. But the few that survive will go on to earn them BILLIONS and change the world.

So this new announcement of $1.75Billion won't change the underlying issue that makes us uncompetitive.

At best, it will go to startups who will flee to the US the very second the money hits

At worse, it will just be another slush fund given to friends of the government 

and I fear its the latter as usual

I’m excited to finally announce the newest edition my Stanford course 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗦𝗼𝗳𝘁𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿. It has been 9 months in the making.

Last November, with the release of Claude Opus 4.5, coding agents experienced a step function improvement in capability. We all felt it. The LLMs were more powerful, could reason for longer, solve harder tasks.

This year’s iteration of my course reflects the 2026 metamorphosis of software engineering.

My core belief is simple: AI-native developers of the LLM era are going to become the most important members of any software organization. I have designed my course to train this next generation of engineers.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱

First, 85% of my Fall 2025 class material is being thrown out. The Fall 2026 syllabus reflects the core capabilities AI-native engineers must have: agent skills, advanced context engineering, MCP portals, agent-ready codebase principles, agentic code review, security, parallelizing background agents, software factories, and more.

Second, I am going to teach my students how to have software taste. Every student will be required to ship pull requests to production-grade, real-world codebases. The course is collaborating with the top open-source AI repos who will offer support and mentorship to students on how to meaningfully contribute to their projects.

This has never been done before in any university course so I am incredibly grateful to our OSS Partners: @browserbase, @HeyGen, @CopilotKit, @semgrep, @OpenHandsDev, @milvusio, @marimo_io, Pi, @crewAIInc, @warpdotdev, @vercel, @cmux, @arizeai, @UnslothAI, and @anyscalecompute.

I’m fortunate to again have AI software engineering leaders and founders as guest speakers to share their learnings from building top coding agent products. Thank you to @leerob from @cursor_ai, @bcherny of @claudeai code, @EnoReyes of @FactoryAI, @silasalberti of @cognition, @0xine of @semgrep, Rajesh Bhatia of @Cloudflare , @amasad of @Replit, and @eladgil.

All resources will be available online. All classes will be available to the public.

9/22 on Stanford campus. See you in class.

从人性的角度看，这些东西有多少人嘴上嫌俗，心里却想拥有？

Pump 找他，我理解就是看中了这一点。他甚至不用懂币圈，只要把自己的日常摆出来，就已经替 Pump 把话说完了：来我战壕玩，下一个过上这种生活的，可能就是你

这套营销厉害的地方，就是把别人的奢靡日常，变成战壕里赌徒下一次下注的理由，毕竟营销先要做的，就是让人先动心

近年来，大语言模型与 AI Agent 的快速发展，正在推动人工智能自主执行时代的到来。当 AI Agent 开始能够独立完成信息检索、服务调用、商业决策乃至商品购买时，支付便不再只是人与商户之间的交易行为，而是逐渐成为机器与机器之间价值交换的重要基础设施。全球支付体系因此也迎来了新的变革。

然而，支付智能化和支付全球化已经成为了一种必然的发展趋势。为了应对这些挑战，中国支付产业一方面持续优化传统支付基础设施，另一方面加速推进新型金融基础设施的研究与试点，试图加快人民币国际化进程，并同步缓解跨境支付效率与成本约束问题，以适应 AI 时代的到来。

在基础设施层面，中国以 CIPS（人民币跨境支付系统）作为核心跨境清算通道，并进一步探索跨境央行数字货币平台 mBridge、数字人民币（e-CNY）的跨境应用，以及港元稳定币等新型结算工具的实践路径。在国内市场，支付宝、微信支付等机构已围绕智能体支付与开放能力体系开展探索与试点。与此同时，中国银联、蚂蚁集团以及各类跨境第三方支付服务商，也正在围绕 AI 原生支付体系的基础设施形态与接入方式展开系统性探索。

text: We've had the pleasure of working alongside Stephanie for over 11 years. She's an incredibly sharp thinker on what technologies will power the future before it's obvious to others. We're excited to support her and her new fund, investing in founders making bold, non-consensus bets.
author: Alfred_Lin
quoted_text:
I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus.

The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future.

I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf.

Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent.

Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade.

Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine.

Why now

We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten.

But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible.

This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition.

More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest.

I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building.

Believing before consensus

My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine.

I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today.

I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?”

Then we work backward together to make it happen.

In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI, before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue.

In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models.

In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point.

The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale.

@linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike.

@tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues.

@Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies.

Making the ambition possible

Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight.

These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work.

This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger.

Thank you

To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together.

Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me.

To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap.

Let’s get to work!

text:
The most valuable lesson from DATA’s evolution is that finding the right problem matters more than pursuing the broadest vision.

Story Protocol initially set out to make intellectual property programmable across industries. But traditional IP markets are deeply entrenched, and permissionless licensing alone couldn’t solve the complexities of commercial adoption. The breakthrough came through @psdnai , where a fundamental problem emerged: AI data buyers often cannot reliably verify data provenance, exclusivity, consent, or licensing rights.

That insight reshaped the strategy. @datafdn is now focused on Trace, an on-chain registry designed to make AI training data auditable, with over 250M contributions and approximately 3–4M receipts processed daily.

The decision to join @SuiNetwork after its $30M strategic investment reflects the same product-first philosophy. Instead of spending resources maintaining an independent L1, DATA can leverage Sui’s execution infrastructure, @WalrusProtocol for decentralized data storage, and Seal for encryption and programmable access control.

Crucially, Trace’s ambition is bigger than becoming another data marketplace. It is to establish a trusted provenance and auditability layer for an AI economy increasingly constrained by copyright, consent, and data-quality concerns.

As a long-term community member, I see this as a meaningful evolution: learning from the original vision, narrowing the focus, and doubling down on a concrete problem.

The next milestone is proving that verification creates measurable economic value.

The future belongs to infrastructure that makes AI data not just abundant, but trustworthy, traceable, and commercially usable.

text:
花 $25.88 先建一套 Memory，结果还不如 $17.84 直接把完整历史交给模型。

《MemoryTax》这篇文章把 Agent Memory 的这笔账摊得很直白。

作者比较了 Full Context、BM25、Mem0、Zep，以及 Pi、Codex、Claude Code 等不同记忆方案。

一个很明显的趋势是：

模型比较弱时，结构化 Memory 确实有帮助。GPT-4o-mini 上，Mem0 准确率 78%，高于 Full Context 的 74%。

但模型变强后，优势开始消失。

GPT-6 Luna 上，Full Context 达到 92%，Mem0 只有 80%；Claude Opus 5.5 上，两者都是 95%。

更关键的是「Memory ceiling」。

如果 Memory 在写入阶段就漏掉了信息，后面换再强的模型来读，也很难把这部分补回来。

反而是保留原始历史、让强模型自己搜索的 Pi，在 Opus 5.5 上做到 99%，成本只有 $6.95。

当然，这组实验规模还很小，只有 LoCoMo 的 1 段对话、152 个问题，不足以下结论说结构化 Memory 已经没用了。

我是觉得 Memory 方案不能脱离模型单独选。给弱模型用的「提前总结」，到了强模型手里可能就成了天花板。

做 Agent Memory、或者正在选 Mem0、Zep 这类方案的可以先参考论文的做法。我会先做一个很便宜的对照：同一批问题，用现有 Memory 和「原始历史 + 让模型自己搜」各跑一遍，再换上最强的模型重跑。如果强模型配 Memory 反而更差，问题多半出在写入阶段丢了信息。

• Tokenized stocks (bStocks) are priced straight off the real share price, so splits and dividends don't break the pool.

Numbers

text:
Ethereum Postpones Glamsterdam Upgrade on Hoodi Testnet Over EIP-8037 Compatibility Concerns

According to the Ethereum Foundation, Ethereum core developers have postponed the Glamsterdam upgrade on the Hoodi testnet, originally scheduled for October 26, to further investigate compatibility concerns between EIP-8037's gas accounting changes and existing mainnet smart contracts. The planned increase of Hoodi's gas limit to 200 million has also been canceled. Node operators must update their clients to prevent activation of the fork as originally scheduled. New dates for the Hoodi upgrade and mainnet activation have not yet been determined.

The hacks over the past few days (PHP, Railway, eMudhra, LiteLLM etc) show how fragile the existing Internet has become. AI agents are challenging the Internet's structure in 3 distinct ways:

1/ On the offense side, agents are a weapon - AI finds and exploits bugs on a scale not seen before, and the cost of attack asymptotes to 0. Bugs that used to take human experts weeks and months are easily found, adapted, and exploited by AI agents. Decades of legacy code that ran on "security by obscurity" no longer holds against agents.

2/ On the defense side, agents are a target - AI generated code is often bug-prone. AI agents themselves, as machines of unconstrained output are liable to prompt injections and other types of attacks that can leak keys, PII, and other pieces of information.

3/ On the identity side, agents are dominating Internet activity - this year, machine traffic has already passed human traffic, and may continue to grow 1000x over the next few years. Content and webpages used to human  requests and behavior are breaking with agents, and it is increasingly difficult to tell human content from AI content.

All this means we will need to see a ground-up redesigning of the Internet, one with more cryptographic verifiability, identity protocols, rule-enforcement, and other security primitives that eliminate bug categories rather than simply patch them - an "Antifragile Internet" that gets stronger and more secure as more agents participate in it.

This is an emerging thesis area for us at @usv, if you're building in the space please reach out!

More thoughts soon.

If Muse, Dot, Grok, and other AI products are trying to become the wallet for commerce, what makes you think they’ll stop at commerce? Eventually, these products will move into retail trading.

I think retail trading will bifurcate into two categories, agentic trading and immersive trading.

Agentic trading is obvious. Major AI front ends will be able to connect directly to your brokerage accounts or onchain vaults, trade on your behalf, and capture a fee along the way.

But imo, the bigger opportunities for startups are in immersive trading and pro agentic trading.

On the immersive side, I believe trading will become gamified, social, and competitive, similar to competitive sports with leagues and communities built around trading.

On the pro side, agentic trading platforms will give advanced traders the tools to build, customize, and deploy their own trading harnesses vs using general purpose AI agents like Muse.

New on our Frontier Red Team blog: using Claude to formally verify software at large scale.

Formal verification can prove that code is free of certain bugs, but historically it has only been feasible for small codebases (or required a lot of expert time).

With AI models, however, this is beginning to change. In collaboration with @theoremlabs, we used Claude to prove security properties in over one hundred real-world open-source libraries over the span of a few weeks.

Read our research in full here: https://t.co/zUyx8CjBEk
